Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.genericPoint_mem_support: The generic point belongs to its component, and the component is contained in the support. Hence the generic point belongs to the support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.genericPoint_specializes: Each point of the component belongs to the closure of its generic point. Membership in that closure means that the generic point specializes to the given point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed: The closure of a component is irreducible and contained in the closed support. Maximality implies that the closure equals the component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPreirreducible_of_isPreirreducible_ima: Write each open of the subspace meeting the subset as the inverse image of an ambient open. Their ambient opens both meet the image of the subset. Preirreducibility of the image gives a point of the image in their intersection. Its preimage lies in the subset and in both original opens.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_vanishingIdeal_of_subset_support: On an affine open, take a section of the ideal and a prime whose point lies in the closed subset. That point lies in the support, so the prime contains the entire section ideal. The chosen section therefore belongs to every prime over the closed subset, which means it belongs to the vanishing ideal there. This holds on all affine opens.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_iff_ideal_le_primeIdealOf: A point lies in the support exactly when its stalk ideal is contained in the maximal ideal. The stalk ideal is obtained by extending the section ideal to the localization at the point’s prime. The maximal ideal contracts to that prime. The extension–contraction correspondence for containment gives the equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_genericPoint_ne_top: In a locally Noetherian scheme, an ideal that is nonzero on every component has finite order at every point. Apply this fact at the generic point of the stated component of the support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_ne_top_of_nonzeroOnComponents: The hypothesis ensures every stalk ideal is nonzero. In a Noetherian local ring, the intersection of all powers of the maximal ideal is zero by the Krull intersection theorem. Infinite order would place the stalk ideal in that intersection, so the order is finite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_ne_bot_of_nonzeroOnComponents: Suppose the stalk ideal is zero at the given point. Choose an irreducible component of the scheme through that point. On an affine neighborhood, the germ at the generic point of that component factors through the germ at the given point, since the generic point specializes to it. Extending the zero stalk ideal along this map gives zero at the generic point. The local ring is nonzero, so the zero ideal is proper and the generic point lies in the support. Closedness of the support puts the whole component in it, contrary to the hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_vanishingIdeal_eq: Choose the affine coordinate neighborhood on which the ideal of the support and the vanishing ideal of this component agree on stalks. Apply the resulting equality at the given point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.vanishingIdeal_ideal_eq_of_restrictIdeal: The section ideal of the coordinate subscheme is radical, so it is the intersection of the primes containing it. Each such prime corresponds to a point of the support in the affine open, and by hypothesis that point belongs to the closed subset. The vanishing ideal lies in all these primes, so it lies in their intersection. Conversely, the closed subset lies in the support, so the original ideal is contained in the vanishing ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.vanishingIdeal_ideal_le_primeIdealOf: On the affine open, the vanishing ideal consists of the sections that belong to every prime representing a point of the closed set. The given point belongs to that closed set, so its prime contains the vanishing ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_ofDigits_le_of_sum_eq: The tuples of degree r form a finite set because each coordinate lies between zero and r. Its subset satisfying P is nonempty. Choose a member of that subset minimizing the weighted digit value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_eq_of_le_of_not_le: The two containments for successive powers translate to order at least n and order strictly below n + 1. An extended natural number between those bounds is exactly n.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_mul: If either ideal is zero the product is zero and both sides are infinite. Otherwise let r and s be the finite orders of I and J. Their product lies in the (r + s)-th power of the maximal ideal. Choose an element of each ideal failing to lie in the power one higher than its order. The nonvanishing result for the product of their leading terms gives an element of IJ outside the (r + s + 1)-st power. The two power bounds imply that the order is exactly r + s.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealOrder_pow: At exponent zero the power is the unit ideal, with order zero. At a successor the next power is the previous power multiplied by I. Apply the order formula for a product and use induction to obtain the stated multiple.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_pow_succ_iff_multiIndex: If f lies in the (r + 1)-st power, every derivative of order r lies in the maximal ideal by the power bound for mixed derivatives. For the converse, the finite index set contains all multi-indices of degree r. The vanishing criterion proved by induction and the Euler argument then puts f in the next power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maximalIdeal_pow_succ_of_multiIndexD: Induct on r. At zero the only required derivative is the identity, so f already lies in the maximal ideal. For a step from r to r + 1, each first derivative of f lies in the r-th power. Its derivatives of total order r are derivatives of f of total order r + 1 because the coordinate derivations commute. They therefore vanish in the residue field. By induction every first derivative of f lies in the (r + 1)-st power. Apply the Euler congruence in degree r + 1 and use the invertibility of r + 1 to conclude that f lies in the (r + 2)-nd power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_multiIndicesOfDegree: The definition keeps precisely the bounded multi-indices of total degree r. If the sum is r, then every entry is at most r because the entries are nonnegative. Thus the bound in the definition follows from the degree condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_notMem_maximalIdeal_pow_add_succ: By the mixed-derivative criterion choose degree r and degree s derivatives of f and g with nonzero residues. Among such indices for each factor choose indices β₀ and γ₀ of minimal weighted digit value in base r + s + 1. Let α be their coordinatewise sum. The residue of the α-th derivative of the product is given by the mixed Leibniz sum over splits α = β + γ of degrees r and s, since all other splits vanish modulo the maximal ideal. For the selected split both derivatives and the positive binomial coefficient are units, so its term survives. For any other split whose first derivative survives, the value of β is strictly larger than that of β₀ by minimality and uniqueness of the base representation. Additivity of the weighted values then makes the value of γ strictly smaller than that of γ₀, so its derivative vanishes. Thus the selected term is the only nonzero residue and the α-th derivative does not vanish. The power bound on derivatives excludes membership of the product in the (r + s + 1)-st power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_add: The weighted sum defining the digit value distributes over coordinatewise addition. Splitting the finite sum gives the sum of the two digit values.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_fin_succ: The first digit has weight one. Each tail weight is the corresponding weight for the shortened tuple multiplied by N. Separate the first term and factor out N from the tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofDigits_injective_of_lt: Induct on the number of digits. For a nonempty tuple compare the two values modulo N. This identifies the first digits because they are less than N. Subtract this common digit and cancel the positive factor N to identify the tail values. The induction hypothesis identifies all the remaining digits.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_notMem_of_unique_notMem: The sum of all terms except the distinguished one belongs to I. If the whole sum belonged to I as well, subtracting that sum of the remaining terms would put the distinguished term in I, a contradiction.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_mem_logDerivIdeal: The given derivation preserves P and the input belongs to J. Its value is therefore one of the generators of the logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_logDerivIdeal: The logarithmic derivative ideal contains J because J is one summand in its definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_logDerivIdealIterate: Every application contains the ideal to which it is applied. Starting with J at iteration zero and composing these inclusions proves the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the composition with the zero-th iterate changes nothing. The successor applies the logarithmic derivative ideal operation once more to both sides of the induction equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_iSup_le: At zero both sides are the sum of the original ideals. At a successor, apply the logarithmic derivative ideal operation to the induction containment using monotonicity. The one-step sum estimate then bounds the result by the sum obtained by applying the operation to each individual iterate. This is the desired sum at the successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_le_of_le: Write r′ as r plus a nonnegative difference. The iteration law expresses the larger iterate as the additional iterations applied to the r-th iterate. These additional iterations contain their starting ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_mono: At zero the operation is the identity and is monotone. At a successor it is the composition of the previous monotone iterate and the monotone logarithmic derivative ideal operation. Induction gives monotonicity at every count.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_one: The first iterate is the logarithmic derivative ideal of the zero-th iterate, which is J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_succ: At a successor the recursive definition applies the logarithmic derivative ideal operation to the previous iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_top_eq_derivIdealIt: At zero both iterates are J. When P is the unit ideal, one application of the logarithmic operation equals one application of the ordinary operation. Apply this equality at each successor step to obtain equality of the iterates.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_zero: By definition zero applications of the operation return the original ideal J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_eq_sup_span: The logarithmic derivative ideal is defined as the sum of J and the ideal generated by derivatives of its elements under derivations preserving P.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_iSup_le: Each J(i) lies in its own logarithmic derivative ideal, so their sum lies in the sum of these enlarged ideals. For a fixed tangent derivation, derivatives of elements from each J(i) lie in its enlarged ideal. Every element of the sum is a finite sum of elements from these ideals, and additivity then puts its derivative in the sum of the enlarged ideals. The containment criterion gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_derivIdeal: The ordinary derivative ideal contains J and the derivatives of its elements under all derivations. Among those are the derivations preserving P. Thus it contains every generator of the logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_iff: The logarithmic derivative ideal is the sum of J and the span of the permitted derivative values. It is contained in K exactly when both summands are contained there. For the span, this means precisely that every stated derivative value belongs to K.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_le_logDerivIdeal: Apply monotonicity for the fixed ideal P to the given inclusion from I to J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_mono: If I is contained in J, every element of I is in the logarithmic derivative ideal of J. Every permitted derivative value from I is also a permitted derivative value from J. The containment criterion gives monotonicity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_top_eq_derivIdeal: Every derivation preserves the unit ideal because all ring elements belong to it. The permitted derivatives in the logarithmic construction are therefore all the derivatives used in the ordinary construction. Both ideals also contain the same original generators.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_tangentDerivations: The tangent derivations are defined to be those that take every element of P back into P. Membership is therefore exactly the stated condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_tangentDerivations_span_singleton: A tangent derivation must take the generator x into its principal ideal. Conversely, if that value belongs to the ideal, then the Leibniz rule puts the derivative of every multiple of x in the same ideal. These multiples are all of its elements.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smul_mem_tangentDerivations: At an element x of P, the scaled derivation takes the value p times D(x). This belongs to P because p belongs to the ideal and ideals absorb multiplication by arbitrary ring elements.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_mem_map_of_forall_mem: The extended ideal is generated by the images of elements of P. Their derivatives lie in the extended ideal by hypothesis. Additivity and the Leibniz rule extend this to the whole span because multiplying a generator or another element of that ideal by a derivative still gives an element of the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_smul_apply: Scalar multiplication of derivations is defined by multiplying their values. Thus evaluation at x gives c times the original derivative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_mul_algebraMap_eq_of_mem_map: An element of an extended ideal in a localization can be written as a fraction with numerator in the original ideal and denominator in the inverted multiplicative set. Multiplying this expression by its denominator gives the displayed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_tangentDerivations_mul_eq: Finite presentation of the differential module clears a common denominator of the restricted derivation, yielding a derivation D₀ of S. Choose finitely many generators of P. Since the original localized derivation preserves the extended P, the image of the value of D₀ on each generator lies in that ideal. For each generator clear another denominator to put that value into P in the source. Multiply these finitely many denominators to get one factor c that works for all generators. The scaled derivation cD₀ then preserves all of P by the Leibniz rule. It agrees with the given derivation on source elements after multiplying by the product of c and the first denominator.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mul_mem_of_algebraMap_mem_map: Write the localized image of y as a fraction with numerator p in P and denominator t from the multiplicative set. The images of ty and p agree in the localization. Some further denominator c therefore gives equality of their products with c in the original ring. Hence cty is a multiple of p and lies in P, and ct belongs to the multiplicative set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_map: At zero both sides are the extension of J. At a successor apply the equality for a single logarithmic derivative ideal, with the previous iterate as input. The induction equality identifies that extended input with the previous iterate after localization.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealIterate_map_away: Localization away from g is localization at its powers. Apply the iterated localization formula to that multiplicative set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map: Extending source tangent derivations proves one inclusion. Clearing denominators using the finite generation of P and finite presentation of the differential module gives the other inclusion. The resulting ideals are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map_away: Use the multiplicative set of powers of g in the formula for localization of a logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdeal_map_le_map_logDerivIdeal: The extension of J already lies in the extension of its logarithmic derivative ideal. Let D preserve the extension of P and take x in the extension of J. Clear a unit denominator m so that on source elements mD is the image of a derivation D₁ preserving P. Choose a numerator y in J and denominator t with tx equal to the image of y. Apply the Leibniz rule to tx and multiply by m. This expresses mtD(x) as the image of D₁(y) minus x times the image of D₁(t). The first term belongs to the extended logarithmic derivative ideal by tangency of D₁, and the second belongs because x lies in the extended J. Since mt is a unit after localization, D(x) belongs to the desired ideal. This establishes containment for the localized logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mapToLocalization_mem_tangentDerivations: An extended derivation agrees with the original derivation on the images of source elements. For each p in P, the derivative of its image is therefore the image of an element of P. The extended ideal is generated by these images, and the Leibniz rule extends the containment from the generators to that entire ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_le: The images of J lie in the localized logarithmic derivative ideal. A derivation preserving P extends to the localization and preserves the extension of P. Its derivative on the image of an element of J is the image of the original derivative. Every generator of the extended logarithmic derivative ideal therefore belongs to the localized one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_derivation_mem_of_span_eq: The scaled derivation has values in P on the given generators. It preserves sums, and its value on a multiple of an element of P is a multiple of that element’s derivative plus a multiple of the element itself. Thus the property extends to all of P by the span property.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_ker_le_derivIde: At the zero-th iterate both sides give the extended J. At a successor apply the one-step quotient containment to the preceding logarithmic iterate. The induction hypothesis and monotonicity of the target derivative ideal bound the result by the next ordinary iterate of the extended J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_le_derivIdealIt: Replace P by the kernel of f using the assumed equality. The iterative quotient containment then gives exactly the stated result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_ker_le_derivIdeal_map: The images of the elements of J belong to the ordinary derivative ideal of its extension. A derivation preserving the kernel of f descends through the surjection. Thus the image of its derivative of an element of J is the derivative of the corresponding image under the descended derivation. It belongs to the target derivative ideal as well. This gives the containment on all generators.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_add: Induct on r. At zero the outer iterate is the identity. At a successor apply one more logarithmic derivative step to both sides and use the recursive definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ideal: At zero both sides are the original section ideal. At a successor take the sections of the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf of the preceding iterate. This applies the ring operation to the section ideal at the previous step, which is the preceding ring-level iterate by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_le_derivIdealS: At zero the two iterates agree. At a successor the logarithmic derivative sheaf of the previous logarithmic iterate lies in its ordinary derivative sheaf. By induction that ordinary derivative sheaf lies in the ordinary derivative sheaf of the preceding ordinary iterate, using monotonicity. This is the desired bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_mono: The zero-th iterate is the identity and preserves inclusions. At each successor the logarithmic operation preserves the inclusion between the preceding iterates, so induction proves monotonicity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_one: The first iterate applies the operation to the zero-th iterate, which is I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_succ: The recursive definition applies the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf operation once more at a successor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_zero: The zero-th iterate is the original ideal sheaf by definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_ideal: On an affine open, the logarithmic derivative ideal sheaf is defined by applying the ring-level operation to the two section ideals, using the base algebra structure on the section ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_le_derivIdealSheaf: On each affine open the tangent derivations used for the logarithmic ideal are among all the derivations used for the ordinary derivative ideal. The latter contains the original ideal and all of the logarithmic generators, giving the inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheaf_mono: An inclusion of inputs gives an inclusion on every affine open. With P fixed, the ring-level logarithmic operation preserves each of those inclusions. This gives the inclusion of ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_basicOpen: The section ring of the basic open is the localization at f, with the same action of the base ring after restriction. The section ideals of P and I on the basic open are extensions of their ideals on U. The section ring on U is Noetherian, so the ideal of P is finitely generated, and its module of differentials is finitely presented. The localization formula for logarithmic derivative ideals now identifies the extended ideal with the ideal assigned to the basic open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.app_comp_sectionsAlgebraMap: The scalar map is obtained by pulling back global sections of the base. Pulling these sections back through the morphism after restricting along p is pullback along the composite structural map. The equality follows from composition of section maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.app_sectionsAlgebraMap: Apply the compatibility of scalar structure maps with pullback to a.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_le_of_map_ideal_le: Let U be affine in X. The inverse image under the affine map is affine, and the ideal of D there is the kernel of restriction to its closed subscheme. By hypothesis the image of each element of the ideal of L on U belongs to this kernel. Its pullback under the composite immersion of that closed subscheme into X is zero. This gives containment of L in the kernel ideal sheaf of the composite. By the adjunction for extension and inverse image of ideal sheaves, the pullback of L lies in D.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ker_le_d: Apply the closed-immersion comparison of the pulled-back logarithmic iterate with the ordinary iterate of the pulled-back ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comp_app_apply: Pullback of sections under a composite is the successive pullback along its two maps. Evaluating at a gives the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_mono_of_le: At zero the inclusion is the original one. At a successor apply monotonicity of the derivative ideal operation to the inclusion for the preceding step.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_le_deriv: For every affine open the ring-level comparison gives the containment of the extended section ideal in the corresponding section ideal of the target sheaf. The affine-morphism criterion for pullback containment then gives the sheaf inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealSheafIterate_ideal_le: The pullback on sections of the affine open is a surjective k-algebra map because the morphism is a closed immersion and scalar maps commute with pullback. Its kernel is the section ideal of the kernel sheaf. Use the ring-level inequality for images of iterated logarithmic derivative ideals along this quotient. The extension of the original section ideal is contained in the section ideal of the pulled-back sheaf. Monotonicity of ordinary iteration therefore bounds the resulting ideal by the stated iterate on the inverse-image open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appLE_sectionsAlgebraMap: Pulling a base scalar section to U and then to V is the same as pulling it back along the composite structural map to V. This follows from composition of the section maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.bijective_appLE_image_of_isOpenImmersion: The open immersion identifies V with its open image. The resulting map of section rings is an isomorphism and is therefore bijective.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.bijective_hom_of_iso: An isomorphism of rings has an inverse ring homomorphism. The underlying functions are inverse, so the forward function is bijective.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_comap_eq_map_appLE: An open immersion identifies an affine source open with its image. On their section rings the map in the statement is the induced isomorphism. The pulled-back section ideal is the inverse image along the inverse ring isomorphism, which equals extension along the forward one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_ideal_of: Take the image affine open of V. The section map from the image to V is an isomorphism, and the ideals of the pulled-back sheaves are extensions along this map. Both sheaf iterates on these opens are the corresponding ring iterates. Transport the ambient ring iterate along the section isomorphism, which sends it to the iterate for the extended boundary and input ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.logDerivIdealSheafIterate_comap_of_isOpe: The two ideal sheaves have the same ideals on every affine open by the section comparison for the open immersion. This determines equality of the sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_appLE_logDerivIdealIterate_of_biject: The section ring on the source side of the ring map is Noetherian and its differential module is finitely presented. In particular P is finitely generated. The section map respects scalars by composition of structural maps. Apply the transport formula for a bijective ring map with these hypotheses.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_eq_comap_of_inverse: Every image of an element of J is sent back into J by the inverse, so the extended ideal is contained in the inverse image under the inverse map. Conversely an element of that inverse image is the forward image of its own inverse, which lies in J. This proves equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_of_bijective: The bijective ring map is a localization away from one. The scalar compatibility makes it a localization of the given base algebra. Use the localization formula for iterated logarithmic derivative ideals.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.finset_sum_derivation_apply: Evaluation is additive and preserves zero, so evaluating the finite sum gives the sum of the evaluations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdealIterate_le_span_pow_mul: At step zero the estimate is the assumed inclusion. At a successor through step m, the remaining exceptional exponent is positive. Apply the one-step logarithmic estimate to the two preceding iterates. It advances both iterates and lowers the exceptional exponent by one, giving the asserted power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_logDerivIdeal_le_span_pow_mul: Write m = e + 1 and denote the exceptional coordinate by b. Each image of f in J has the form b to the m-th power times f₁ in J₁. The original images satisfy the bound because the logarithmic ideal contains J₁. For a tangent source derivation, expand its value on f in the coordinate partials, with coefficients its values on the coordinates. In the distinguished boundary direction i the coefficient is divisible by the old boundary coordinate. Its image is therefore divisible by the new boundary coordinate and the exceptional coordinate, so the chart formula contributes a multiple of the coordinate-scaled tangent partial of f₁. Every other nonexceptional partial in the chart is tangent, and the formula leaves at least the e-th exceptional power. In the exceptional direction the remaining bracket is a sum of f₁ and weighted partials of f₁, including the scaled tangent partial in direction i. All these remaining factors lie in the new logarithmic ideal. The bound holds for the derivative generators and hence for their ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_mem_sup_of_span_pow_mul_eq_: Let b be the exceptional coordinate. On generators coming from J, the chart partial in a nonexceptional center direction acts as b times the image of the source partial. The assumed bound for source derivatives therefore puts these chart derivatives in the product of the (c + 1)-st power of b with L + L′. The extended J itself is also contained there. The Leibniz rule extends the derivative bound to the span of the generators. For g in L apply it to the product of g with the (c + 1)-st power of b, which belongs to the extended J. The chosen partial kills b, so it leaves exactly that power times its derivative of g. Cancel the power, which is a nonzerodivisor, to get the derivative in L + L′.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smul_derivation_apply: Scalar multiplication of a derivation multiplies each of its values by the scalar, giving the formula.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_mem_pow_sub_one: Induct on n. At zero the derivative lands in the unit ideal. In the successor step write the higher power as the product of the preceding power and J. For a product ab from these two factors, the term a times the derivative of b lies in the preceding power. The other term lies in J times the power given by induction for the derivative of a, which is contained in the same preceding power. Additivity handles sums of such products.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_natCast_mul: Multiplication by the image of a natural number is repeated addition. Since a derivation is additive, it commutes with this multiplication.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.fin_cons_self_tail: At the first position the reconstructed tuple agrees with β by its choice of head. At each later position it agrees by the definition of the tail. Hence the functions agree at every index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_comm_of_comm: The result for an empty composition is immediate. In a nonempty composition commute E past the first map by hypothesis, then commute it past the composition of the tail by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_eq_of_eq_id_of_ne: All factors except the distinguished one are identities. This follows recursively by removing the first factor. If it is the distinguished factor, the tail is an identity composition. If it is an identity, the tail contains the distinguished factor and gives the desired map by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_eq_self_of_forall_eq_self: The empty composition fixes x. In a nonempty list the composition of the tail fixes x by induction, and the first map fixes that value by hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_iterate_mem_pow_sub: Induct on the ordered family of derivations. The empty family makes no change. In a nonempty family the tail reduces the exponent by the sum of its iteration counts. Applying the first derivation its prescribed number of times reduces the exponent by that additional count. Truncated subtraction in succession is subtraction of their sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_mem_pow_sub: With zero iterations the original containment is unchanged. Each application lowers the available ideal-power exponent by one, with truncation at zero. Apply the one-derivative estimate and the induction hypothesis to get the exponent n minus the total number of applications.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_mul: At order zero the product is unchanged. Differentiate the formula at order n. The derivative commutes with the finite sum and the natural coefficients, and the Leibniz rule adds one application to either factor in each term. Reindex and combine the two sums by Pascal’s identity, obtaining the coefficients for order n + 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_natCast_mul: The identity map commutes with multiplication by the natural scalar. The single-derivation compatibility is preserved by composing with another application, so induction gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_derivation_sum: The identity preserves the finite sum. Each further derivative is additive and commutes with the sum, proving the identity by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mul_pow_sub_one_le: At n equal to zero the right side is the unit ideal. For positive n, the product of J with its preceding power is exactly the n-th power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add: Apply composition of mixed derivatives for a family of pairwise commuting derivations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add_of_comm_forall: Induct on the size of the family. In the nonempty case split off the first derivation and apply induction to the tail. The first derivation commutes with each tail derivation and hence with every iterate and their ordered composite. Its powers can therefore move past the tail factors. Group its applications into the two prescribed counts, using the addition rule for powers of a single map. The resulting two successive mixed derivatives have indices β and α in that order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_add_unitMultiIndex_apply: The addition rule for commuting derivations splits the mixed derivative into the unit-index derivative followed by the derivative with index α. The unit-index derivative is the single application at i.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_fun_zero: The function constantly zero is the zero multi-index. Apply the identity for that index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mem_pow_sub: The mixed derivative is the ordered composition of the iterated derivatives. The power estimate for that composition subtracts the sum of all entries of the multi-index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mul: Induct on the number of derivations in the family. With no derivations the only split is empty and the product stays unchanged. For a nonempty family, expand the tail derivative of the product by induction. Apply the prescribed iterate of the first derivation to each term, taking the natural coefficient outside and using the one-variable Leibniz formula on the two factors. Combining the split of the first count with each tail split gives all allowed multi-indices. The coefficient is the product of their coordinate binomial coefficients. The order of application in both factors is the same as in the original mixed derivative.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_mul_sub_sum_mem: The mixed Leibniz formula expands the product derivative over all splits of α. Remove those splits whose first part has total order r. In every remaining term, either the first part has order less than r or the second part has order less than s, since their orders add to r + s. The corresponding derivative then lies in a positive power of J by the order estimate. Thus each remaining product, and hence their sum, lies in J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_of_isEmpty: There are no derivations to apply. The empty composition is the identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_succ: By definition the composition for a nonempty index first acts with the tail of the family and then applies the first derivation the specified number of times.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_unitMultiIndex: A unit multi-index prescribes one application at i and zero elsewhere. The ordered composition is therefore the derivation at i.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.multiIndexDeriv_zero: Every entry of the zero multi-index prescribes zero applications of its derivation. Each factor in the composition is the identity, so the composite fixes f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_choose_succ_mul_eq: Separate the last term in the first sum and the first term in the second. The remaining terms have the same products after shifting the index by one. Their coefficients add by Pascal’s identity, giving the interior binomial coefficients for n + 1. Each boundary term already has coefficient one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_piFinset_succ: A tuple of allowed values consists uniquely of an allowed first value and a tuple of allowed tail values. Reindex the sum by this bijection and then sum over the first value and the tail in succession.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_unitMultiIndex: All entries except the designated one are zero, and the remaining entry is one. Thus the sum is one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.unitMultiIndex_apply: The unit multi-index is defined to have value one at its designated index and zero elsewhere.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coord_mem_primeIdealOf_of_mem_support: If the coordinate lay outside the prime corresponding to the point, it would become a unit in the stalk. Its germ generates the stalk ideal, so the stalk ideal would be the entire local ring. This contradicts membership in the support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_etaleChart_genericPoint_mem: The maximal irreducible subset is closed in the scheme and has a generic point in the support specializing to the given point. Choose a chart around the given point. Since the point lies in the support, the divisor there is defined by a single coordinate. Shrink to an affine basic open around the point. The generic point also lies in it by specialization. To prove minimality of its prime over the coordinate, let a smaller prime contain the coordinate. Its point belongs to the support and specializes to the generic point. The closure of this point is irreducible, lies in the support, and contains the original component. Maximality makes the two closed sets equal. The original generic point therefore specializes back to the point of the smaller prime, proving equality of the primes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_primeIdealOf_eq_of_isPrime: The affine open is canonically identified with the spectrum of its section ring. The given prime determines a point in that spectrum and the corresponding point of the affine open. The inverse identification associates the original prime to this point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mul_mem_of_map_mem_map: In the localization, write the image of the element as a fraction with numerator in the original ideal and denominator in the multiplicative set. After cross-multiplication the equality in the localization becomes an equality in the original ring upon multiplication by one further element of the multiplicative set. The product of the two denominators therefore sends the original element into the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_of_maximal_irreducible_subset_s: The closure of the given subset is irreducible and stays inside the support, which is closed. Maximality forces the closure to equal the subset.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrime_span_germ_coord: The affine chart ring is étale over the polynomial ring. After quotienting by the chosen coordinate, the ring is étale over the polynomial ring with that variable removed. Localizing at the prime corresponding to the point gives a regular local ring, since the base polynomial ring is regular and étale maps preserve regularity. This quotient is a nonzero domain because the coordinate lies in the prime. Thus the germ of the coordinate generates a prime ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isUnit_germ_iff_notMem_primeIdealOf: The stalk on the affine open is the section ring localized at the point’s prime. Elements outside that prime become units by localization, and elements in the prime map into the maximal ideal and so are nonunits.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isUnit_map_of_mem_of_isLocalization: A localization makes each element of the specified multiplicative set invertible. Its inverse is the fraction with numerator one and that element as denominator.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_iff_forall_stalkIdeal_le: A sheaf inclusion extends to an inclusion on each stalk. Conversely, take a section of the first ideal on an affine open. At every point its germ belongs to the second stalk ideal. Since the stalk is localization at the corresponding prime, clearing denominators gives a section that is a unit at that point and whose product with the original section belongs to the second ideal. The basic opens of these sections cover the affine open, so the sections generate the unit ideal. A combination of them equal to one shows that the original section belongs to the second ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_of_span_mul_mem_eq_top: Multiplication by the given element sends every generator of the span into the ideal. By additivity and compatibility with scalar multiplication, it sends the entire span into the ideal. The span contains one, so the original element belongs to the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_span_pow_of_mul_mem_span_pow: Induct on the exponent. At exponent zero the ideal is the whole ring. At a positive exponent, membership of the product in the power first puts the product in the prime principal ideal. The first factor lies outside that prime, so the second is divisible by the generator. Substitute this multiple and cancel one copy of the generator, using that it is a nonzerodivisor. The induction hypothesis shows that the remaining factor of the second element is divisible by the preceding power, giving the desired divisibility.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.notMem_support_of_mem_opens_of_restrictI: Under the open inclusion, the support of the restricted ideal is the inverse image of the original support. The unit ideal has empty support, so no point in the given open can lie in the original support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.not_stalkIdeal_le_pow_succ_genericPoint: At the generic point the divisor stalk ideal equals the maximal ideal. Containment in its next power would force the order to be at least that next exponent. This contradicts the given value of the order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAtGenericPoint_eq_orderAt: The order at the generic point is defined by evaluating the pointwise order at that point. Substitution gives the equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.primeIdealOf_eq_comap_span_germ_coord: The prime of the generizing point contains the coordinate and is contained in the prime of the specialized point. The coordinate germ at the specialized point generates a prime ideal, so its contraction is prime and contains the coordinate. For an element of the contraction, clearing denominators gives a multiplier outside the prime of the specialized point whose product with the element belongs to the coordinate ideal downstairs. The multiplier is also outside the prime of the generizing point. Primality puts the element in this latter prime. By the assumed minimality, the contraction equals that prime.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.primeIdealOf_le_of_specializes: If a section is outside the prime of the specialized point, its basic open contains that point. Any open containing the specialized point also contains the point that specializes to it. The section is therefore outside the prime of the latter point. Taking contrapositives gives the inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.span_eq_top_of_forall_mem_basicOpen: The stated condition says that the basic opens of the sections cover the entire affine open. Under its identification with the spectrum of the section ring, a prime containing the ideal generated by these sections would give a point missed by the cover. Every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal, so the generated ideal is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.specializes_of_primeIdealOf_le: Take an open neighborhood of the point with the larger prime and choose a basic-open neighborhood inside it on the affine chart. Its defining section lies outside the larger prime, hence outside the smaller prime. The point of the smaller prime is in the basic open. Thus every open neighborhood of the point of the larger prime contains the other point, which gives the stated specialization.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_eq_maximalIdeal_of_minimal: At the generizing point, the stalk ideal is proper and generated by the coordinate germ. The contraction formula applied at that point says that the contraction of this principal ideal is its point prime. The contraction of the maximal ideal is contained in the same prime, since every element outside the prime becomes a unit. In a localization, extending the contraction of an ideal recovers it. The maximal ideal is therefore contained in the stalk ideal, and the reverse inclusion holds because the stalk ideal is proper.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_eq_span_germ_coord: On the affine chart the ideal is generated by the indicated coordinate. Its stalk is the extension of that section ideal along the germ map. Extension of a principal ideal is generated by the image of its generator.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_genericPoint_eq_maximalIdeal: Choose a point in the component, which is nonempty by irreducibility. The local chart construction gives a chart containing the generic point with its prime minimal over the coordinate. At such a point the stalk ideal of the coordinate divisor is the maximal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_le_pow_of_le_orderAt_genericP: Use the chart through the point and the component’s generic point provided by the local coordinate hypothesis and maximal irreducibility. In that chart the generic prime is minimal over the coordinate ideal. Apply the stalk containment for a minimal prime with the given bound on the order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_le_pow_stalkIdeal_of_minimal: At the generizing point the divisor’s stalk ideal is the maximal ideal generated by the coordinate germ. The order bound puts the germ of every section of the given ideal in the appropriate power of that maximal ideal. Clear denominators to multiply the section by an element outside the generizing prime and obtain a multiple of the coordinate power in the affine ring. In the stalk at the specialized point, the multiplier lies outside the prime generated by the coordinate germ, by the contraction formula. The coordinate germ is a nonzerodivisor, so the cancellation result for powers of a principal prime gives membership of the section’s germ in the coordinate power. These germs generate the desired stalk ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_commuting_dual_derivations: Give A the polynomial algebra structure that sends the variables to w. The unit differential determinant implies formal étaleness of this evaluation map over the polynomial ring. The coordinate partial derivations then take the dual values on w, and they commute by the vanishing of their commutators on coordinates.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_regularParameters_of_formallyEtal: Use adapted coordinates on S whose selected members generate the maximal ideal after localization at q. Their full differential determinant lies outside q, so its image in A is a unit. Base change of the coordinate differential basis to A identifies this image with the determinant for the images of the adapted coordinates. The local algebra is formally smooth over k by composition of localization with the original formally étale coordinate structure. Construct commuting dual derivations for the full family. Restrict the coordinates and derivations to the selected indices and enumerate them by a finite initial segment. The selected coordinates generate the maximal ideal, and their paired derivations remain dual and commute.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_regularParameters_stalk_of_smooth: Choose an affine étale chart containing x. The section ring is formally étale over the polynomial coordinate ring, and its localization at the point prime is the stalk. The stalk is Noetherian by smoothness, and its residue field is formally smooth over the characteristic-zero field. The scalar structures are compatible under both maps. Apply the adapted-parameter construction for a prime localization to obtain the stated generators and commuting dual derivations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.natCast_mul_le_mul_iff: If a is infinite, multiplication by positive c leaves it infinite, so both inequalities hold. If a is finite, the equivalence is cancellation of the positive common factor c in an inequality of natural numbers.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAtLeastLocus_pow_mul: By the order formula for powers, a point satisfies the threshold c times m for the power precisely when c times the original order is at least c times m. Cancel positive c to obtain the original threshold.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_mul: The product sheaf has the product of the two stalk ideals at x. The smooth stalk has parameters with commuting dual derivations, and positive natural scalars are units. The multiplicativity formula for ideal order in this local ring gives the order of the product as the sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_pow: Taking the stalk takes the sheaf power to the corresponding power of the stalk ideal. Use the order formula for powers in the local ring with the commuting dual derivations provided by smoothness and the invertibility of the positive natural scalars.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_comm: The commutator of the two partial derivations is a derivation. It vanishes on every coordinate because each first derivative of a coordinate is either zero or one, and both are killed by any derivation. Coordinate values determine a derivation, so the commutator is zero. Evaluating at a gives commutativity.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.germ_comp_appLE: Pulling a section back to V and taking its germ commutes with taking the original germ and then applying the stalk map. This follows from naturality of the germ maps under the morphism, since restricting within a neighborhood does not change its germ.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_natCast_or_succ_le: Infinity is at least r + 1. In the finite case the ordinary natural value is either at most r or, by discreteness, at least r + 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.one_le_orderAt_of_one_le_orderAt_comap: Order at least one for the pullback puts the extension of the original stalk ideal inside the target maximal ideal. The inverse image of that maximal ideal is the original maximal ideal because the stalk map is local. Thus the original stalk ideal is contained in it, giving order at least one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAtLeastLocus_comap: At each point the order of the pulled-back ideal equals the order of the original ideal at its image. The two membership conditions at threshold m are consequently equivalent.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_comap: Pullback cannot lower the order. If the original order is infinite this already gives equality. Otherwise let it be r. If the pullback order were at least r + 1, its r-th derivative iterate would have order at least one by the lower bound for derivative iterates. Smooth pullback commutes with taking that iterate, and order at least one for a pulled-back ideal implies order at least one for the original. This would make the original r-th iterate have positive order, but its order is r − r by exact order decrease. Thus the pullback order is at most r.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_le_orderAt_comap: Take any natural lower bound n for the original order. The original stalk ideal lies in the n-th power of its maximal ideal. Extend along the stalk map, which sends the original maximal ideal into the target maximal ideal because it is local. Extension commutes with powers, so the pulled-back ideal lies in the target n-th power. Every finite lower bound is thus preserved.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_comap: Choose an affine U around the image point and an affine V around y mapping into U. The section ideal of the pulled-back sheaf on V is the extension of the original ideal on U along the section map. Passing to germs commutes with this map through the stalk map. Since extension of ideals commutes with composition, the pulled-back stalk ideal is the extension of the original stalk ideal along the stalk map.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coord_mul_partialDeriv_mem_logDerivIdeal: The coordinate-scaled partial derivation preserves the distinguished principal ideal. Its value on g is the stated scaled derivative and is a generator of the logarithmic derivative ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coord_smul_partialDeriv_mem_tangentDeriv: The scaled derivation takes every element to a multiple of the distinguished coordinate. It therefore preserves the ideal generated by that coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealIterate_le_iSup_logDerivIdealI: At stage zero use the summand with zero partial and zero logarithmic steps. At a successor, the ordinary derivative of the previous iterate is contained in the sum of ordinary derivatives of the summands by monotonicity and the derivative estimate for sums. For each summand, split this next derivative into a logarithmic step and a possible partial step in direction h. The logarithmic step keeps the count of partial steps unchanged. In the other term, move the partial step across all the preceding logarithmic steps by the iterated containment. It increases the partial count by one and leaves the logarithmic count unchanged. Both terms are among the summands at the new total count, proving the bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdeal_le_logDerivIdeal_sup_partialD: The sum on the right contains I. Expand any derivation in the basis of partial derivations. Its term in the distinguished direction lies in the chosen partial derivative ideal. Each other partial preserves the boundary, so its term lies in the logarithmic derivative ideal. The sum therefore contains every derivative generator.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_eq_sum_partialDeriv: The coordinate differentials form a basis. Expanding the linear map associated to D in its dual basis expresses D as the sum of partial derivations with coefficients its values on the coordinates. Evaluate that sum at g.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_sum_apply: Addition of derivations is pointwise, so evaluation at g carries their finite sum to the sum of their evaluations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_partialDerivIdeal: The partial derivative ideal is a sum with J as a summand, so it contains J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_idealInfComapPartialDeriv_iff: The auxiliary ideal consists by definition of the elements of K whose chosen partial derivative also belongs to K.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdealIterate_one: The first iterate applies the partial derivative ideal to the zero-th iterate, which is J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdealIterate_succ: At a successor the recursive operation applies the partial derivative ideal once to the previous iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdealIterate_zero: With zero iterations the operation returns J by definition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_def: The partial derivative ideal is defined by adjoining to J all the values of the chosen partial derivative on elements of J and taking their ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_le: The hypotheses give containment of the original ideal and every derivative generator in K. The containment criterion then gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_le_iff: The partial derivative ideal is contained in K if and only if both the original ideal and the span of the derivative values are contained in K. The latter condition is equivalent to membership of each individual derivative value.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_logDerivIdealIterate_l: At zero the logarithmic operation is the identity. At a successor move the partial derivative operation past the outer logarithmic step using the one-step containment. Apply the induction containment to the remaining logarithmic steps, using monotonicity of the outer step.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_logDerivIdeal_le: Let K be the logarithmic derivative ideal of the partial derivative ideal of I. It suffices to put the generators of the logarithmic derivative ideal of I in K with their h-th derivatives, because the elements with these two properties form an ideal by the Leibniz rule. For an element of I this follows from the definition of the partial derivative ideal. For a tangent derivative of y in I, its value belongs to K by monotonicity. Expand it in the basis of partial derivations and differentiate in direction h. The terms differentiating the coefficients multiply first derivatives of y, which already lie in K, in the distinguished direction by the partial ideal and in the other directions by tangency. For terms differentiating the partials of y, the directions different from h commute with h and are tangent, hence send the h-th derivative of y into K. The coefficient in direction h is a multiple of the distinguished coordinate by tangency. Its second partial therefore belongs to K via the coordinate-scaled tangent derivation applied to the h-th derivative of y. All differentiated terms lie in K, giving the containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDerivIdeal_mono: Under inclusion from I to J, every element of I and every chosen partial derivative of such an element belong to the partial derivative ideal of J. This is enough for containment of the partial derivative ideal of I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_mem_logDerivIdeal_of_ne: The partial derivation at i preserves the boundary ideal because i differs from h. Its value on g in J is therefore one of the logarithmic generators.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_mem_partialDerivIdeal: The derivative of g is among the generators adjoined to J in the chosen partial derivative direction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.partialDeriv_mem_tangentDerivations_of_n: The partial derivation at a different index kills the distinguished coordinate. The Leibniz rule then shows that it preserves the principal ideal of that coordinate.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_point_primeIdealOf_eq: The affine open is isomorphic to the spectrum of its sections. Send q to the corresponding point of the open. The inverse affine identification takes this point back to q.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_top_of_disjoint_support: A proper affine ideal of Z would be contained in a maximal ideal. The point of that maximal ideal would belong to the support inside W. The disjointness hypothesis excludes this, so the ideal is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_le_of_support_subset: Each prime containing the affine ideal of Z is the prime of a point of its support. The support inclusion puts that point on the support of J, so the prime also contains the affine ideal of J. Intersecting over all the primes containing the ideal of Z gives its radical, which is the ideal itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_le_pow_of_restrictIdeal_eq_coordId: At m equal to zero the containment is automatic. For positive m, write C for the affine ideal of Z, generated by the selected coordinates with their dual partial derivations. The (m − 1)-st derivative iterate of I has support containing the support of Z on U by the order-locus formula. Since C is radical, the section ideal of that iterate is contained in C. Induct on j from one to m to show that the (m − j)-th ring iterate of the affine ideal of I lies in C to the j-th power. The case j = 1 is the support argument. At the next step an element of the (m − j − 1)-st iterate and all its selected partial derivatives lie in the (m − j)-th iterate, hence in the j-th power by induction. The Euler criterion uses the invertibility of j over the characteristic-zero field to put the element in the (j + 1)-st power. At j = m the iterate is the original affine ideal, proving the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isRadical_ideal_of_restrictIdeal_eq_coor: The chart identifies the ideal of Z with the extension of the selected coordinate ideal from the polynomial ring. Quotienting by it is therefore étale over the polynomial ring in the remaining coordinates. Every localization of this quotient at a maximal ideal is regular local, hence a domain and reduced. Reducedness can be tested at these localizations, so the quotient is reduced and the ideal of Z is radical.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isUnit_natCast_of_algebra_of_charZero: The positive integer maps to a nonzero element of the characteristic-zero field k, and hence to a unit there. The algebra map sends that unit to the required scalar in R.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_pow_of_forall_le_pow_basicOpen: On an affine V, suppose a section a of I does not belong to the m-th power of the section ideal of Z. The ideal of multipliers taking a into that power is then proper. Choose a maximal ideal containing it and consider its point. Choose the basic neighborhood provided by the hypothesis there, with defining section g outside this maximal ideal. On this neighborhood a belongs to the localized ideal power. Clearing a power of g makes a multiple of a belong to the original ideal power. This puts that power of g in the multiplier ideal, hence in the maximal ideal, contradicting primality. The containment holds on every affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_pow_of_hasStrictNormalCrossingsWith: The strict normal crossings hypothesis gives, around every point of the center, a chart in which the center ideal is a coordinate ideal. These are the charts required by the power-containment criterion for the given order-locus inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.le_pow_of_support_subset_orderAtLeastLoc: Around any point of the support choose the given chart and a basic open of the current affine contained in it. Restrict the chart and apply the coordinate-ideal power containment using the order-locus hypothesis. Outside the support choose a basic open disjoint from it. The ideal of Z there is the unit ideal, so containment in its power is automatic. The local containment criterion for basic opens then gives the sheaf inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_iff_ideal_le_primeIdealOf_of: The stalk ideal is the extension of the affine section ideal to the localization at the point prime. The inverse image of the maximal ideal in that localization is the point prime. Thus containment of the extended ideal in the maximal ideal is equivalent to containment of the section ideal in the point prime. The former is the support criterion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.notMem_primeIdealOf_of_mem_basicOpen: The section has a unit germ at a point of its basic open. If the section belonged to the point prime, its germ in the localization would belong to the maximal ideal and could not be a unit.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_subset_orderAtLeastLocus_of_le_p: At a point of the support of Z, its stalk ideal is contained in the maximal ideal. The inclusion of I in the m-th power of Z passes to the stalk, and taking stalk ideals commutes with powers. Thus the stalk ideal of I is contained in the m-th power of the maximal ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivIdealSheafIterate_le_biSup_logDeriv: Prove the inclusion on affine neighborhoods. Over the center the local blowup-chart estimate supplies the required inclusion. Away from it, the blowup is an isomorphism and the exceptional ideal is the unit ideal. The assumed identities then identify the section ideal of every chosen transform with the extension of the corresponding derivative iterate downstairs. Iterated ordinary differentiation commutes with pullback on this neighborhood, so the left-hand side equals the transform indexed by the derivative count. This is exactly the summand at that index, where zero logarithmic differentiations are taken. The local inclusions give the global containment.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineOpen_derivIdealSheafIterate: Use strict normal crossings to choose affine étale coordinates downstairs with the center cut out by a subset of the coordinates. Take an affine neighborhood of the point in a blowup chart. If the strict-transform boundary has unit ideal there, logarithmic differentiation agrees with ordinary differentiation, so the term indexed by zero already contains the left-hand side. Otherwise the boundary is generated by the chart coordinate for a center index distinct from the exceptional index. The exceptional coordinate is a nonzerodivisor. Evaluate the assumed identities on the chart to express each extended derivative ideal as the corresponding exceptional-coordinate power times the section ideal of the chosen transform. The blowup coordinate equations now give the hypotheses of the ring-level estimate comparing ordinary derivatives with the sum of logarithmic derivatives. Translate each summand back to a section ideal and use its inclusion in the stated supremum of sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_affineOpen_eq_top_of_restrictIdeal: The restriction of the unit ideal sheaf is the unit ideal sheaf on the open. The hypothesis therefore identifies the restrictions of the given ideal and the unit ideal. On the affine open their section ideals agree, so the original section ideal there is the whole ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_ideal_eq_ideal_pow: On an affine open, evaluating a product gives the product of the evaluated ideals, and the unit sheaf evaluates to the unit ideal. These facts give the equality for every exponent, including zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_top: Restriction is pullback along the open inclusion. Pullback of the unit ideal sheaf gives the unit ideal sheaf because extension along a section map sends one to one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.top_ideal_eq_top: The largest ideal sheaf has the whole section ring as its value on every affine open. Its value on this open is the unit ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coeff_eq: The coefficient is defined as the image of the iterated derivative multiplied by the image of the inverse factorial.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.factorial_inv_mul_choose: Start with the binomial identity that the coefficient times the two factorials of the split sizes equals the factorial of j. The factorials are nonzero in the rationals, so dividing by their product and by the factorial of j gives the equation there. Apply the algebra map to the target ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_deriv_mul: In the repeated-addition formula, an integer count acting on a ring element is multiplication by its image in the ring. Replace each repeated-addition coefficient by that scalar factor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iterate_deriv_mul_eq_sum_nsmul: Induct on the number of applications. The formula at zero has only the original product. At each successor, apply additivity and the Leibniz rule to every term. Each term produces one term with an extra derivative on the first factor and one with an extra derivative on the second. In the interior, Pascal’s identity combines the two neighboring coefficients. The two endpoint products have coefficient one. This proves the iterated product rule with coefficients acting by repeated addition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_add: The truncated series preserves addition. The quotient map also preserves addition, giving the displayed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_mul: The difference between the truncated series of the product and the product of the two series lies in J. Their classes are therefore equal, and the quotient map carries a product to the product of its classes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_one: The truncated series of one is one for positive N, and its class in the quotient is one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mk_truncatedSeries_zero: The truncated series of zero is zero, and its class in the quotient is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_Ico_mul_pow_eq_sum_range: Set j = i + k. The interval from i up to, but excluding, N corresponds to 0 ≤ k < N − i, and j − i becomes k. This changes the summand to exactly the one on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_convolution_sub_mul_mem: Expand the product of the two truncated sums into terms indexed by pairs i,k each below N. The convolution sum uses precisely the pairs with i + k < N, by setting the total degree to i + k. Their difference is the negative of the terms with i + k at least N. Each of those terms contains β to a power at least N and hence is a multiple of β to the N-th power. They all lie in J, as does their signed sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_range_sum_range_succ_eq_sum_sum_Ico: Both sums run over pairs with 0 ≤ i ≤ j < N. The first groups by the larger index j, and the second groups by the smaller index i. Equivalently, increasing N adds the same terms with j equal to the old bound on both sides.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeriesRingHom_apply: The ring homomorphism is defined by evaluating the truncated series and taking its class modulo J. This gives its value at f.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_add: Every iterate of the additive derivation preserves addition. Apply this to every coefficient and use additivity of σ, then distribute the scalar factors and split the finite sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_apply: By definition the truncated series is the sum over degrees below N, with coefficient the image of the iterated derivative divided by its factorial, multiplied by the corresponding power of β.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_mul: At each degree j expand the derivative of the product by the iterated Leibniz rule. The ring map transports this sum and its products to S. For each split i and j − i, the binomial coefficient divided by j factorial becomes the product of the inverses of the two split factorials. Thus the coefficient of β to the j-th power is the sum of products of the two individual Taylor coefficients.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_mul_sub_mem: Use the convolution formula for the Taylor series of the product and express each individual Taylor series as the sum of its coefficients times powers of β. The difference is the convolution error, which belongs to J because β to the N-th power does.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_of_deriv_eq_zero: All positive iterates of D on f vanish because the first is zero and D fixes zero. Since N is positive, the sum contains the constant term. This is the only term left, and it equals σ(f).
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_one: Every derivation kills one. The series of an element killed by the derivation equals its constant term when N is positive, and σ sends one to one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_sub_mem_span_singleton: Subtracting σ(f) removes the degree-zero term since N is positive. Every remaining term has a positive power of β, hence has β as a factor. Their sum lies in the principal ideal generated by β.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_zero: Every iterate of D sends zero to zero, including the identity iterate. Each term is consequently zero after applying σ, so the sum vanishes.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.derivation_apply_eq_zero_of_formallyUnra: A derivation factors through the module of relative Kähler differentials. Formal unramifiedness makes this module zero, so every such derivation vanishes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mul_deriv_pow_eq_pow_mul: At exponent zero the derivative is zero, so take coefficient zero. At a successor apply the Leibniz rule to b times the previous power. After multiplication by b, the term differentiating the old power uses the induction coefficient. The other term adds the derivative of b to that coefficient.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isTaylorExpansionOn_mvPolynomial: For positive N reduce both maps modulo the N-th maximal-ideal power. The truncated Taylor formula gives a ring homomorphism into this quotient because β to the N-th power vanishes there. It agrees with the second map on coefficients, since the derivation kills those coefficients and the original maps agree there. The variable hypothesis gives agreement on all variables modulo the same power. Thus the two homomorphisms agree on the polynomial algebra, giving the congruence on every element.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_le_map_of_pow_mul_iterate_deriv_mem: For g in J, if the extension along φ is the unit ideal the conclusion is automatic. Otherwise this extension is proper and lies in the maximal ideal. For each positive length N, weighted derivative stability puts the truncated Taylor series of g in the extension along φ because φ(b) = β. The comparison with φ′ gives that φ′(g) lies in the sum of this extension and the N-th maximal-ideal power. This also holds for N equal to zero. The quotient and Krull intersection argument gives membership in the extension along φ. This works for every generator of the extension along φ′.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_of_forall_mem_sup_maximalIdeal_pow: Quotient by J. This is a Noetherian local ring because J lies in the maximal ideal. The image of the maximal ideal is the maximal ideal of the quotient. The image of x belongs to every power of it since the J summand vanishes. Krull intersection makes that image zero, so x belongs to J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pow_mul_iterate_deriv_mem_of_mul_derivId: At zero this is membership of g in J. If the weighted j-th derivative is in J, then b times its derivative is in J by the assumed product containment. Expand this derivative by the Leibniz rule. Its term from differentiating the power of b is a ring multiple of the previous weighted derivative, because b times the derivative of the j-th power is divisible by that power. Subtract that term to leave the next weighted derivative, still in J.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sub_mem_iInf_span_sup_maximalIdeal_pow: For every positive N the comparison gives membership in the corresponding ideal sum. For N equal to zero the power is the unit ideal, so membership is automatic. Hence the element lies in the intersection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sub_mem_of_isTaylorExpansionOn: The Taylor comparison puts the difference in the ideal generated by β. That ideal lies in I because β belongs to I.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sub_mem_pow_succ_of_sub_mem_pow: Work modulo the (k + 1)-st power. The two maps are additive and agree on base scalars and the unit. Their difference satisfies the Leibniz rule with the module structure given by φ′. Indeed the multiplicativity error already vanishes, and the product of the two differences lies in the 2k-th power, contained in the (k + 1)-st because k is positive. Agreement on the base gives linearity over P. The difference is therefore a P-derivation into the quotient, which is zero by formal unramifiedness.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sub_mem_span_singleton_of_isTaylorExpans: The difference lies in the sum of the principal ideal of β and each maximal-ideal power. Since the principal ideal lies in the maximal ideal, the quotient and Krull intersection argument puts the difference in that principal ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sub_mem_span_sup_maximalIdeal_pow: Insert the truncated series between the two values. Its difference from φ(f) is in the principal ideal of β, and its difference from φ′(f) is in the N-th maximal-ideal power. Subtract the first difference from the second to express φ(f) − φ′(f) in the sum of these ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_length_one: Only the degree-zero term occurs. Its factorial and power factors are one, so it equals σ(f).
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.truncatedSeries_mem_map: Each weighted derivative of g belongs to J by stability.
