Conversely, local containment includes a nonempty open part of the selected component through the image point. That part is dense in the component, so closedness of the divisor implies containment of the whole component. The old index is then among the chosen center indices. The total sum therefore splits into the exponents of the selected strict transforms and the exponents of the chosen center indices. The latter sum is the order along the selected center component, giving the claimed equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_transform_eq_of_genericPoint_: The order along the upper component is the order at its generic point. Its image has irreducible closure, and the image of the generic point is generic for that closure by continuity. The order along the image is therefore the order at this image point. The upper generic point is off the exceptional divisor, so the equality of orders for the controlled transform at that point equates the two values.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_transform_eq_of_not_mem_exceptio: The exceptional ideal is the pulled-back center. At the given point its stalk is the unit ideal. Taking stalks in the controlled-transform product identity therefore makes the transformed ideal stalk equal to the total-transform stalk. Off the exceptional divisor the blowup preserves the order of the total transform from its image downstairs. These equalities give the stated order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransformIndex_injective: The strict-transform index map retains the numeric value of each index. Equal images thus imply equal original numeric values and hence equal original indices.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.binaryEncode_transport_lt_iff: The two sets have the same cardinality, and transport preserves both cardinalities. The strict code comparison is therefore equivalent to comparison of the sorted index lists in lexicographic order. The original lists and their transports are obtained from the same two filtered sets of matching positions by applying the first and second strictly increasing index maps. Each map preserves and reflects the lexicographic comparison, yielding the equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_eq_minIndexCard_of_isMaxOrderIndexS: The witness for a maximizing index set is a candidate at the minimum size. The size condition for this candidate is the stated equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_transport: The filter set maps injectively to both lists because the two index maps are strictly increasing. Its first image is the original selected set, since all those indices are matched, and its second image is the transported set. Both images have the cardinality of the filter set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.get_ne_top_of_isMaxOrderIndexSet: A maximizing index set is witnessed by a candidate component. That component belongs to the selected intersection, so none of the selected ideals is a unit.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.get_ne_top_of_mem_intersectionComponents: If a selected ideal were the unit ideal, the intersection ideal would be the unit ideal and its support would be empty. An irreducible component is nonempty and lies in that support, which is impossible.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.get_ne_top_of_mem_lexMaxIndices: If there is a set of maximum order, the chosen set is also of maximum order, so each of its selected ideals is nonunit. Otherwise the chosen set is empty and there are no entries to check.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.iSup_orderAlong_le_of_orderedMatchingOfN: Every term in the first supremum comes from a candidate component for a set of the specified size. Transport the set and keep the component. The same value is a term in the second supremum, which therefore bounds the first.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.image_toFirst_preimage: The first image of a retained matching position belongs to the selected set by the filter condition. Conversely, every index of the selected set is nonunit, so the matching provides a position for it. That position belongs to the filter. This proves equality with the selected set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionComponents_congr: Equal intersection ideals have equal supports. Maximal irreducible subsets of those supports therefore form the same family.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionIdeal_eq_top: The intersection ideal is the sum of the selected ideals. It contains the selected unit ideal, so it is itself the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionIdeal_transport: Every original selected index is nonunit and hence occurs in the matching. The corresponding second index is selected after transport and has the same ideal. Conversely, every transported index comes from an original selected index with equal ideal. The two sums of selected ideals thus have the same summands.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isCandidateComponent_transport: A candidate has a nonempty intersection component, so all selected boundary entries are nonunit. Transport preserves their number and the intersection ideal. The same component lies in the transported intersection, and its order for the original marked ideal is unchanged. The transported selection therefore satisfies each candidate condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxOrderIndexSet_lexMaxIndices: There is at least one code from a set of maximum order. The codes are bounded by the sum of the powers of two for all boundary indices, so the supremum of these natural numbers is attained. The chosen index set is a witness attaining it, hence has maximum order and has code at least the code of every other maximum-order set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMaxOrderIndexSet_transport: Transport the candidate witness to the other list. Its size remains the minimum, since the minimum sizes agree, and its component keeps the same order, which is still maximal because the maximum orders agree. The transported set is therefore maximizing.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lexMaxIndices_eq_empty: If no set of maximum order exists, there can be no such set attaining the maximum code. The definition takes its empty-set branch.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lexMaxIndices_eq_of_binaryEncode_le: The given set and the chosen set are both of maximum order. Each has code at least that of the other by their maximal-code properties. Equal codes imply equal sets because the binary encoding is injective.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lexMaxIndices_transport: If a maximum-order set exists, transport the chosen one. It remains of maximum order. Any competing maximum-order set in the second list can be transported back to the first, where its code is bounded by that of the first choice. Both sets have the minimum size and contain only nonunit entries. Transport preserves their strict code comparison and sending the competitor back and forth recovers it. Thus the transported choice has maximal code in the new list and equals the new choice by injectivity. If there is no maximum-order set in the first list, there is none in the second by reverse transport. Both choices are empty, and the transport of the empty set is empty.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxCandidateOrder_eq_of_orderedMatchingO: The minimum candidate sizes coincide under the matching. At this size the order supremum in the first list is at most the one in the second by candidate transport. Reversing the matching gives the reverse inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_preimage: All matching positions belong to the finite set before filtering. The filter keeps a position exactly when its first index belongs to the selected set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_transport: A second index lies in the transported set exactly when it is the image of a matching position retained by the filter. The filter retains exactly the positions whose first index belongs to the original set, giving the stated witness in both directions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_eq_of_orderedMatchingOfNonT: A positive size is realized by a candidate in the first list exactly when it is realized in the second. In one direction transport the candidate through the matching, and in the other use the reversed matching. Both constructions preserve size. The sets of possible positive sizes agree, so their infima agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_eq_of_sameNontrivialBoundar: The common list of nonunit entries gives an ordered matching of their indices. The minimum-size invariance for such a matching gives the equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenterSet_eq_of_orderedMatchingO: The two lists give the same minimum size and maximum candidate order. Their chosen index sets correspond by transport. Transport a component with the required order to the new chosen set, keeping the component and its order. Conversely, transporting back recovers the old index set because all its selected entries are nonunit. The two selections therefore give the same family of components, and their unions agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_eq_of_orderedMatchingOfNo: The matching preserves the minimum size, the union of selected components and the ideal of the intersection at the chosen indices. Thus the two center definitions have the same conditions of positive size and openness. If those conditions hold, both centers are the kernel for the same open in the same intersection. If the conditions fail, both centers are the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_eq_of_sameNontrivialBound: Use equality of the filtered boundaries to construct an ordered matching of all nonunit positions. The center ideal is invariant under that matching, giving the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonempty_orderedMatchingOfNonTop: The boundary relation asserts equality after removing unit entries. Apply the matching construction with the sum of the two lengths as its bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonempty_orderedMatchingOfNonTop_of_leng: Induct on the bound for the sum of the lengths. At zero both lists are empty and have the empty matching. When a list begins with the unit ideal, remove that entry. Its removal does not change the filtered list of nonunit ideals. The induction matching extends to the original lists by increasing all indices in the shortened list by one. If neither head is a unit, equality of the filtered lists forces both lists to be nonempty and the two heads to agree. Apply induction to their tails, then match the two heads and shift the remaining positions. An empty list against a nonunit head is excluded by equality of the filtered lists. In every extension the matched positions stay strictly increasing and cover all nonunit entries.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.openSublocusIdeal_congr: Identify the ideal sheaves and the ambient subsets using the given equalities. The intersection subschemes coincide, and the open preimages define the same open. Their inclusion morphisms and hence their kernels agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sameNontrivialBoundary_append: Filtering unit entries commutes with concatenation. The filtered lists for each pair of factors agree, so concatenating the first factors' filtered lists with the second factors' filtered lists gives equality for the two concatenations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sameNontrivialBoundary_refl: Removing the unit entries from either occurrence of the same list gives identical filtered lists, so the relation holds.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_top_eq_empty: The unit ideal has a unit stalk at every point. Its support therefore has no points.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.symm_symm: Reversing the matching exchanges its two index maps and reverses the equality of corresponding entries. Doing it twice restores both maps and their matching conditions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.transport_symm_transport: An index carried back and then forward comes from two occurrences of a common first-list position. The first index map is injective, so these occurrences correspond to the same matching position and recover the original second index. Conversely, every selected second index is nonunit and hence appears in the matching. Its matching position carries it back and then returns it to the selected set.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_depth: The rank field is filled with the smallest positive size of an index set supporting a candidate component, as given by the minimum-size function.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_indices: The selected position set is defined to be the index set obtained by maximizing the binary code among the candidates of the chosen size and order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_order: The order field is filled with the supremum of the orders of candidate components among index sets of the chosen minimum size.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_sortedIndices: The sorted list of an invariant is the sorted list of its position set. For this invariant that position set is the selected set of indices.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_sortedIndices: An entry of the sorted list is the natural-number value of a member of the original finite set. Sorting retains every member, so any such value also occurs in the list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sortedIndices_eq_map_sort: By definition, the list of indices is obtained by sorting the finite set in increasing order and then taking the natural-number value of each index.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentUnionIdeal_eq_openSubschemeKer: Both ideals are the kernel of the morphism obtained by including the chosen open into the intersection subscheme and then including the intersection into the ambient scheme. Their descriptions therefore agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hasStrictNormalCrossingsWith_componentUn: Let x lie in the support of the component union. Choose an ambient open around x whose inverse image in the intersection subscheme lies in the selected open and closed part. On this ambient open the union ideal and the intersection ideal agree. Intersect the open with an étale coordinate chart for the boundary around x. Every selected divisor meets x, since x lies in their intersection. Each is therefore given by a coordinate equation on the chart, and the coordinate indices are distinct by the normal-crossings assumption. The intersection ideal is the sum of these coordinate ideals, which defines their common coordinate subspace. The chart thus exhibits the union ideal and the boundary in strict normal-crossings position near x.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_componentUnionOpens: The union of selected components is closed in the ambient scheme. Its preimage under the continuous inclusion of the intersection subscheme is closed, and that preimage is the underlying set of the indicated open subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_sUnion_intersectionComponents: Admissibility ensures that the intersection has finitely many irreducible components. The selected family is a subset of this finite set, and every selected component is closed in the ambient scheme. Its union is a finite union of closed sets.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_componentUnionIdeal: The intersection subscheme of the selected boundary divisors is smooth over the base by the étale chart description. The chosen union defines an open and closed part of that intersection. The kernel of its inclusion into the ambient scheme defines the same part as a closed subscheme. Its map to the base is smooth by restriction to the open.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isPrime_between_notMem_of_mul_mem: Consider the multiplicative set of products of an element outside P and a nonnegative power of g. Primality of P makes this set multiplicatively closed. It is disjoint from I, since repeatedly cancelling g in such a product in I would put the outside factor in I and hence in P. Choose a prime Q containing I and avoiding this set. The set contains every element outside P, so Q lies inside P. It also contains g, so Q excludes g.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.false_of_restrictIdeal_eq_coordIdeal: On the affine chart let I be the ideal generated by the selected coordinates, and let g be the different coordinate defining the additional divisor. In the polynomial ring g acts injectively modulo the selected variables, and étale flatness preserves this injectivity after extending the ideal to the chart ring. The prime of the given point contains I. The prime-avoidance construction supplies a prime between I and that prime which omits g. It defines a generalization of the given point in the support of the first ideal and outside the other divisor, contradicting the hypothesis on all such generalizations.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionComponents_subset_support_if: If the divisor is selected, its ideal is a summand of the intersection ideal, so the intersection support and the component it contains lie in the support of the divisor. If it is unselected, containment would contradict the argument at the component's generic point using the extra boundary coordinate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_basicOpen_iff_notMem_asIdeal_primeId: Identify the affine open with the spectrum of its section ring. The point there is the corresponding prime and the given basic open pulls back to the basic open of the section in that spectrum. Membership in this basic open means that the section is outside the prime.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_map_of_mul_mem_of_etale_of_isSMulReg: Pass to the quotient of the target ring by the extended ideal. It is flat over the source quotient because the quotient map between the rings is obtained by base change of an étale map. Multiplication by the class of w is injective in the source quotient, and flatness preserves this injectivity in the target quotient. The given product vanishes there, so the class of x vanishes. Thus x belongs to the extended ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_mvPolynomialCoordIdeal_of_X_mul_mem: Set the variables in the chosen index set to zero and fix all other variables and coefficients. This endomorphism kills the coordinate ideal and induces the same quotient map as the identity. The distinguished variable is fixed because its index is outside the selected set. If its product with the polynomial belongs to the coordinate ideal, evaluating gives the product of this nonzero variable and the evaluated polynomial equal to zero. The polynomial ring over the field is a domain, so the evaluated polynomial is zero. Its original quotient class is therefore zero as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_of_mul_pow_mem: Induct on the exponent. For exponent zero the product is the initial element. For a successor exponent, rewrite the product as g times the product for the preceding exponent. Cancel one g using the ideal membership hypothesis and apply induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_iff_ideal_le_asIdeal_primeId: On an affine open, the support of the ideal sheaf is the common zero locus of the sections in its ideal. A section vanishes at the point precisely when the corresponding prime contains it. Applying this condition to every section of the ideal gives the claimed inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.not_subset_boundary_support_of_notMem: Suppose the component lies in the additional divisor. At its generic point choose an affine neighborhood in an étale boundary chart. The selected divisors containing the point give distinct chart coordinates, and their sum ideal is generated by those coordinates. The additional divisor also contains the point and has a different coordinate, since its index is outside the selected set. A generalization of the generic point inside the intersection support must remain in the component, because its closure is an irreducible subset containing the component and maximality gives equality. It would therefore lie in the additional divisor. The affine coordinate argument produces a generalization outside that divisor, a contradiction.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_biSup_finset: Induct on the finite index set. The empty sum is the zero ideal, and its pullback is zero. Inserting an index adds one ideal to the sum. Pullback preserves the sum of two ideals, so the induction formula for the smaller set extends to the larger one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordIdeal_eq_biSup_singleton: On affine space the coordinate-subspace ideal is the sum of the single-coordinate ideals. Pull it back along the étale chart. Pullback preserves the finite sum, and each summand pulls back to the corresponding chart ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordSubspaceIdeal_eq_biSup_singleton: Induct on the finite set. The empty coordinate subspace ideal is zero. Inserting a coordinate adds its principal ideal, so the induction formula gives the sum of the single-coordinate ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coordSubspaceIdeal_insert: The ideal of a coordinate subspace is generated by the coordinates in the selected index set. Inserting one index adds its principal coordinate ideal to the previous ideal. Passing from these global ideals on affine space to ideal sheaves preserves the sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ofIdealTop_sup: On any affine open, the ideal sheaf associated to a global ideal has sections given by extension along the restriction map. Extension of ideals preserves binary sums. The two ideal sheaves therefore have the same section ideals on all affine opens.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_boundary_eq_one: Take an étale chart giving the boundary equations near the point. Since the point lies in the specified divisor, the restricted divisor is defined by one chart coordinate. Restrict further to an affine chart neighborhood to use the coordinate order calculation. The vanishing coordinate has order one there, giving order one for the divisor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.restrictIdeal_biSup_finset: Restriction to the open is pullback along its inclusion. Apply preservation of finite sums under pullback.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_intersectionIdeal_subscheme: At a point in the support of the intersection ideal, every selected divisor contains the point, since its ideal is a summand of the intersection ideal. Choose an étale boundary chart there. Each selected divisor has a coordinate equation, and the restricted sum of their ideals is the chart ideal defined by all those coordinates. Thus near every point of its support the intersection subscheme is the étale inverse image of a coordinate subspace. Coordinate subspaces are smooth over the field, and the local description proves smoothness of the intersection.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_lt_krullDimSucc_of_mem_intersection: Choose a point of the given irreducible component. It lies in the support of the sum of the selected boundary ideals and hence in the support of each summand, since a unit summand would make the sum the unit ideal. Take an étale boundary chart at the point and an affine open inside it containing the point. Each selected divisor is defined there by a coordinate vanishing at the point, and distinct divisors have distinct coordinates. Thus the point's prime contains as many distinct chart coordinates as there are selected divisors. The coordinate dimension bound gives at least that many dimensions in the stalk. The stalk dimension bound then puts this cardinality strictly below the dimension successor of the ambient scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_lt_krullDimSucc_of_nonempty: Choose one component from the nonempty intersection-component set. The cardinality bound for a selected family admitting such a component applies to it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lt_krullDimSucc_of_le_ringKrullDim_stalk: The Krull dimension of the stalk is bounded by the topological Krull dimension of the scheme. The latter is at least the given natural number, so it cannot be the dimension of the empty space. By the finiteness assumption it is also below infinity. Write it as a natural number d. The given number is at most d and therefore strictly below d + 1, the dimension successor of the scheme.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentUnionIdeal_support_eq_sUnion: The composite inclusion of the chosen open part of the intersection into the ambient scheme has image the selected union, because the union is contained in the range of the intersection embedding. The composite is quasi-compact on the Noetherian schemes in question, so the support of its kernel is the closure of its image. The selected union is a finite union of closed components and hence already closed. This gives the claimed support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionComponents_disjoint_of_smoot: Lift both sets to irreducible components of the intersection subscheme. A point of their intersection would lift to points in both components. The embedding is injective, so these are the same point. Smoothness forces the two components through that point to agree, contrary to the distinct images.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionComponents_finite: The admissible ambient scheme is Noetherian, as is its closed intersection subscheme. The latter has finitely many irreducible components. Their images are exactly the members of the desired family, so that family is finite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.irreducibleComponents_eq_of_inter_nonemp: Choose a point common to the two components. Smoothness over the base field gives a regular local ring at the point, hence a domain. A domain has a unique minimal prime, so the two irreducible components through the point coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_of_mem_intersectionComponents: Take the irreducible component of the intersection subscheme whose image is the given set. Irreducible components are closed in their spaces, and the closed embedding of the subscheme sends closed sets to closed sets in the ambient scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_preimage_sUnion_intersectionCompo: By the component correspondence and injectivity of the embedding, the inverse image is the union of precisely the irreducible components whose images were selected. In the Noetherian intersection subscheme there are finitely many irreducible components, each closed, and smoothness makes them pairwise disjoint. The complement is the finite union of the unselected components, hence is closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maximal_irreducible_subset_range_iff: The closed embedding identifies its source with its image. For a maximal irreducible subset of the image, the inverse image is irreducible. A larger irreducible subset of the source would map to a larger irreducible subset of the image, which maximality excludes. Conversely, the image of an irreducible component is irreducible. Any irreducible extension of it inside the image has an irreducible inverse image containing the component and so equals it. Taking images proves maximality in the range.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_intersectionComponents_iff_exists_ir: The intersection subscheme embeds as a closed subset whose range is the support of the intersection ideal. Maximal irreducible subsets of this range correspond to irreducible components of the intersection subscheme under the embedding.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_irreducibleComponents_iff_isIrreduci: An irreducible component is a maximal irreducible subset. In terms of inclusion, maximality requires that any irreducible set containing the given subset be contained in it as well. These are exactly the two conditions on the right.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsIrreducibleComponentOf.closure_image_g: Take the closure of the image of the upper generic point. It is irreducible, lies in the closed target set, and contains the image of the upper component by continuity. Suppose it is contained in a larger irreducible subset of the target set. A generic point of the larger subset's closure generalizes the image of the upper generic point. Lift this generalization upstairs using the generalizing property. Its closure lies in the inverse image of the target set and contains the upper component, so it equals that component by maximality. The image of the lift then belongs to the original image closure. Thus the larger subset is contained in that closure, proving maximality downstairs.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsIrreducibleComponentOf.exists_isGeneri: The closure of the component is irreducible and stays in the given closed set. Maximality therefore makes the closure equal to the component. An irreducible closed subset of a scheme has a generic point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comapSubschemeHom_comp_subschemeι: The square of the two closed subschemes over the ambient morphism is a pullback and therefore commutes. The two routes to the original ambient scheme are the stated composites.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_biSup_finset_fin: Pullback of ideal sheaves is left adjoint to the corresponding map on ideals and therefore preserves suprema. The finite sum is such a supremum, so it pulls back to the sum of the pulled-back terms.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_componentUnionIdeal_of_flat: The union of upper components mapping into selected lower components lies in the inverse image of the selected union. For the reverse inclusion, start with an upper point mapping to a selected lower component. Flatness lifts it into an upper component whose generic point maps to the generic point of the selected component. This upper component maps into a lower component with that same generic point, so its image lies in the selected component. The two unions therefore have the required inverse-image relation. The intersection ideal also pulls back, since it is a sum of selected boundary ideals. The inclusion of the selected open into the lower intersection and then the ambient scheme is quasi-compact by Noetherianity. Apply flat base change to its kernel and the two inverse-image descriptions. This gives the upper open and identifies its component-union ideal with the pulled-back ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_intersectionComponents_mapsTo_of_: The support of the new intersection is the inverse image of the closed original intersection support. The upper component has a generic point there. Flatness makes the underlying map generalizing, so the closure of the image of that point is a component of the original support and contains the upper component's image. The image point is generic in this closure, and the generic point of each component is unique.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isIrreducibleComponentOf: Order the irreducible subsets of the specified set by inclusion, starting with the given irreducible subset. A nonempty chain has an upper bound given by its union. The union is nonempty, stays in the set, and is preirreducible by the chain property. The supplied initial subset handles the empty chain. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal irreducible set containing the initial one, which is a component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isIrreducibleComponentOf_preimage: Choose the generic point of the given downstairs component. It generalizes the image of the specified upper point, so lift it to a generalization of that upper point. The closure of the lift lies in the preimage of the closed set. Choose a component containing this closure and thus the specified point. The image closure of a generic point of the chosen upper component is a downstairs component and contains the original downstairs generic point, since the lift lies in the upper component. By maximality it equals the given downstairs component. The upper component maps into it and its generic point maps to the downstairs generic point by uniqueness.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isOpen_comap_ker_of_flat: Replace the new ideal and the new set by their given pullback descriptions. The square of closed subschemes commutes, so the part over the inverse image of the ambient set is the inverse image of the original open part under the comparison of closed subschemes. It is open by continuity. Base change of that open immersion, pasted with the closed-subscheme square, gives the pullback square for the composite inclusion into the ambient scheme. This inclusion is quasi-compact by base change of the original inclusion. Flat base change then identifies the kernel of the new composite with the pullback of the original kernel.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isPullback_comapSubscheme: The closed subscheme defined by the pulled-back ideal is canonically isomorphic to the scheme pullback of the original inclusion. Its map to the original subscheme is the isomorphism followed by the corresponding pullback projection. The other projection is the inclusion of the new subscheme. These are the arrows of the pullback square.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_intersectionComponents_pullba: Flatness gives a generalizing map. View the given downstairs component as a component of the closed original intersection support. The component-lifting result gives a component of its inverse-image support containing the specified upper point and carrying its generic point to the downstairs one. The inverse-image support is exactly that of the pulled-back intersection ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionIdeal_pullbackOverField: Both intersection ideals are sums over their selected boundary positions. Pullback preserves this sum. Every new selected index is the image of an old selected index and carries the pullback of that old ideal. Conversely, each old selected index contributes its corresponding new entry. Thus the sums agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPreirreducible_sUnion_of_isChain: Suppose two opens meet the union. Choose a point of each intersection and a member of the chain containing that point. The larger of the two members contains both points, so each open meets it. Preirreducibility of that member gives a point of the intersection of the opens in the union.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullback_comapSubschemeHom: The comparison morphism is chosen from the existence of a map that makes the square of closed subschemes a pullback. It therefore has the required pullback property.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_intersectionComponents_pullbackOverF: A member of the intersection-component family is a maximal irreducible subset of the support of the intersection ideal. For the new boundary this support is the inverse image of the old intersection support, giving the equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_boundary_get: The pulled-back boundary is obtained by applying pullback to each entry of the original list. The corresponding index has the same numeric position, so its entry is the pullback of the old entry.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.quasiCompact_comp_of_noetherianSpace: The composite of the open immersion and the closed immersion is a topological embedding, so the source is a subspace of the Noetherian target and is itself Noetherian. Every subset of the source is quasi-compact, in particular the inverse image of each quasi-compact open of the target. The composite is therefore quasi-compact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_intersectionIdeal_pullbackOverFi: The ideal of the pulled-back intersection is the pullback of the original intersection ideal. The support of a pulled-back ideal is the set-theoretic inverse image of the original support.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.binaryEncode_eq_sum_image: The code sums powers of two with exponents obtained by reversing the selected indices. The reversal map is injective, so every exponent occurs once when the sum is reindexed over the image.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.binaryEncode_injective: Write each code as a sum of distinct powers of two over the set of reversed indices. If the exponent sets differed, the largest exponent in their symmetric difference would give unequal sums, so equal codes imply equal exponent sets. Injectivity of index reversal then gives equality of the original sets.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.binaryEncode_lt_iff: When comparing two sums of distinct powers of two, the highest exponent present on just one side decides the order. Its term exceeds the sum of all lower powers. Thus the code of J is larger exactly when an exponent from J alone exceeds every exponent from J′ alone. Reversing the indices converts this into an index of J alone smaller than every index of J′ alone. The same argument in reverse proves sufficiency.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.binaryEncode_lt_iff_lex_of_card_eq: Sort the two sets into increasing lists. Equal cardinality gives equal list length. The reversed binary-code criterion says that an entry of the first list alone is smaller than every entry of the second alone. For increasing lists of equal length this is exactly lexicographic precedence. Taking natural-number values preserves and reflects that comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lex_iff_exists_min_mem: Compare the heads of the two increasing lists of equal length. If the first head is smaller, it is absent from the other list and is smaller than each of its entries, so it witnesses the set condition. If the second head is smaller, that head is absent from the first list and prevents any entry of the first from witnessing the condition. If the heads agree, they occur in both lists, and all tail entries are strictly greater than the common head. The comparison and the set condition both reduce to the tails. Two empty lists satisfy neither strict condition, which completes the induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lex_map_iff_of_strictMono: Compare the lists recursively. The comparison with an empty list depends only on which lists are empty, which the map preserves. For two nonempty lists, a strict comparison of their heads is preserved and reflected by strict monotonicity, and equality of their mapped heads is equivalent to equality of their heads by injectivity. In the equal-head case apply the induction statement to the tails.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lex_sortedIndices_image_iff: The sorted index lists of the images are obtained by applying the increasing index map and then taking natural-number values. Both this composite and the original natural-number value map are strictly increasing. Lexicographic comparison for either pair is therefore equivalent to comparison of the original sorted lists.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.reversedIndex_injective: The two indices lie between zero and n − 1. If their differences from n − 1 agree, adding back these indices shows that their natural-number values agree. The indices are therefore equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.reversedIndex_lt_reversedIndex_iff: Both indices are at most n − 1, so subtracting either from n − 1 uses ordinary nonnegative differences. Subtracting from the same bound reverses the strict comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sort_image_of_strictMono: A strictly increasing map carries the sorted list to a strictly increasing list. This mapped list and the sorted image have the same entries, since an element of the image comes from an element of the original set and conversely. A strictly increasing finite list is determined by its set of entries, so the lists coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sortedIndices_image_of_strictMono: Sorting the image gives the same list as sorting the original indices and mapping the strictly increasing function over them. Taking each resulting index's natural-number value gives the stated list.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_orderAt_le: The stalk ideals are nonzero, so the order at each point is finite. The loci where the order is at least a given natural number are closed under the admissibility hypotheses. They form a decreasing family with empty intersection, since no finite order exceeds every natural number. The scheme is quasi-compact because its structural morphism is quasi-compact and the base is the spectrum of a field. Finitely many of these closed loci already have empty intersection. At the largest of the chosen thresholds, taking zero if the family is empty, the order is bounded above by that threshold everywhere.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyNoetherian_of_isAdmissible: The base is a field, hence Noetherian, and the structural morphism of an admissible object is locally of finite type. Thus the section ring of any affine open in the scheme is Noetherian, which is the required local property.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_setOf_stalkIdeal_eq_bot: At a point where the stalk ideal is zero, choose an affine neighborhood. Its ring is Noetherian, so the section ideal has finitely many generators. Each generator has zero germ and therefore restricts to zero on some smaller open neighborhood of the point. Intersect those finitely many neighborhoods. At every point of the intersection all generator germs vanish, and they generate the stalk ideal. The vanishing locus of the stalk ideal is therefore open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_ne_bot_of_isAdmissible_of_non: Suppose the stalk ideal vanishes at x. Its vanishing locus is open by local Noetherianity. Choose an irreducible component through x. Since the ideal is nonzero on components, this component also meets the open complement of the support. The two nonempty opens of the component have a common point by irreducibility. There the stalk ideal is both zero and the unit ideal, which is impossible in a local ring of a scheme point.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyMonomialPrincipalization_monomi: Use the monomial principalization theorem for the center, invariant, local monomiality, resolution and empty-locus properties. The flat comparison for a field extension gives the field-base-change property, and the smooth comparison theorem gives compatibility with smooth pullback. For a surjective comparison map these comparisons are strict because each lower blowup center has nonempty support. Field extension supplies a surjective projection, and surjectivity is assumed in the strict smooth comparison. These are the required properties for every permitted marking.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPullbackBlowupSequence_monomialPrincip: The projection from the extension of the base field is flat, by base change of the flat map between spectra of fields. The assumed order invariance for field extension supplies the pointwise preservation of order on each compatible pullback square required by the flat pullback theorem. The given relation between the pulled-back and replacement boundaries can be read in either direction. Apply the flat pullback theorem to these data to obtain the comparison of the two principalizations.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.appendProjectionToBase_of_lt: Beyond the first length, the projection first identifies the stage with the second sequence's stage at the difference of the indices. It then goes to the base of that sequence and through the last projection of the first. The difference is the given second index, giving the claimed composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.append_center_eq_appendToBlowupSequenceD: The marked append uses the center ideals of its appended underlying blowup data. Thus at any index its center agrees with the underlying center.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_boundary_of_le: The admissible step is an append. At a stage up to the old length, the boundary formula for appends takes the original boundary and pulls each ideal back along the stage identification. This gives the stated list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_boundary_succ: For an admissible center the new sequence is the append of the monomial step. Its new last boundary is the strict transforms of the old last boundary with the exceptional ideal added, transported along the new scheme identification by the boundary formula for an append.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_center_of_eq_length: At the old last index, the append takes the initial center of the single step. This center is formed by pulling back through the inverse initial isomorphism of that step and through the identification of the joining scheme. The inverse initial isomorphism itself is the identification with the zero stage. Combining the two identifications gives the supplied equality of schemes. The initial center of the single step is the old last center, yielding the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_center_of_lt: If a new blowup is appended, every center strictly before the old length belongs to the first part of the append. Its ideal is the former center pulled back along the identification of the stages. If the center is inadmissible, the sequence is unchanged and the identification pullback is the identity. The formula holds in either case.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_eq_append: The last center is admissible, so the operation chooses the branch appending a single blowup at that center. The appended sequence is the given monomial step.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_ideal_succ: At the new last stage, the ideal of the append is the ideal at offset one of the single step, pulled back along the equality of the stage schemes. The single-step calculation identifies that ideal as the controlled transform by the exceptional power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_length: The operation appends the single-step sequence when the center is admissible. The length of an append is the sum of the lengths, so the new length is the old length plus one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_projectionToBase_succ: Use the appended projection formula with offset one in the single step. Its projection to the joining scheme is the blowup projection. The projection to the original base is therefore the stage identification followed by the blowup projection and the original last projection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_schemeAt_of_le: If the center is admissible, the operation appends a single step and the stages up to the old length continue to use the original schemes. If the center is inadmissible, the operation returns the sequence itself. Both cases give the stated equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_schemeAt_succ: The index one greater than the original length belongs to the appended part with offset one. At that offset the single-step scheme is the blowup of the original last scheme along its last center.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.boundary_eq_map_comap_of_index_eq: Use the equality of indices to replace the index on the second sequence with the specified index on the first. The boundary formula at that common index then applies with the given scheme identification.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.boundary_succ_of_eq_append: Replace the given sequence by its description as the append. The boundary one stage beyond the old length is obtained by transporting the boundary at offset one of the single step along the specified stage identification. At offset one that boundary consists of the strict transforms followed by the exceptional ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.center_monomialBlowupIterate_blowupAtCen: The first added blowup increases the length to the given index plus one. At the given index its center is the former last center under the joining identification. Further iterations preserve all centers strictly within this new length, transporting them by their stage identifications. Composing with the join identification gives the stated pullback.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_eqToHom_comap_eqToHom_symm: The two identification morphisms come from opposite equalities of schemes and are inverse. The successive pullbacks therefore compose to pullback along the identity, giving the original ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_eqToHom_comp: The changes of scheme identification along the two equalities compose to the change along their combined equality. By functoriality the two successive pullbacks equal the single pullback along that composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_eqToHom_self: An equality of the scheme with itself induces the identity morphism. Pullback of the ideal along that morphism leaves it unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_eq_comap_of_isPrefix: Identify the index with the length of the prefix. The prefix relation expresses its ideal at that stage as the pullback of the longer sequence's ideal under the prefix identification. Pull back along the inverse identification. The two transports cancel, yielding the given ideal on the longer sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isAdmissibleCenter_of_lt_monomialStallIn: If this center were inadmissible, its index would be stationary. The infimum of the stationary indices would then be at most that index, contradicting the strict inequality with the defined stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrefix_monomialBlowupIterate_of_le: Induct on the later index. At equality the iterate is its own prefix. If the earlier index is strictly below a successor, apply induction to the predecessor, then use the consecutive prefix relation and transitivity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isPrefix_monomialBlowupIterate_succ: If the current center is admissible, the next iterate is formed by appending its single blowup, so the current sequence is its prefix. Otherwise the next iterate equals the current one, which is a prefix of itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isStationaryAt_iff_not_isAdmissibleCente: If the current center were admissible, the successor would have one more blowup and the two lengths could not agree. Conversely, an inadmissible center makes the step return the current sequence, so the lengths agree. This is precisely stationarity at the given index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isStationaryAt_monomialStallIndex: The stationary indices form a nonempty set of natural numbers by hypothesis. Its infimum is its least member, so the defined stationary index is stationary.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.length_le_blowupAtCenter_length: The operation appends one blowup if the center is admissible and otherwise returns the original sequence. The length either increases by one or stays equal, giving the inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_comap_eqToHom_comp: For each list entry, the two successive ideal pullbacks along the scheme identifications equal pullback along the combined identification. Applying this equality at every position gives equality of the lists.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_comap_eqToHom_self: Every boundary entry pulls back to itself along the identity induced by the equality. Therefore the mapped list equals the original list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_add: Induct on the second iteration count. A zero second count returns the first iterate. For a successor, both expressions apply the same center step to the preceding expression, and those preceding expressions are equal by induction and associativity of addition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_boundary_of_le: Induct on the number of further steps. With zero steps the identification is the identity. In a successor, the earlier stage is still within the preceding sequence because its length has grown. The latest admissible step transports the preceding boundary, and induction identifies that preceding boundary with the transported original boundary. Combining the two identification morphisms gives the stated direct pullback of each original entry.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_center_of_lt: Induct on the number of further iterations. At zero the center is the original one under an identity pullback. At a successor, the earlier index stays strictly within the preceding length by its lower bound. The one-step center formula identifies it with the transported preceding center, and induction identifies that center with the transported original one. Compose the two pullbacks along the identifications.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_length: Induct on the number of iterations. At zero the sequence is the initial one. At a successor all earlier centers satisfy the induction hypothesis, and the current admissible center appends exactly one blowup. This increases both the actual length and the formula by one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_length_le_and_sche: At zero both claims are immediate from the initial sequence. Induct on the number of steps. The next step does not reduce the length, so it preserves the lower bound. Each original index still lies within the preceding sequence by that bound. Its scheme survives the new step and agrees with the original scheme by induction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_boundary: The iterate at the given index has length equal to that index. Express the full sequence as this iterate followed by the remaining iterations to the first stationary index. Each remaining step before that index has an admissible center, so iteration preserves the earlier boundary under the stage identification. At the given index that boundary is the earlier iterate's last boundary, giving the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_center: Before the first stationary index the iterate at the chosen index has length equal to that index and an admissible last center. Split the full iteration into that iterate, its next blowup and the remaining steps. The next blowup uses the last center of the iterate, and the remaining steps preserve it by the earlier-center formula. Transporting it to the stage of the complete sequence gives the claim.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_eq_monomialBlowupItera: The monomial sequence is defined by iterating from the empty sequence for the infimum of its stationary indices. That number is the stated stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_eq_monomialIterateUnti: Start with the empty marked sequence. The monomial sequence and the construction that iterates until stationarity both run it for the infimum of the same set of stationary indices.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_ideal: The iterate at the chosen index has that index as its length because every earlier center is admissible. It is a prefix of the full iteration to the stationary index. The ideal formula for a prefix therefore identifies the full sequence's ideal at that index with the transported last ideal of the chosen iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_length: Before the first stationary index every center is admissible. Apply the iteration length formula from the empty sequence through that index. The initial length is zero, so the resulting length equals the stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupSeq_schemeAt: Up to the given index, every step before it has an admissible center, so its iterate from the empty sequence has length equal to the index. Split the iteration to the stationary index into this iterate and the remaining iterations. Later iterations preserve all its stages. Thus the given stage in the full sequence is the last scheme of that earlier iterate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_blowupMorphism_zero: The first step is the blowup along the last center. Its morphism is the projection from this blowup to the scheme carrying the center.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_boundary_one: The boundary rule for a single blowup replaces each old divisor by its strict transform in the same order and adds the exceptional ideal at the end. The old boundary here is the last boundary of the input sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_center_zero: The center used to form the single blowup is the given last center. It is the center at index zero of the single-step sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_ideal_one: The marked ideal at stage one is the controlled transform under the single blowup. Pull back the last ideal and remove the mark-th power of the exceptional ideal, which is the pullback of the center. The residual ideal is the stated stage-one ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_isoObjZero_inv: The single step's initial scheme is the old last scheme by construction. Its inverse initial isomorphism is exactly the morphism given by this identification in the indicated direction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_length: The monomial step is constructed as the single blowup at the admissible last center. The single-blowup sequence has one step.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_projectionToBase_one: The projection from stage one to the base of the single step is the blowup projection followed by the initial identification. That identification is the identity on the last scheme of the old sequence, leaving the blowup projection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_schemeAt_succ: In the single-step data each positive index uses the scheme of the blowup. This blowup is along the last center of the input sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupStep_schemeAt_zero: The single-step sequence starts on the last scheme of the input sequence. Its zero stage is therefore that scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialIterateUntilStall_eq_monomialBlo: Iteration until stationarity is defined as iteration for the stationary index of the supplied sequence. This is the expression on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialStallIndex_eq_monomialStallIndex: Both expressions take the infimum of stationary indices for the iteration whose initial sequence is empty. They therefore agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialStallIndex_eq_of_isStationaryAt: The given index is stationary, so the least stationary index is at most it. The least stationary index is itself stationary, because the set is nonempty. If it were smaller, the assumption on earlier centers would make its center admissible, contradicting stationarity. The indices are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialStallIndex_eq_sInf: The stationary index of a sequence is defined as the infimum of the indices where the next step leaves its length unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialStallIndex_eq_zero_of_not_isAdmi: With an inadmissible initial center, the sequence is stationary at iteration zero. Its stationary index is the infimum of a set of natural numbers containing zero, so that infimum is zero.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.blowupAtCenter_eq_self_of_not_isAdmissib: The step appends a blowup only when the last center is admissible. In the other branch it returns the existing sequence. The given hypothesis selects that branch.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerAtLast_eq_monomialCenter: The last center is obtained by applying the monomial center construction to the last ideal, the original mark and the last boundary. This gives the stated formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_le_comap_eqToHom: Identify the two pairs of schemes by their equalities. Both pullback maps are then identities and preserve the ideal and the boundary on each side. Thus the invariant comparison is exactly the given one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_le_of_lt: The weak comparison includes the strict comparison as its first case. The hypothesis provides that case.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_eqToHom_refl: The identification of a scheme with itself is the identity morphism. Pullback of the ideal along the identity gives the same ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isStationaryAt_emptyMarkedBlowupS: Suppose that no iteration is stationary. Then every last center is admissible and every last triple has positive minimum candidate size. The triples remain locally monomial, and each one is obtained from the preceding triple by blowing up its monomial center. Their dimension successors are bounded by that of the original scheme, by induction using the dimension bound for one blowup. With this fixed dimension bound the monomial invariant strictly decreases at every step, since the successor minimum is also positive. The invariant takes values in a well-founded lexicographic order on triples of natural numbers. An infinite strictly decreasing sequence there is impossible, proving existence of a stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isAdmissibleCenter_of_minIndexCard_tripl: Apply the specification of the monomial center to the locally monomial last-stage triple and its positive minimum size. It gives a proper smooth center with strict normal crossings lying in the cosupport, and it gives a controlled transform. These are the admissibility conditions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyMonomialTriple_tripleAtLastBlow: If the center is admissible, one blowup is appended. The formulas for its final scheme, projection, ideal and boundary identify its last-stage triple with the blowup of the former last-stage triple at its monomial center. The former minimum size is positive, so the monomial blowup theorem preserves local monomiality and admissibility. If the center is inadmissible, the sequence remains the same and the given property applies directly.

Induct on the iteration number. At zero the sequence is empty, and its final scheme, ideal and boundary are the original ones, with identity projection. Thus the final triple is the original locally monomial triple. The rule for a succeeding iteration takes one center step, and local monomiality survives that step by the preceding result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialCasePrincipalization_monomialP: Use the stage results for containment of the centers in the boundary locus, the corresponding certificates and equality of each center with the monomial center. They also give positive minimum size before the final stage, the successive invariant comparison, local monomiality on every cosupport and nonempty center supports. The final cosupport is empty, so the sequence resolves the triple, and an initially empty cosupport gives length zero. Together these are the required properties of monomial-case principalization.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialNear_comap_eqToHom: Identify the two schemes by their equality. The ideal and boundary pullbacks are then the originals. The given point lies in the original cosupport, so the assumed local monomial expression applies there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_comap_eqToHom_refl: The identification morphism is the identity. Pulling back each listed ideal leaves it unchanged, so the entire list is unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.markedIdealWithBoundary_mk_comap_eqToHom: Identify the two underlying schemes using their equality. The identification morphism then becomes the identity, so composing the structural morphism and pulling back the ideal and boundary along it leaves the data unchanged. The base field and mark already agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_comap_eqToHom: After identifying the schemes by their equality, the pullback morphism is the identity. It preserves every ideal in the calculation and every position of the boundary. Thus the minimum size is unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_monomialIterateFromEmpty_ne: Every iterate strictly before the first stationary index has an admissible center. Such a center is proper, which forces positive minimum candidate size in its last-stage triple.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_monomialIterateFromEmpty_st: A stationary index exists, so the first stationary index is stationary and its center is inadmissible. The last-stage triple at that iterate remains locally monomial. If its minimum size were positive, the center specification for such a triple would make its last center admissible. Hence the minimum is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_tripleAtLastBlowup_ne_zero_: At minimum size zero the monomial center is the unit ideal. The last center is the monomial center of the last-stage triple, and admissibility requires a proper ideal. Hence the minimum size cannot be zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_comap_eqToHom: Identify the two schemes using their equality. Pullback along the identification becomes pullback along the identity, which leaves the ideal, the boundary and the resulting center unchanged. The two expressions coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_centerInvariant: Both consecutive stages precede the first stationary index. The earlier iterate has an admissible center and a locally monomial last triple, and its successor is the blowup of that triple at its monomial center. The one-step comparison gives either zero minimum size at the successor or a strict comparison of the center invariants in the stated direction. The successor minimum is positive, so the strict comparison holds and implies the weak one. Finally, the ideal and boundary of each principalization stage are transported from the corresponding iterate. These identifications preserve the comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_center_eq_monom: The stage precedes the first stationary index. Its center agrees with the last center of the corresponding iterate under the stage identification, and its ideal and boundary come from the same iterate under the same identification. The last center is the monomial center calculated from that ideal and boundary. The construction commutes with transport along the identification, giving the formula on the principalization stage.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_center_subset_b: Identify the principalization stage with the last stage of its corresponding iterate. The principalization center and boundary are the last center and boundary of the iterate transported along this identification. Any point of the transported center support maps into the original center support, and hence into a listed boundary support. The corresponding transported boundary ideal has the original point in its support, which places it in the boundary locus.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_center_support_: The stage occurs before the first stationary index. Its corresponding iterate is locally monomial and has positive minimum candidate size, so the selected center set is nonempty and equals the support of its monomial center. The principalization uses this center transported along the identification of the stage schemes. This transport preserves nonempty support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_isMonomialNear: Every reconstructed stage up to the length is identified with the last stage of the corresponding iterate. Its ideal and boundary are obtained by transport along that identification. The iterate's last triple is locally monomial, giving a monomial expression around each point of its cosupport. The identification transports the expression to each point of the principalization stage's cosupport.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_isResolution: At the first stationary index the final triple is locally monomial and has minimum size zero. The zero-minimum result then gives empty cosupport for its ideal. Reconstruction keeps that final ideal, and empty final cosupport is the criterion for the marked sequence to resolve the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_length: The principalization reconstructs the marked sequence at the first stationary iterate. Reconstruction preserves length, and the iteration starting with the empty sequence has one blowup for each index before the first stationary one. Its length is therefore the stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_length_eq_zero_: An empty cosupport gives minimum candidate size zero. The last triple of the empty sequence is the original triple. An admissible center for that sequence would have positive minimum size, so the empty sequence is stationary already at zero. The principalization length equals this first stationary index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_minIndexCard_ne: A stage before the length occurs before the first stationary index. The last triple of the corresponding iterate therefore has a positive minimum size. The ideal and boundary in the reconstructed stage are obtained by pulling back those of the iterate along the stage identification, which preserves the minimum size.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_principalizatio: Every center support is contained in the boundary locus at its stage. The boundary-memory form of the principalization certificate takes exactly this containment, giving the required certificate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_centerAtLast_subset_iUnion_bound: The iterate before the stationary index is locally monomial with a positive minimum size. Its last center is the monomial center of its last triple, whose support lies in the union of the boundary supports by the center specification.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_comap_eqToHom_nonempty: After using the equality to identify the two schemes, the pullback morphism is the identity. Any point in the original support then belongs to the pulled-back support, proving nonemptiness.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_baseField: The construction of the last-stage triple keeps the base field of the original marked ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_blowupAtCenter: An admissible center increases the length by one. At that new index the scheme is the blowup at the former monomial center, the ideal is its controlled transform, and the boundary consists of the strict transforms and the new exceptional ideal. The projection is the new blowup projection followed by the old last projection. These formulas give the structural map, ideal and boundary of the blown-up triple under the scheme identification. Transport along the identification gives equality of the triples.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_boundary: The boundary of the last-stage triple is the list of boundary ideals at the last stage of the sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_eq_mk_of_length_eq: Replace the length of the sequence by the equal given index. Each last-stage field is then the corresponding scheme, projection, ideal or boundary at that index, with the original field and mark.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_ideal: The construction uses the transformed ideal at the last stage as the ideal of the triple.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_mult: The last-stage triple uses the same mark as the original triple, as in the definition of a marked transform.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_scheme: The last-stage triple is defined on the scheme at the last index of the blowup sequence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.tripleAtLastBlowup_structureMorphism: The structural map of the last-stage triple is defined by projecting the last stage to the original scheme and then using its structural map to the base field.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_eq_minIndexCard_of_isMaxOrderIndexS: A maximizing selection has a candidate witness at the minimum size. The candidate size condition says that the selection has exactly that cardinality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.card_lexMaxIndices: At positive minimum size, the index-selection result says that the chosen selection has maximum order. Every maximum-order selection has minimum candidate size, so the chosen one has that cardinality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerComponents_subset_intersectionComp: A member of the center family is a candidate for the chosen index set. The candidate condition places it among the components of the intersection for that set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_controlledTransform_monomialCente: The center has strict normal crossings with the boundary, and its support lies where the original ideal has order at least the mark. The power containment theorem puts the original ideal inside the center ideal raised to that mark. After blowing up the center, the pulled-back center ideal is the exceptional ideal. The controlled transform exists by the blowup factorization theorem for this containment, giving the required product with the exceptional power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isCandidateComponent_minIndexCard: A nonzero minimum means that the set of positive candidate sizes is nonempty. The minimum-size specification gives a selection and component that attain it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isIrreducibleComponentOf_mem: Work in the subspace of the specified set. The singleton of the given point is preirreducible, so it is contained in a maximal preirreducible subset of the subspace. That subset is nonempty and hence irreducible. Its image under the subspace inclusion is irreducible in the ambient scheme and contains the given point. Any larger irreducible subset inside the specified set would give a larger preirreducible subset in the subspace, contradicting maximality. Thus the image is an irreducible component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isMaxOrderIndexSet: Take a candidate at the minimum size whose component attains the maximum order. Its chosen index set has the required witness for maximum order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_intersectionComponents_of_mem: Apply the existence of a component through a point to the support of the intersection ideal. Being an irreducible component of this support is the membership condition for the intersection-component family.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.finite_maxOrderCandidatePairs: A maximum-order pair is still one of the candidate pairs, witnessed by the minimum size. All candidate pairs form a finite set, so the subset of maximum-order pairs is finite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.finite_setOf_isCandidateComponent: There are finitely many subsets of the finite boundary index set. For each subset its intersection has finitely many components by admissibility and the geometry hypotheses. All candidate pairs lie in the finite union of these pairs of a subset with one of its components. The candidate set is therefore finite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.genericPoint_mem_support_iff_mem: A closed boundary support contains the generic point exactly when it contains the generic point's entire closure, which is the given component. The component containment criterion identifies this with membership of the divisor index in the chosen set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hasStrictNormalCrossingsWith_monomialCen: Identify the center ideal with the ideal of the selected component union. The normal-crossings property for these component-union ideals gives strict normal crossings with the given boundary.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.indicator_one_eq_one_of_mem: On the set the indicator retains the value of the underlying constant function, which is 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.indicator_one_eq_zero_of_notMem: The indicator of the constant function 1 takes value zero outside the set. The point is outside by hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isClosed_intersectionComponents_of_mem: The closure of the component is irreducible and lies in the closed support of the intersection ideal. It contains the component, so maximality makes it equal to the component. The component is therefore closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isGenericPoint_genericPoint_of_mem_inter: The chosen point for the irreducible set has singleton closure equal to the closure of the set. The intersection component is already closed, so this singleton closure is the component itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isIrreducible_of_mem_intersectionCompone: An intersection component is a maximal irreducible subset of the intersection support. Irreducibility is part of this condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_preimage_monomialCenterSet: Replace the center set by the union of its selected components. The inverse image of this union is open in the chosen intersection subscheme by the component-union result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isOpen_preimage_sUnion_centerComponents: The center family consists of components of the chosen intersection. The geometry hypotheses make the preimage of the union of any such family open in that intersection subscheme. Apply this to the center family.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lexMaxIndices_spec: The family of maximum-order selections is nonempty. Their codes form a finite set of natural numbers, so its supremum is attained. The chosen selection attains that code and thus is of maximum order. All maximum-order selections have the same cardinality. If another one had a lexicographically smaller increasing index list, the reversed binary encoding would give it a larger code than the chosen one. This contradicts maximality of the chosen code, proving the stated lexicographic property.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lt_top_of_le_natCast: The bound is a natural number and hence is strictly below infinity in the extended natural numbers. Anything at most that bound is also strictly below infinity.
