Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxBinaryCode_eq_sSup: The maximum code is defined as the supremum of the binary codes of selections admitting a component of maximum candidate order. This is the stated set of codes.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxCandidateOrder_eq_iSup_orderAlong: The maximum-order expression is defined as the supremum of the orders of components whose selected indices make them candidates at the minimum size. Indexing the supremum by the selection, component and candidate condition gives the stated formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxCandidateOrder_spec: Positive minimum size gives at least one candidate at that size. There are finitely many candidate pairs, so the orders of the pairs at the minimum size attain a maximum. This maximum is the defined supremum since it occurs among the terms and bounds all terms. The attaining component has order at least the mark by candidacy and has finite order by the order bound. These facts give the existence, upper bound and two bounds on the maximum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_centerComponents_iff: The center family consists of those components that are candidates at the minimum size for the chosen index set and whose orders attain the maximum. Membership is exactly these two conditions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_intersectionComponents_of_isCandidat: A candidate meets three requirements, including that its component belongs to the intersection-component family for the selected boundary indices. Apply this condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_maxOrderCandidatePairs_iff: The family is defined by the condition that the pair is a candidate at the minimum size and that its component order equals the maximum. This is exactly the right-hand condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_supportIndices: The index set is obtained by filtering the boundary positions for membership of the given point in the corresponding support. This is exactly the stated condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_bot: The zero ideal sheaf has zero stalk at every point. That stalk is contained in the maximal ideal, so the point belongs to the support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_finsetSup_of_forall_mem: Induct on the finite selection. The zero ideal from the empty sum has full support. When one ideal is added, the point belongs to its support by hypothesis and to the support of the smaller sum by induction. It then belongs to the support of their sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_intersectionIdeal: The intersection ideal is the finite sum of the selected boundary ideals. At the specified point each summand has stalk contained in the maximal ideal, so the sum does as well. This is membership in the intersection support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_support_sup_of_mem: Both stalk ideals lie inside the maximal ideal. The stalk of their sum is the sum of the stalk ideals, which is contained in the maximal ideal as well. This gives membership in the support of the sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_eq_sInf: The minimum selection size is defined as the infimum of the positive natural numbers for which a set of that cardinality and a candidate component exist. This is the stated infimum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_eq_zero_iff: Every size in the defining set is positive. If the set is nonempty, the infimum is an element and is positive. If the set is empty, its natural-number infimum is zero. Thus zero occurs precisely when there is no candidate of positive size.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_eq_zero_of_orderAtLeastLocu: If a positive-size candidate existed, its component would have order at least the mark at its generic point. The whole component would then lie in the closed marked order locus. An irreducible component is nonempty, contrary to emptiness of this locus. Thus no positive-size candidate exists and the minimum is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_spec: The set of positive sizes realized by candidates is nonempty by hypothesis. Its infimum in the natural numbers is one of its elements, so it is positive and realized by a candidate. As the infimum, it is at most every other positive size realized by a candidate.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenterSet_eq_sUnion_centerCompon: Both sets are the union over components that are candidates of the minimum size for the chosen indices and have maximum order. A point's membership in either union is witnessed by the same component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenterSet_nonempty: The chosen index set has a candidate component of maximum order. This component belongs to the center family and is irreducible, hence contains a point. That point belongs to the union defining the center set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_eq_componentUnionIdeal: The minimum size is positive and the preimage of the center set is open. The center therefore uses the branch taking the kernel for this open in the intersection subscheme. The center set is the union of the selected components, so the resulting ideal is the component-union ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_eq_top_of_minIndexCard_eq: The center definition uses an open part of the intersection only if the minimum size is positive and the requisite preimage is open. When the size is zero its other branch gives the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_ne_top: The center support is the selected center set, and this set contains a point. The unit ideal has empty support, so the center ideal is proper.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_spec: The preceding center results give a proper ideal, smoothness of its subscheme, strict normal crossings with the boundary and containment of its support in the marked order locus. The controlled-transform theorem supplies an ideal upstairs whose product with the required exceptional power is the total transform. These establish all the specified conditions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.openSublocusIdeal_eq_componentUnionIdeal: Replace the open subset by the equal preimage of the component union. Both ideal constructions are then the kernel of the inclusion of this same open into the intersection subscheme followed by its inclusion into the ambient scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_eq_of_closure_eq: The singleton closures of the two generic points are the two given closures and hence are equal. Scheme spaces distinguish points by their closures, so the two points coincide. The order along each set is the order at the common point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_eq_orderAt_genericPoint: With irreducibility supplied, the order-along definition selects the branch evaluating the ideal's order at the generic point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_eq_orderAt_of_mem_intersectio: The component is irreducible. The definition of order along an irreducible set gives the order at its generic point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_eq_sum_of_monomial: The open neighborhood meets the given component, so it contains the component's generic point. The order along the component is the order at this point. In the local monomial order formula only boundary supports through that point contribute. By the generic-point criterion their indices are exactly the chosen set, and each contributes its exponent. Summing them gives the finite natural-number sum in the statement.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_lt_top_of_isCandidateComponen: The candidate belongs to the intersection-component family, so its order is the order at its generic point. The geometry hypotheses give a finite global order bound for the ideal, which is nonzero on components by admissibility. The order at this point is therefore finite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAtLeastLocus_eq_empty_of_minIndexCa: Suppose a point belongs to the marked order locus. Take a local monomial expression there. The order is the sum of the exponents for the boundary divisors through the point. The mark is positive, so this set of indices is nonempty. The point belongs to the support of their intersection, and a component of that support contains it. The generic order along this component is the sum of the same exponents by the component order formula. It is at least the mark, so the index set and component give a candidate of positive size. This contradicts the zero minimum size.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_eq_sum_indicator_support: Restriction to an open preserves order at its points. On the given neighborhood, apply additivity of order to the product expression for the ideal, and use that raising a factor to its exponent multiplies its order by that exponent. A boundary divisor has order one on its support and zero off it. Thus each contribution equals the exponent times the indicator of the divisor support, giving the sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_eq_sum_supportIndices: Apply the local formula expressing the order as a sum weighted by the support indicators. Terms outside the support index set are zero and each term inside it is its exponent. Removing the zero terms gives the claimed sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_foldr_mul: Induct on the list. The empty product is the unit ideal of order zero, equal to the empty sum. For a nonempty list, the order of the product of its first factor and the remaining product is the sum of their orders. Use the induction formula for the remaining product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_monomialCenter: The monomial center ideal is the ideal of a union of components of one boundary intersection. By the smoothness property of such component unions in the geometry hypotheses, its closed subscheme is smooth over the base.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.subset_orderAtLeastLocus_of_le_orderAlon: The hypothesis places the generic point of the component in the locus of order at least the threshold. Over the characteristic-zero base with smooth structural map this locus is closed. It therefore contains the closure of the generic point, which is the component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.subset_support_iff_mem_of_mem_intersecti: Use the boundary-component property from the geometry hypotheses for the admissible triple. It says that the component lies in the support of exactly the boundary divisors indexed by the selected set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_monomialCenter: Express the center as the ideal of its selected component union. The support property in the geometry hypotheses identifies the support of that ideal with the union. This union is exactly the center set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_monomialCenter_subset_boundary: The chosen index set has positive cardinality, so select one of its indices. Each selected component belongs to the corresponding boundary intersection and is contained in the support of this chosen divisor. Every point of the center support lies in such a component and therefore in the union of the boundary supports.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_monomialCenter_subset_orderAtLea: Take a point of the center support and a selected component containing it. Its order at its generic point is at least the mark by the candidate condition. The locus of points with order at least the mark is closed and contains the generic point, so contains the whole component and the given point.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_le_iff: The weak comparison holds when the first invariant is strictly smaller or all its comparison entries coincide with those of the second. Substituting the minimum size, maximum order and sorted chosen indices into these entries gives the right-hand condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerInvariant_lt_iff_lex: Expand the strict comparison of the invariant entries. A smaller minimum size gives the comparison first. At equal size a larger maximum order gives the comparison, and at equal order the increasing lists of chosen indices are compared lexicographically. These are the stated cases.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_monomialCenter_eq_top: Suppose an upper point maps into the lower center. Its image lies in a selected lower component. Lift this component through the upper point using the component comparison and pull back its chosen index set. This keeps the size, generic order and numeric index positions. The resulting positive-size upper candidate rules out a zero upper minimum and bounds the upper minimum by the lower one. Thus a strict invariant comparison cannot arise from a larger upper minimum. If sizes agree, the lifted candidate bounds the upper maximum order below by the lower maximum, ruling out strict comparison by a smaller upper order. If orders agree as well, the lifted selection maximizes the upper order and has the same sorted positions as the lower choice. Optimality of the upper choice then rules out strict comparison by the index list. This contradiction excludes all upper points from the inverse image of the lower center support. The pullback center has empty support and hence is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentUnionIdeal_congr: Replace the two index sets and the two component families by their common values. The open parts of the intersection and their inclusions then agree, so their defining kernels coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.lexMaxIndices_pullbackOverField_eq_image: An index belongs to either chosen set exactly when its position occurs in the corresponding sorted list. The lists agree by hypothesis. Each position in the upper set is therefore the position of a lower chosen index, and the pullback map carries that lower index to the given upper one. Conversely, pulling back a chosen lower index gives the same position in the upper list and hence an upper chosen index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.maxCandidateOrder_le_of_minIndexCard_eq: The common minimum size is positive. Choose an upper component attaining the maximum order at that size. Send its indices downstairs without changing their number and use the component comparison to send its generic point to a lower component's generic point. Order preservation gives the same order there. This is a lower candidate at the common minimum size, so the lower maximum is at least its order, which is the upper maximum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_ne_zero_and_le_pullbackOver: Since the upper minimum size is positive, choose an upper component attaining it. Send its selected indices to their counterparts in the lower boundary. This preserves cardinality and recovers the original selection after pulling back the indices. The component comparison gives a lower component whose generic point is the image of the upper generic point. Order preservation at that point gives the same order downstairs, so the lower component is a candidate of the same positive size. The lower minimum is therefore positive and at most the upper one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_pullbackOverField_eq_zero_o: A zero upper minimum gives the first outcome. Otherwise the lower minimum is positive and at most the upper one. Strict inequality gives the strict invariant comparison by size. If sizes agree, the upper maximum order is at most the lower one, and strict inequality gives the comparison by the reversed order entry. If these orders also agree, transport a component attaining the upper choice to the lower selection with the same positions. It remains of maximum order and the same size. The lower choice is lexicographically at most that selection by its optimality, and the sorted positions of that selection equal the upper choice's positions. This gives strict comparison by the index list or equality of all entries.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialCenter_pullbackOverField_eq_coma: If the common minimum size is zero, both centers are unit ideals, and pullback preserves the unit ideal. Otherwise write the centers as ideals of the selected component unions. Under the given index identification, an upper selected component maps into a lower intersection component with the same generic order. Equality of the maxima and minima makes this lower component selected. Conversely, an upper intersection component mapping into a selected lower one has the same generic order as the component supplied by the comparison. That lower component equals the selected one, since their intersection contains the image of an upper point and distinct lower components are disjoint. The upper component therefore also has the required order and is selected. This identifies the two component families used by the pullback property of the union ideal, which gives the center equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlong_pullbackOverField_eq_orderAlo: Order along each component is order at its generic point. By the generic-point comparison, the upper generic point maps to the lower one. The assumed preservation of order under pullback equates these two values.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackAlongIndex_val: The comparison at the original base field uses the index map for pullback over that field. It keeps the numeric position in the list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndexSymm_injective: Equal images under the inverse index map have equal numeric positions. The map preserves positions, so the two original upper indices have equal positions and are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndexSymm_pullbackIndex: Both index maps preserve the numeric position. Their composite has the original numeric value and therefore equals the original finite index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndexSymm_val: The inverse index map uses equality of the boundary lengths to reinterpret an upper position in the lower list. Its natural-number value stays the same.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndex_pullbackIndexSymm: Sending a pulled-back index downstairs and then upstairs leaves its numeric value fixed. Equality of these values identifies the original index with the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndex_strictMono: The order on finite indices is the order of their numeric values. Since the pullback index map preserves these values, it preserves strict inequality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackIndex_val: Pulling back the boundary preserves list positions. The new index has the same natural-number value as the original index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sortedIndices_image_pullbackIndex: A strictly increasing map commutes with sorting the index set. Taking numeric positions after applying the pullback index map gives the same entries as taking them before, so the two sorted lists coincide.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentUnionIdeal_eq_ker: First include the open union of components into the intersection subscheme. Then include the intersection into the ambient scheme. The component-union ideal is defined as the kernel of this composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exceptionalIndex_val: The list has one more position than the original boundary. Its last position, numbered from zero, equals the length of the old list, and this is the exceptional index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_intersectionComponents_iff: Membership means that the set is irreducible, lies in the support of the intersection ideal and is maximal with these properties. These are the defining conditions for an irreducible component of the support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_preimageStrictTransformIndex_iff: The preimage set is formed by keeping exactly those original indices whose strict-transform indices belong to the given set. This filter is the membership condition on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackAlongIndex_val: Identify the two index bounds using equality of the boundary lengths. This changes only the bound, leaving the numeric position unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackAlong_boundary_length: Pulling back along the morphism applies ideal pullback at every position of the old list. This keeps the original list length.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverFieldIndex_val: The boundary lengths agree, so the corresponding new index has the original numeric position, now regarded as an index in the pulled-back list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_baseField: The construction stores the field supplied for the source scheme as its base field. This is the stated field.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_boundary: The new boundary is defined by pulling back each ideal in the original list along the given morphism, keeping the list order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_boundary_length: The pullback boundary is obtained by replacing each entry with its pullback, so there is one entry for each original position and the lengths agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_eq_pullbackAlong: When the field is the original one, both constructions use the same source scheme and structural morphism. They pull back the same ideal and boundary along the given morphism and carry over the same mark. Their data coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_ideal: The construction sets the ideal of the new marked object to the pullback of the original ideal along the given scheme morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_mult: The pullback construction copies the mark of the original object. The multiplicities therefore agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_scheme: The construction uses the source scheme of the given morphism as its underlying scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.pullbackOverField_structureMorphism: The structural morphism of the constructed marked object is the supplied map from the source scheme to the spectrum of its field.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictTransformIndex_val: The strict transforms occupy the old positions in the enlarged list. The new index for a strict transform is the old position with the larger bound, so its numeric value is unchanged.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.transformedBoundary_length: The strictly transformed ideals have one entry at each old boundary position. The exceptional ideal adds one entry at the end, giving the stated length.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_prod: The empty product is the unit ideal, which pulls back to the unit ideal. At a successor size, split the first factor from the product. Pullback preserves multiplication, and induction pulls back the remaining product term by term.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_mem_intersectionComponents_orderA: Since the exceptional index is excluded, the upper selection is the image of its old indices under the strict-transform map. The transformed-component property gives an old intersection component outside the selected center family, identifies the image of the upper generic point with its generic point and places the upper generic point off the exceptional divisor. The controlled and original orders agree at these points. Taking the orders along the two components gives the required equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_mul_ofFn_eq_prod: Both products use each member of the finite family once. Formally, at size zero both are the unit ideal, and at a successor size both multiply the first entry by the product of the remaining family. Induction gives the equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.get_transformedBoundary_exceptionalIndex: The exceptional index is the last position of the enlarged list, after all strict transforms. Its entry is the exceptional ideal, which equals the pullback of the center.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.get_transformedBoundary_strictTransformI: The strict-transform index has the old numeric position and lies in the initial list of strict transforms. The entry there is the strict transform of the old boundary ideal at that position.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.image_strictTransformIndex_preimageStric: Every image index belongs to the selection by definition of its preimage, and is below the exceptional position. Conversely, a selected index other than the exceptional one lies below the old length and so has an old index at the same position. This old index lies in the preimage. Hence the image equals the selection with its exceptional position removed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.injective_strictTransformIndex: The strict-transform index map preserves numeric positions. Equal images therefore have equal original positions, so the original finite indices coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyMonomialTriple_blowupTripleAtCe: The monomial center is smooth, has strict normal crossings with the boundary and lies in the cosupport. It admits a controlled transform, so it defines a single admissible marked blowup. The stage-admissibility property applies at its sole successor and identifies that stage with the blown-up triple. The center support is the selected component union and the residual ideal satisfies the controlled-transform identity. The local monomiality theorem for that blowup then supplies a monomial expression at every point of the new cosupport.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialNear_transformedBoundary_of_is:
First put the image point in the lower cosupport. On the exceptional divisor this follows because the image is in the center. Off the exceptional divisor, the order of the total transform equals the lower order and is at least the order of the controlled transform. Choose a lower monomial expression near the image, with old boundary exponents aᵢ. For each old divisor the local total transform is its strict transform times the exceptional ideal to exponent εᵢ, where εᵢ is zero or one. Pass to a common neighborhood upstairs where all these formulas and the pulled-back monomial expression hold. The total transform there is the product of the strict-transform factors with exponents aᵢ and the exceptional factor with exponent e = ∑ εᵢaᵢ.

The exponent e is at least the mark. Over the center, the chosen center indices all have εᵢ = 1, and the sum of their exponents is the order along the selected component containing the image, which is at least the mark. Off the center, the local containment criterion for εᵢ = 1 holds vacuously on the complement of the center, so e is the sum of all exponents. It bounds the order at the image and hence the mark. The exceptional ideal is locally generated by a nonzerodivisor, so cancel its mark-th power from the two expressions for the total transform. This leaves the strict-transform factors and the exceptional factor with exponent e minus the mark. These are the transformed boundary ideals with nonnegative exponents, giving local monomiality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.krullDimSucc_blowupTripleAtCenterIdeal_l: Positive minimum size gives an admissible single blowup at the monomial center. The scheme of the blown-up triple is its stage-one scheme. The stage-one dimension bound yields the assertion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.krullDimSucc_schemeAt_one_le_dim: Reconstruct the marked sequence from its data. The length bound ensures its stage one is defined within the sequence. Apply the geometry hypothesis bounding the dimension successor of every such stage by that of the original triple. Reconstruction identifies its stage one with the scheme in the data.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_blowupTripleAtCenterIdeal_e: If the transformed minimum size is zero, take that case. Otherwise the transformed triple is locally monomial and its ideal satisfies the controlled-transform identity. The center is the ideal of the chosen component union. Apply the one-blowup comparison of minimum size, maximum order and sorted positions to these data. Its alternatives are exactly the strict comparison of the two center invariants.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_le_card_add_one_of_exceptio: The upper generic point lies on the exceptional divisor. Its image lies in a selected center component, where there is a local monomial expression. Let S be the old indices represented by strict transforms in the upper selection, and let A be the chosen lower center indices. The order formula says that the upper order plus the mark equals the sum of the exponents on S plus the sum on A. All these quantities are finite, and the upper order is at least the mark. If the size of S is already at least the old minimum, the size bound follows. Otherwise its exponents sum to less than the mark, since all the corresponding old divisors contain the image point. The order formula then gives upper order strictly below the sum on A, which equals the old maximum. To obtain the size bound in this case, choose an index of A outside S, possible because A has the old minimum size. Removing this index from A leaves a sum less than the mark by the same small-selection argument. Since the combined sums on S and A are at least twice the mark, adding the chosen index to S gives a sum of at least the mark. All these divisors contain the image point. An intersection component through it has that sum as its generic order, so it is a positive-size candidate downstairs. The old minimum is therefore at most the size of S plus one.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_lt_or_maxCandidateOrder_lt_: Consider any positive-size upper candidate. If its indices omit the exceptional position, its component comes from a lower component of the same order and the same selection size. If they include it, the size bound for an exceptional selection again gives size at least the lower minimum. Thus the upper minimum is at least the lower one. A strict inequality gives the first outcome. At equality, take a component for the chosen upper selection that attains the upper maximum. If the selection contains the exceptional index, its old preimage has one fewer index and hence has size below the common minimum. The exceptional order bound gives a strict drop in the maximum. Otherwise it comes from a lower candidate of the same size and order whose component is outside the center family. The upper maximum is therefore at most the lower one. A strict inequality gives the second outcome. If the maxima also agree, the preimage selection is a maximum-order lower selection and its sorted positions are those of the upper choice. The lower choice is lexicographically at most these positions by optimality. Equality would make the old selection the lower choice and put its maximizing component in the center family, a contradiction. Hence the lower sorted list is strictly lexicographically smaller.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialInvariant_blowupTripleAtCenterId: The transformed minimum is positive, so the one-step center comparison gives either a larger minimum size, a smaller maximum order at equal size, or equal sizes and orders with a strict comparison of sorted positions. In the first case a candidate attaining the upper minimum has cardinality below the transformed dimension successor, which is at most the old dimension successor and hence at most D. Subtracting the larger upper size from D gives a smaller first entry. In the second case the lower maximum is finite, so the strict order drop gives a smaller second entry and equal first entries. In the final case the size and order entries agree, and the count of maximizing pairs strictly drops under the blowup. In each case the new lexicographic invariant is smaller.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialInvariant_lt_of_lex_lt: The invariant is the lexicographic triple of the specified natural-number entries. A smaller first entry gives a strict comparison. At equal first entries the second entries are compared, and at equal second entries the comparison passes to the third entries. The given disjunction provides exactly one of these comparisons.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_controlledTransform_eq_of_notMem: At the given point the pulled-back center ideal has unit stalk, since the point is outside its support. The controlled-transform identity then identifies the controlled and total transform stalks. The blown-up point is outside the exceptional support, so the total-transform order is the original order at its image. Combining the equalities gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_pow_comap_transformedBoundary_eq: The transformed list has exactly the old positions and one final position. Split its finite product at the final position. For every old position the list entry is the corresponding strict transform and its exponent is the old exponent. The last position carries the exceptional ideal and has the new exponent. This gives the two factors on the right.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sortedIndices_image_strictTransformIndex: Sorting commutes with the strictly increasing strict-transform index map. Each new index has its old numeric value, so taking the sorted numeric positions gives the original list.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.strictMono_strictTransformIndex: The comparison of indices is the comparison of their numeric positions. The map keeps both values, so any strict comparison is preserved.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sum_lt_mult_of_card_lt_minIndexCard: Suppose the sum of the exponents on the chosen indices reaches the mark. These indices are nonempty because the mark is positive. The point lies in the intersection of their supports, so choose a component of that intersection through it. The local monomial formula for its generic order gives precisely the stipulated sum. It therefore makes a candidate with positive size equal to the chosen cardinality, contradicting the strict bound below the minimum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.toNat_lt_toNat_of_lt_of_ne_top: The larger order is finite by hypothesis, and the smaller is finite because it is below it. Writing both as natural numbers preserves the strict comparison. Taking their natural-number values returns those same numbers.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsMonomialNear.congr_sameNontrivialBound: The boundary relation implies equality of the sets of nonunit boundary ideals. Apply the result that local monomiality is preserved by such equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsMonomialNear.congr_setOf: Equality of the two sets of nonunit boundary ideals implies that each nonunit ideal from the first list belongs to the second. The monotonicity result transfers the local monomial expression.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsMonomialNear.mono: Keep the neighborhood on which the monomial expression holds. Each nonunit boundary ideal in the old list occurs in the new one, so its restriction belongs to the new generated submonoid. A unit ideal restricts to the multiplicative identity and also belongs. Thus the old generators, and hence the restricted monomial ideal they generate, belong to the new submonoid.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.foldr_mul_ofFn_eq_prod: Listing the values of the finite family in index order gives the factors of its finite product. The unit ideal is the multiplicative identity, so multiplying that list with the unit as the initial value gives this product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.image_comap_eq_range_get: A boundary ideal in the list occurs at some index, so its restriction is a value of the indexed family. Conversely, every value of that family is the restriction of a listed ideal. This proves equality of the two sets.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyMonomialTriple_withBoundary: The geometry hypotheses preserve admissibility when the boundary is replaced by one with the same nonunit entries. At each point of the cosupport the original triple provides a local monomial expression. The ideal and mark are unchanged, and equality of the nontrivial boundary entries lets that expression be read with the new boundary.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialNear_iff_exists_pow_prod: The definition of being monomial near the point asks for an open neighborhood where the ideal is a product of powers of the restricted boundary ideals. Writing the powers in boundary index order gives precisely the stated product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialNear_iff_mem_closure: On a proposed neighborhood, the restrictions of the listed boundary ideals are the finite indexed family of generators. A product of nonnegative powers of that family belongs to the generated submonoid. Conversely, a finite product of generators can be collected by index because ideal multiplication is commutative. The resulting exponents give the required monomial expression on the same neighborhood.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.coe_orderAlongComponent_eq_orderAt_gener: The ideal is nonzero on the ambient components, so the order at the generic point of the given component is finite. Taking its natural-number value and inserting that value back into the extended natural numbers recovers it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_ι_eq_of_forall_affineOpens_ideal_e: Take any affine open of the open subscheme. Its image is an ambient affine open contained in the specified open. On the chosen affine open of the subscheme, each restricted ideal is obtained by extending the section ideal on the image. Those section ideals agree by hypothesis. Hence the restricted ideals agree on every affine open and are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentPowerIdeal_of_isIrreducibleComp: The component is a closed irreducible subset of the divisor's support. The construction thus takes its vanishing ideal to the power given by the order of the marked ideal along that component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.componentPowerIdeal_of_not_isIrreducible: The component-power construction uses the unit ideal in the branch where the given subset is not an irreducible component of the divisor's support. The hypothesis selects that branch.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_affineOpens_ideal_comap_ι_eq_map: Take the image of the affine open under the open inclusion. It is affine, lies inside the original open, and its inverse image contains the given affine open. The affine formula for pullback of ideal sheaves expresses the restricted ideal there as extension along the indicated map on sections.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isMonomialSplitting: Take the monomial factor to be the product of the contributions along all boundary divisors and the residual factor to be the ideal quotient by that product. Their product is the original ideal by the factorization result. Off all listed divisor supports each contribution has unit stalk, so the monomial factor has support contained in the boundary. Around each point the neighborhood formula writes the section ideals of the monomial factor as a product of powers of boundary ideals. Equality on all affine opens of the neighborhood gives equality after restriction, and restriction preserves products and powers. It remains to check the residual support. At the generic point of a boundary component the monomial factor is the maximal ideal raised to the original order along that component. If the residual support contained the component, its stalk would be contained in the maximal ideal there. The product identity would force the original stalk into the next power, contradicting its order. Thus no boundary component is contained in the residual support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_nhds_ideal_monomialPartAlongDivis: If the point lies on a divisor component, choose an affine étale chart that meets the divisor only along this component and where its vanishing ideal equals the divisor ideal. On any affine open inside the chart, its contribution is the divisor ideal raised to the order along that component. Other components miss the chart and contribute unit ideals. The intersection of the component-power ideals lies between their product and the chosen power, which have equal section ideals there. If the point lies on no component, take the complement of the finite closed union of components. Each contribution is the unit ideal on all affine opens inside it, so the intersection agrees there with the zeroth power of the divisor.

If the point lies on a component, take an affine étale chart in which the divisor is a coordinate divisor and all its support in the chart belongs to that component. On every affine open inside the chart the component's vanishing ideal agrees with the divisor ideal, generated by the restricted coordinate. The component-power ideal is therefore generated by the corresponding power of this coordinate, a nonzerodivisor. Every other component is disjoint from the chart, so its contribution is the unit ideal. The intersection is bounded above by the chosen component ideal and below by the product of all component ideals, which has the same sections there. If the point is off every component, take the open complement of their finite closed union. On any affine open inside it every component power is the unit ideal, so the product and the intersection are the unit ideal, generated by 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_prod_monomialPartAlongDivisor_eq_: Induct on the size of the finite family. The empty products agree on the whole scheme. For a nonempty family, find a neighborhood and exponent for the first divisor, and a neighborhood and exponents for the remaining product by induction. Intersect the neighborhoods. On every affine open in the intersection, multiply the established section equalities for the first and remaining factors. This gives the product of the powers with the combined exponents.

Induct on the list of divisors. For the empty list, use the whole scheme and the unit generator. Otherwise intersect the neighborhoods giving a single nonzerodivisor generator for the first divisor's contribution and for the product of the remaining contributions. On every affine open inside this intersection the full product is generated by the product of their generators, which remains a nonzerodivisor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_comap_one: The multiplicative identity is the unit ideal sheaf. Its pullback to an open is the unit ideal sheaf there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_comap_prod: Induct on the number of factors. The empty product pulls back to the unit ideal. Split a nonempty product into its first factor and the remaining factors. Pullback preserves the product of two factors, and induction handles the remaining factors.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_listProd: Induct on the list. The empty product gives the unit section ideal. For the head and tail, take sections of their product using the affine multiplication formula and substitute the induction formula for the tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_mul: On the given affine open, the product of ideal sheaves is defined by multiplying their section ideals. This gives the equality there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_one: The multiplicative identity for ideal sheaves is the unit ideal sheaf. Its section ideal on the affine open is the unit ideal, the multiplicative identity for ideals in the section ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_pow: Induct on the exponent. At zero both sides are the unit ideal by the section calculation for the identity sheaf. At a successor, use preservation of products of section ideals and then the induction hypothesis for the preceding power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_ideal_top: The section ideal of the unit ideal sheaf contains the unit section on every affine open. Thus it is the unit ideal of that section ring.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_listProd_le_of_mem: Induct on the list. If the specified ideal is its head, the product is contained in the head ideal. If it occurs in the tail, the full product is contained in the tail product, which is contained in the specified ideal by induction. The empty list has no specified member.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_mul_le_left: Check inclusion at each stalk. Products of a section from the first stalk ideal with any element of the second belong to the first ideal. Thus the product ideal is contained in the first.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.idealSheafData_mul_le_right: At each stalk, a product with a factor in the second ideal belongs to that ideal. Hence the product of the stalk ideals is contained in the second stalk ideal, and the sheaf inclusion follows.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_componentPowerIdeal_eq_top_of_disj: If the subset is a support component, its vanishing ideal has unit sections on the disjoint affine open. Thus its specified power has unit sections there. If it is not a support component, the component-power ideal is already the unit ideal sheaf.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_vanishingIdeal_eq_top_of_disjoint: The section ideal consists of elements lying in every prime of the affine open corresponding to a point of the closed set. There are no such primes because the open is disjoint from the set. The unit satisfies the defining condition and the ideal is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isEtaleLocallyCoordinateDivisor_of_inStr: Choose the listed index of the divisor and take an étale normal-crossings chart around the given point. The chart assigns to this entry either the unit ideal or the ideal of a single coordinate. Use that chart for the local description of the divisor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isLocallyGeneratedByNonZeroDivisor_monom: Every listed divisor is étale locally a coordinate divisor by strict normal crossings. The product calculation gives a neighborhood of each point where every affine open has a nonzerodivisor generator for the product. Choose an affine basic neighborhood of the point inside it. The generator on that basic open gives the required local generation of the monomial factor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_prod_map_of_forall_mem_span: Induct on the list of principal ideals. For the empty list the product is the unit ideal. Otherwise write the given element as the first generator times a coefficient, using its membership in the first principal ideal. For each remaining ideal, membership of this product and the cancellation hypothesis show that the coefficient belongs to that ideal. The tail satisfies the same pairwise cancellation assumptions, so the coefficient belongs to the product of the tail by induction. The original element then belongs to the full product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_span_algebraMap_of_mul_mem: Write the localized element and the coefficient of the generator as fractions. Clear their denominators in the equality expressing divisibility, multiplying by one further denominator to obtain the equality in the original ring. The original cancellation property shows that the numerator times the necessary denominators is divisible by d. In the localization this says that the localized element times a product of denominators belongs to the extended principal ideal. These denominators become units, so the localized element itself belongs to the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_span_germ_coord_pow_of_mul_mem: On the affine étale chart, the coordinate with the second index acts injectively modulo the given power of the coordinate with the first index, because the indices are distinct. The stalk is the localization of the chart ring at the point's prime. Apply preservation of the cancellation property under localization. The image of the first coordinate power is the same power of its germ, giving the stated membership.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.mem_span_of_pow_mul_mem_span: Induct on the power of the factor being cancelled. At zero the membership is the conclusion. For a successor power, factor off one copy and apply the assumed cancellation in the principal power ideal. Then use the induction hypothesis on the remaining power.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialFactorIdeal_eq_prod_monomialPart: The monomial factor is defined as the product of the contributions along the listed boundary divisors. Applying the divisor-contribution operation to the list gives the factors in the stated product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialFactorIdeal_mul_nonMonomialFacto: First show that the original ideal is contained in its proposed monomial factor by testing stalks. Choose an affine étale boundary chart at a point. A boundary entry that misses the point contributes the unit ideal. An entry through the point contributes the principal ideal generated by its coordinate germ raised to the order along the component through the point. The original stalk is contained in each of these principal ideals by the generic-order bound along a divisor. Distinct boundary entries through the point have distinct coordinates. Each coordinate germ can be cancelled modulo any power of another, and repeated cancellation gives the same property for their powers. Unit generators satisfy the cancellation condition as well. The product membership lemma now puts the original stalk inside the product of all these principal ideals, which is the monomial stalk. The monomial factor is locally generated by a nonzerodivisor. For an ideal contained in such a factor, multiplying the factor by the ideal quotient recovers the ideal. This is the proposed product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPartAlongDivisor_eq_inf_componen: The contribution along a divisor is defined by intersecting the component-power ideals for its finite set of support components. This intersection is their infimum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.natCast_add_one_le_of_not_le: The hypothesis says that the extended natural number is strictly greater than n. Every such value, including infinity, is at least n + 1.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonMonomialFactorIdeal_eq_idealSheafColo: The residual factor is defined as the ideal quotient of the original ideal by the monomial factor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.not_mem_support_of_stalkIdeal_eq_maximal: Suppose the point also lies on the second divisor. Its coordinate germ then belongs to the maximal ideal, which by hypothesis is generated by the first coordinate germ. Express the second germ as a multiple of the first. Clear the coefficient's denominator in the affine localization, then clear any remaining localization equality by another element outside the point's prime. This puts the second coordinate times a product of denominators in the affine ideal generated by the first coordinate. Because the coordinates are distinct on the étale chart, the second coordinate acts injectively modulo that ideal. Thus the product of denominators lies in the first-coordinate ideal. Its germ is therefore in the maximal ideal, yet it is a unit because every denominator is outside the prime. This is a contradiction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAlongComponent_eq_orderAt_genericPo: By definition, the natural-number order along the component is obtained by taking the natural-number value of the order at its generic point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_monomialFactorIdeal_genericPoint: At the generic point the monomial factor's stalk is the maximal ideal raised to the finite order of the original ideal along the component. This gives a lower bound on its order by that exponent. If its order were greater, the maximal-ideal power would lie in the next power. The original ideal's stalk is contained in the maximal-ideal power with the original order as exponent, so it would then lie in the next power too. That contradicts the exact finite order of the original ideal at the generic point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_map_eq_apply_getElem_of_forall_ne: The specified position is the only one whose mapped entry can differ from the identity. Removing all the identity factors leaves the mapped entry at that position. This works even when the original list contains repeated entries, since the hypothesis is imposed on positions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_map_eq_apply_of_nodup_of_forall_ne: The distinguished element occurs exactly once by membership and the absence of repetitions. Every other entry maps to the identity. Multiplying the mapped entries therefore leaves only the value at the distinguished element.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.prod_map_eq_one_of_forall_eq_one: Each entry of the mapped list is the image of a listed element and therefore equals the multiplicative identity. Their product is the identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_componentPowerIdeal_of_mem: For this component the defining ideal is the specified power of its vanishing ideal. At the given point on the component, the étale coordinate-divisor description identifies the stalk of its vanishing ideal with the divisor stalk. Taking stalks of the power gives the formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_componentPowerIdeal_of_not_me: If the subset is not a component, the ideal is already the unit ideal. If it is a component, its vanishing ideal has precisely the component as support. At a point outside it the vanishing ideal has unit stalk. Stalks commute with powers, so its specified power also has unit stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_finsetInf_eq_top: Induct on the finite set of indices. The empty intersection is the unit ideal. Inserting one index intersects the previous ideal with the additional ideal, both of which have unit stalk at the chosen point. The binary intersection then has unit stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_inf_eq_top: The product of the two ideals is contained in their intersection. Its stalk is the product of two unit stalk ideals, hence is the unit ideal. By monotonicity the stalk of the intersection contains the unit ideal and is therefore equal to it.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_listProd: Induct on the list of ideal sheaves. The empty product has the unit ideal as its stalk. For a nonempty list, take the stalk of the head multiplied by the tail product, then use preservation of multiplication and the induction formula for the tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_monomialFactorIdeal: Take the stalk of the finite product of the contributions along the boundary. Stalks preserve list products, so the result is the product of the stalks of those contributions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_monomialFactorIdeal_genericPo: Take an étale boundary chart at the generic point of the given divisor component. The chosen divisor stalk is the maximal ideal. Any other boundary entry is the unit ideal on the chart or is given by a distinct coordinate. In the latter case its support cannot contain the point, since the second-coordinate argument excludes this when the chosen divisor generates the maximal ideal. All these other divisor contributions therefore have unit stalk. The product stalk reduces to the chosen divisor's contribution, which is its stalk raised to the order along the component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_monomialPartAlongDivisor_of_m: The intersection of the component-power ideals is contained in the ideal for the component containing the point. Its stalk is therefore contained in the stated power. For the reverse containment, use the product of all component-power ideals, which is contained in their intersection. Distinct components of this étale coordinate divisor are disjoint, so all other factors have unit stalk at the point. The product stalk is exactly the power for the chosen component, giving the other inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_monomialPartAlongDivisor_of_n: Each support component lies in the divisor support, so none contains the given point. Each component-power ideal has unit stalk there by the calculation away from its component. Their finite intersection therefore has unit stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_one: Multiply the identity for sheaf multiplication by the full structure sheaf ideal. The result is the full structure sheaf ideal. Taking stalks and using the known stalk of the unit ideal gives the product of the sought stalk ideal with the unit stalk ideal equal to the unit ideal. This product is contained in the sought stalk ideal, forcing it to be the unit ideal.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.intersectionIdeal_eq_iSup: The ideal defining the common intersection is defined as the sum of the boundary ideals with the selected indices. The supremum of these ideals is their sum.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_succ: The recursion takes the next iterate by applying one center-selection and blowup step to the preceding iterate. This is exactly the successor formula.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialBlowupIterate_zero: The recursion starts with the given sequence. Thus the iterate with zero additional steps is that sequence itself.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_apply: Evaluate the assignment at the marked ideal. It takes the structural morphism, ideal, mark and boundary as inputs to the monomial blowup sequence and then forms the associated marked sequence. This is the expression on the right.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.centerAtLast_ne_top_of_isAdmissibleCente: Admissibility of the last center includes the condition that its ideal is proper. Hence this ideal differs from the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_sequenceOfBlowupsPullback_monomia: Induct on the number of lower steps up to the first stationary index. At zero take the two empty sequences, which compare over the base map and have no centers. At a successor, compare the preceding lower iterate with an upper iterate by induction. All earlier upper centers are admissible, and the preceding lower center is admissible since it occurs before the lower stationary index. Both final triples are locally monomial. The one-step comparison either extends only the lower sequence, keeping the upper index and its admissibility history, or extends both sequences by one admissible blowup. In the latter case add the new upper center to its history. This gives the claimed comparison and upper index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.false_of_mem_support_of_comap_eq_top: If the image point is in the support, the given point is in the support of the pulled-back ideal by the inverse-image formula for support. That ideal is the unit ideal and has empty support, a contradiction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.false_of_mem_support_top: The unit ideal has empty support. Membership of the given point in that support is therefore impossible.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.flat_lastMap: The comparison square at the last stages is a pullback of the original base morphism. The last-stage map is therefore flat by stability of flatness under base change.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isNoetherian_schemeAt_of_le_length: Induct on the stage number. The zero stage is isomorphic to the given Noetherian base scheme. At a successor stage within the length, the preceding stage is Noetherian by induction and its blowup is again Noetherian.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.length_monomialIterateFromEmpty_zero: The iteration begins with the empty blowup sequence. At iteration zero this is still the sequence, so the length is zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.minIndexCard_ne_zero_and_monomialCenter_: Replace the upper boundary by the directly pulled-back boundary. Admissibility and local monomiality survive this replacement, and the minimum size and center are unchanged because the nonunit entries are the same in order. Flatness and order preservation supply the component-compatible comparison. A positive upper minimum forces a positive lower minimum. For a positive lower minimum, either the upper minimum is zero or the lower invariant is weakly below the upper one. The lower center pulls back to the unit ideal if the upper minimum is zero or the invariant comparison is strict. If all entries agree, the chosen indices agree under the boundary index map. Then the upper minimum is positive and the upper center is the pullback of the lower one. Transfer these conclusions back to the given upper boundary.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.monomialPrincipalization_isPullbackBlowu: Apply the iterative comparison at the lower first stationary index, obtaining a comparable upper iterate whose earlier centers were all admissible. At the lower stationary index the minimum candidate size is zero. If the current upper center were admissible, the one-step comparison would force the lower minimum to be positive. Thus the current upper center is inadmissible, and this is the first stationary upper index. The two principalizations are the sequences at these stationary indices. The constructed comparison of the iterates therefore supplies the pullback relation for the principalizations.

The given smooth morphism is flat, and at the original field its pullback triple agrees with the specified same-field construction. The boundary equality can be read in either direction. In every comparison square required by the flat theorem the map on the lower stage is a base change of the original smooth morphism, hence smooth. The lower structural morphism is smooth over a characteristic-zero field by admissibility. Order is preserved under such smooth pullback, which supplies the remaining hypothesis of the flat comparison theorem.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonempty_sequenceOfBlowupsPullback_blowu: Both last centers are admissible, so each appended step is a single blowup with a proper center. The last-stage map is flat by base change. The new stage-zero identifications are identities, so the given equality of the center ideals is the comparison required for the length-one pullback construction. Append the resulting comparison of single steps to the comparison of the given sequences to get the two extended sequences.

The admissible lower center appends a single blowup. Its pullback to the upper last stage is the unit ideal. Thus no upper point maps into the support of the lower center. The omitted-center construction compares the empty upper extension with this single lower step over the last-stage map. Concatenate that comparison with the existing one. Identifying the upper append of the empty sequence with the original upper sequence gives the required comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.nonempty_sequenceOfBlowupsPullback_of_le: Both single steps are blowups of their initial centers. The upper initial center is the pullback of the lower one along the flat stage-zero comparison. Flat base change of blowups gives a pullback square for the blowup morphisms. The initial identifications express the stage-zero comparison by the original base map, and the upper center is proper. These data give the comparison of the length-one sequences.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.sequenceOfBlowupsPullback_blowupAtCenter: The final comparison of the existing sequences is a pullback square, with a flat last-stage map. The transformed upper ideal is the pullback of the lower one, and its boundary has the same nonunit ideals in order as the pulled-back lower boundary. This follows from the comparison of marked transforms on the Noetherian stages. The assumed preservation of order applies to the final square. Use the flat center comparison on the final triples. Admissibility upstairs implies a positive upper minimum, hence a positive lower one. If the lower center is admissible, it has positive minimum. The center comparison either makes its pullback the unit ideal, allowing the single lower step to be omitted upstairs, or identifies it with the upper center at a positive upper minimum. In the latter case the upper center is admissible and the single steps on both sides extend the comparison.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.smooth_fst_of_isPullback: The indicated projection to the lower scheme is obtained by base change of the given smooth morphism. Smoothness is preserved by base change.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsMonomialIn.comap_of_isMonomialIn: At the image of the given point, choose an open on which the ideal is a product of powers of boundary ideals. Take its inverse image as the neighborhood upstairs. Restriction and pullback commute, and pullback preserves products and powers. The pulled-back boundary has one entry at each original index, so the original exponents give the required product upstairs.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_comap_ι: The inverse-image open, the original open and the two ambient schemes form the commutative restriction square. The two successive ideal pullbacks are pullbacks along the two composites in that square. Those composites are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.comap_finset_prod: Induct on the finite set. The pullback of the empty product is the unit ideal. Inserting an index introduces one factor, and pullback of the resulting product is the product of the pullbacks. Apply the induction hypothesis to the remaining factors.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.generalizingMap_base_of_flat: Flat morphisms satisfy going-down. Applied on affine neighborhoods, it lifts a generalization of the image of a point to a generalization of that point. Thus the underlying point map is generalizing.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.irreducibleComponents_not_subset_support: Let an upstairs component of a pulled-back boundary support have generic point ξ. Its image belongs to the downstairs boundary support. The closure of that image is a component there: if a larger irreducible subset contained the closure, take a generic point of the larger subset's closure. It generalizes the image of ξ, so the generalizing map lifts it to a generalization of ξ. This lift lies in the upstairs boundary support and its closure contains the upstairs component. Maximality puts the lift back in the component. Its image therefore lies in the closure of the image of ξ, forcing the larger set to be contained in that closure. If the upstairs component were contained in the pulled-back residual support, the image of ξ would be in the residual support, and its whole closure would be there by closedness. This contradicts the condition on the downstairs component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialSplitting_comap_of_flat: A flat morphism gives a generalizing map on points by going-down. Apply preservation of monomial splittings under pullback along a generalizing map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialSplitting_comap_of_generalizin: Pullback preserves the product identity for the monomial and residual factors. It preserves the containment of the monomial support in the boundary and carries each local monomial expression to one in the pulled-back boundary. Since the map lifts generalizations, the component argument also preserves the condition that the residual support contains no boundary component. These give the four properties of the pulled-back splitting.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialSplitting_comap_of_smooth: Smooth morphisms are flat, so preservation of the splitting under flat pullback gives the result.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.support_comap_subset_biUnion: A point in the pulled-back support maps into the original support. The assumed inclusion places its image in some listed boundary support. Thus the point belongs to the support of that pulled-back boundary ideal, which occurs in the pulled-back list.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_monomialFactorIdeal: At every point the stalk of the splitting's monomial factor equals the stalk of the canonical factor. Stalk ideals test inclusion in both directions, giving equality of the ideal sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_nonMonomialFactorIdeal: The monomial factor equals the canonical one and is locally generated by a nonzerodivisor. The original ideal is contained in that factor by the product identity. Multiplying the canonical factor by its ideal quotient into the original ideal recovers the original ideal. This is also the product with the given residual factor. Cancel the canonical factor locally using its nonzerodivisor generators to conclude equality of the residual factors.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_of_ideal_map_eq_of_ringHom_leftInvers: Extend the equal ideals along the left inverse. Successive extension is extension along the composite, which is the identity on the original ring. The resulting equality is the equality of the original ideals.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exponent_eq_orderAlongComponent: The open contains the generic point of the chosen boundary component because it meets that component. At this point, any other boundary entry whose support misses the point contributes a unit stalk. If another boundary entry contains the point, its local exponent is bounded by the original ideal's order along one of its components through the point. In the canonical monomial factor, this other entry's contribution is therefore contained in the power of the maximal ideal with that local exponent. The chosen entry's contribution is contained in the power given by the original order along the chosen component. If the other exponent were positive, the product of these two contributions would force the canonical factor to have larger order than the original ideal at the chosen generic point. The canonical factor's order there equals the original order, so the other exponent is zero. Thus the local product for the monomial factor consists, up to unit factors, of just the chosen boundary stalk raised to its exponent. This boundary stalk is the maximal ideal because the divisor is étale locally a coordinate divisor and the point is generic on its component. The order of this maximal-ideal power equals its exponent, since the order is finite. The splitting gives equality of monomial and original orders at the generic point, so the exponent is the original order along the component.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exponent_le_orderAlongComponent: The open meets the component and therefore contains its generic point. At that point the monomial stalk is a product and is contained in the factor for the chosen boundary index. That boundary stalk is contained in the maximal ideal, so the monomial stalk is contained in the power of the maximal ideal with exponent given by the local expression. The order of the monomial factor is at least that exponent. The original ideal is contained in its monomial factor by the product identity, so its order is at least as large. Its generic order is the finite order along the component, proving the bound.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.hom_apply_hom_apply_of_comp_eq: Evaluate the equality of the composite ring morphism and the given ring morphism at the specified element. Evaluation of a composite is successive evaluation.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_listProd_finRange_eq_of_ne_eq_top: The list contains one factor for each finite index. All except the specified factor are the unit ideal. Removing these unit factors leaves exactly that factor.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_listProd_le_mul_getElem_of_lt: Induct on the list. Two ordered indices cannot occur in the empty list. If the first index is the head, the product of the tail is contained in the factor at the second index, which proves the claim after multiplying by the head. If both indices are in the tail, the entire product is contained in the tail product and the induction bound applies there.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_listProd_le_mul_getElem_of_ne: Order the two distinct positions. The ordered-index bound puts the product inside the product of the entries in that order. Commutativity of ideal multiplication gives the stated order of the factors.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_listProd_le_pow_add: The full product is contained in the product of the two distinct listed factors. Substitute the bounds by the corresponding powers of the given ideal and use monotonicity of ideal multiplication. The product of the two powers is the power with the sum of the exponents.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.ideal_map_listProd: Extension of ideals along a ring map preserves multiplication and the unit ideal. Apply it successively to the factors of the list to obtain the product of their extensions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.inv_hom_apply_hom_apply: The ring morphism followed by its inverse is the identity. Evaluating this composite at the element returns that element.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.isMonomialSplitting_unique: The monomial part of each splitting equals the same canonical monomial factor. The residual part of each equals the same canonical ideal quotient. Equality through these canonical factors proves uniqueness of both parts.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.map_finRange_get_eq_map: Both lists have the same length as the original list. At each position both contain the value of the function on the original entry at that position, so they are equal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_eq_of_stalkIdeal_eq_maximalIdeal: Write the finite order as n. The stalk ideal is the a-th power of the maximal ideal, so n is at least a. If n were larger, that power would be contained in the next power. Multiplication by the maximal ideal would then leave the a-th power unchanged. Nakayama's lemma applies because the stalk is Noetherian and forces that power to vanish. This would make the order infinite, a contradiction. Hence n equals a.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_genericPoint_eq_of_isMonomialSpl: The residual support does not contain the whole boundary component. Since the support is closed, it cannot contain the generic point either. The residual factor has order zero there. The order of the product is the sum of the orders at this point, so the original ideal and its monomial factor have the same order.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_eq_prod_of_isMonomialOnOpen: Choose the point of the open subscheme corresponding to the given ambient point. Take stalks of the monomial identity on the open. Stalk ideals preserve products and powers, and the stalks of restricted ideals are extensions along the stalk map of the inclusion. This stalk map is an isomorphism. Applying its inverse to the resulting equality gives the product formula in the ambient stalk.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.stalkIdeal_eq_stalkIdeal_monomialFactorI: Choose a local monomial expression at the point and take its stalk. If a boundary divisor contains the point, choose a component of its support through the point. The exponent formula identifies its local exponent with the order of the original ideal along that component, and the canonical factor along the divisor has the same stalk power. If the point is off the divisor, both factors have unit stalks. The stalk products for the local monomial expression and the canonical monomial factor therefore agree factor by factor.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.IsComponentCompatiblePullback.of_flat: Apply the geometry hypotheses to the given flat map and the two admissible objects. They identify pullbacks of the chosen component-union centers and give both directions of the correspondence between downstairs and upstairs intersection components. The remaining compatibility, preservation of order, is the assumed equality at each point.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.orderAt_comap_eq_of_notMem_exceptionalId: The exceptional ideal is the pullback of the center ideal, so their supports are related by inverse image. Thus a point off the exceptional support maps outside the center. The blowup is an isomorphism there, and its map on stalk rings at the given point is an isomorphism. It identifies the two ideal stalks and the powers of the maximal ideals, so the orders agree.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.eq_of_isBlowupAlongIdealSheaf_of_notMem_: On the complement of the center the blowup is an isomorphism, since it is the blowup of the unit ideal there. Both points are in the preimage of this complement. The restricted blowup is injective on points, so equality of their images gives equality upstairs.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_eq_closure_of_isIrreducibleCompon: The component of the strict-transform support is closed by maximality, so it has a generic point. A Noetherian component has an ambient open meeting the strict-transform support only within that component. The support is the closure of the inverse image of the divisor away from the center, so this open meets that inverse image. Its intersection with the component shows that the generic point lies off the exceptional locus. Its image lies on the divisor because the inverse image of the divisor is closed and contains the strict-transform support. Take the closure of this image point inside the divisor. To prove maximality, suppose an irreducible subset of the divisor contains that closure and take a generic point of its closure. This point lies off the center, since it specializes to the image point off the center. The blowup is an isomorphism off the center, so lift it to a point specializing to the chosen upper generic point. The lift is in the strict-transform support. Its closure contains the original upper component and must equal it by maximality. Mapping back shows that the larger downstairs subset lies in the closure of the original image point. That closure is therefore an irreducible component of the divisor and meets the complement of the center.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Em.exists_isOpen_inter_subset_of_maximal: Write the closed set as a finite union of irreducible closed subsets using Noetherianity. Remove the union of those pieces that are not contained in the given maximal irreducible subset. The complement is open, and its intersection with the original closed set lies in the maximal subset. If that intersection were empty, the removed pieces would cover the maximal subset.
