Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exceptionalIdeal_eq_comap: The exceptional ideal is defined to be the pullback of the center ideal along the blowup.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosedImmersion_lift_comp: The lift through the closed immersion is defined to factor the given map. The defining identity says that its composite with the immersion is the given map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.ker_le_ker_pullbackFst: The map from the pullback to the intermediate scheme, followed by the given factorization to the first source, has the same composite to the base as the first projection. Cancel the monomorphism to identify it with that projection. Thus the projection factors through the indicated morphism to the first source, whose kernel is contained in the kernel of the projection.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.schemeImageIdeal_eq_ker: The image ideal of the subscheme is the scheme-theoretic kernel of its inclusion followed by the given morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.strictTransformImmersion_eq: The defining map first includes the open part in the total-transform closed subscheme, then includes that subscheme in the blowup scheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.strictTransformOpens_eq: In the closed subscheme of the total transform, the defining open for the strict transform is the inverse image of the complement of the exceptional support.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.strictTransform_eq_ker: The strict-transform ideal is the ideal of the scheme-theoretic image of the open part off the exceptional support. By definition it is the kernel of the map from this open part to the blowup scheme.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_affineOpens_mem: The union of all affine opens is the whole scheme. Membership in this union gives an affine open containing the given point.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_affineOpens_mem_le: The affine opens form a basis. Refine the given open neighborhood to a basis member containing the point and contained in that neighborhood.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_isAffineOpen_mem: Affine opens form a basis for the topology of a scheme. Apply this basis property to the point in the whole scheme to obtain an affine neighborhood.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.appLE_congr_hom: Identify the two morphisms. The induced restriction on the specified opens is then the same map of sections.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.appLE_mem_comap_ideal: The image of the given section belongs to the extended ideal by the definition of extension. The affine pullback formula includes that ideal in the pullback section ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.appLE_top_eq_appTop: For the whole source and target, the restriction after applying the map on sections is the restriction from the whole source to itself. It is the identity, so the restricted map is the global map.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_finset_prod: Induct on the finite indexing set. For the empty set use preservation of the unit ideal. Inserting a new index multiplies the old product by its factor. Pullback preserves this multiplication, and the induction hypothesis applies to the old product.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_iSup: Ideal pullback is the left adjoint in the ideal-sheaf image and pullback Galois connection. Left adjoints preserve suprema, giving the stated equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ideal_eq_ker_pullbackFst: The pullback ideal is the scheme-theoretic kernel of the first projection from the pulled-back closed subscheme. This projection is affine as a base change of a closed immersion. On an affine open its ideal of sections is therefore the kernel of the induced ring map on sections.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ideal_eq_map_appLE: On the affine source open the pullback ideal is the kernel of the map on sections of the pulled-back closed subscheme. The extended ideal is contained in this kernel because its generators vanish on that subscheme. Conversely the quotient by the extended ideal factors through the section map of the pullback, so every element of the kernel belongs to the extended ideal. Together the inclusions give equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ideal_eq_span_image: By the affine pullback formula the new ideal is the extension of the old one. Extension sends an ideal generated by a set to the ideal generated by the images of the set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ideal_top_eq_map_appTop: Apply the affine section formula with each open equal to its whole scheme. The restricted section map for those opens is the map on global sections.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ker_comp_of_isOpenImmersion: On an affine open of the intermediate scheme its image under the open immersion is affine, and the section map from this image is an isomorphism. The inverse images of these corresponding opens under the two remaining maps are the same. Functoriality of section maps therefore identifies the map of the composite with the intermediate scheme's map after transport by section isomorphisms. Its kernel extends to exactly the kernel on the intermediate affine open. This holds on all of its affine opens and proves the ideal-sheaf equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_listProd: The empty product is the unit ideal, preserved by pullback. For a nonempty list, pullback preserves the product of the head with the tail product. Apply induction to the tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_mul: Cover the source by affine opens each mapping into an affine open of the target. Such neighborhoods exist because affine opens form a basis in both schemes. On each source open the affine pullback formula is extension of the target section ideals, which commutes with products. Equality on this cover gives equality of the sheaves.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ofIdealTop: The two ideal sheaves have the same global section ideal by the affine pullback formula and the affine ideal correspondence. Since affine ideal sheaves are determined by their global section ideals, the sheaves agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_pow: At exponent zero both schemes have the unit ideal, which pullback preserves. The successor power is a product of the preceding power with the original ideal. Apply preservation of products and the induction hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_subschemeι_self: The ideal is the image of the zero ideal along its closed-subscheme inclusion, since this image is the kernel of that inclusion. Pulling back an image ideal is contained in the starting ideal by the general pullback-image inequality. Thus the restriction is contained in the zero ideal, and equality follows.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ι_comp_eq_of_comap_ι_eq: The map from the source open into the target factors through the chosen target open. Pulling back either ideal along that composite is thus pulling back its restriction to the target open. These restrictions are equal by hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_ι_eq_top_iff_ideal_eq_top: On the affine open the pulled-back ideal sheaf is determined by its global section ideal. This ideal is the extension of the original section ideal along the section-ring isomorphism for the open inclusion. A ring isomorphism preserves and reflects the unit ideal. Use the affine correspondence on the open subscheme to conclude the equivalence.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.eq_top_iff_support_eq_empty: The ideal-sheaf support is the least closed subset exactly for the unit ideal. The least closed subset is the empty set.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_hom_comp_eq_appLE_comp: Compose the section map with the given map to the target ring. The kernel hypothesis makes this composite vanish on the original ideal. It therefore factors through the quotient by that ideal. Identify this quotient with the sections of the closed subscheme on the inverse image of the affine open. The quotient lift gives the desired map and composite identity.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_hom_pullbackFst_app_comp_eq: The two specified ring maps give maps from the spectrum of the target ring to the affine source open and to the corresponding affine open of the closed subscheme. Their composites into the original target agree because the given equality of ring maps reverses to that equality of scheme morphisms. The two maps therefore lift to the pullback, with projection to the source the map from the first ring homomorphism. The whole spectrum maps into the inverse image of the source open under this projection. Take the resulting map of sections and identify the global sections of that spectrum with its ring. Compatibility of the lift with the first projection says that the resulting map factors the original ring homomorphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_iso_subscheme_comap_of_isIso: For an isomorphism, the kernel of the pulled-back subscheme inclusion followed by the isomorphism pulls back to the original pulled-back ideal by the open-immersion kernel comparison. Pullback along the inverse shows that the kernel before pulling back was the original ideal. The closed immersions into the target thus have the same kernel, so the universal property gives an isomorphism between their sources commuting with both inclusions.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.idealSheafData_prod_cons: A list product is defined recursively by multiplying its first factor by the product of its tail.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.idealSheafData_prod_nil: The empty product is the multiplicative identity of ideal sheaves, which is the unit ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isReduced_of_ringEquiv: The image of a nilpotent element under the ring isomorphism is nilpotent and hence zero in the reduced target ring. Injectivity forces the original element to be zero.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isReduced_stalk_of_radical: Choose an affine neighborhood of the image of the point in the ambient scheme. Its inverse image under the closed immersion is affine, with section ring the quotient by the corresponding ideal. This quotient is reduced because the ideal is radical. An affine scheme with reduced section ring has reduced local rings, since localization preserves reducedness. The stalk of this open at the point is the original stalk on the closed subscheme.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isReduced_subscheme_vanishingIdeal: On each affine open, the vanishing ideal is an intersection of primes and therefore radical. The radical-ideal argument shows that every stalk of its closed subscheme is reduced. Reducedness is local on stalks, so the subscheme is reduced.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.ker_pullbackFst_le_map_appLE: Take the quotient of the affine source section ring by the extended ideal. The quotient map vanishes on extensions of the original ideal. It therefore factors through the section ring of the pulled-back closed subscheme by the two factorization lemmas. Any section vanishing under the pullback projection also vanishes in this quotient, so it belongs to the extended ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.map_appLE_le_comap_ideal: The affine pullback formula identifies the extended ideal with the pulled-back section ideal. The quoted inclusion follows from this equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.map_appLE_le_ker_pullbackFst: The commutative pullback square identifies the two composites on sections, after restricting to the inverse image of the indicated source open. A section in the original ideal maps to zero on its closed subscheme. It therefore maps to zero along either composite. All generators of the extended ideal are in the kernel of the section map of the first projection, giving the inclusion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.mem_basicOpen_iff_notMem_primeIdealOf: The affine identification sends the corresponding prime ideal to the given point. The inverse image of the scheme's basic open is the basic open of the same element in the affine spectrum. A prime lies in this basic open exactly when it does not contain the element.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.mem_support_comap: The closed support of the pulled-back ideal is the inverse image of the original support. The two membership statements are the defining property of inverse image.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.mem_support_iff_ideal_le_primeIdealOf: On the affine open the support is the zero locus of the ideal of sections. A point is in this locus precisely when it belongs to none of the basic opens of the ideal's sections. Under the affine identification this says that every section of the ideal belongs to the point's prime ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.ne_top_of_mem_support: If the ideal were unit, its support would be empty. The given point in the support contradicts this.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.noetherianSpace_subscheme: The closed immersion identifies the subscheme topologically with a subspace of the ambient scheme. Subspaces of a Noetherian space are Noetherian.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.notMem_support_of_comap_ι_eq_top: If the given point were in the original support, its representative on the open would lie in the restricted support by the inverse-image formula. The restricted ideal is unit, and thus has empty support, a contradiction.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.ofIdealTop_ideal_top: The affine correspondence takes an ideal sheaf to its ideal of global sections. The construction from the chosen ideal is the inverse correspondence, so taking its global sections recovers the ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.ofIdealTop_mul: On each affine open, building a sheaf from a global ideal extends that ideal along the restriction of global sections. Extension commutes with products. Thus the two proposed sheaves have the same ideal on every affine open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.support_nonempty_iff_ne_top: A support is nonempty exactly when it differs from the empty set. By the unit ideal criterion this is exactly the condition that the ideal is nonunit.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.exists_sigmaι_base_eq: Take the union of the open images of the summand inclusions. Every inclusion factors through this open. The factorizations assemble into a map to the union by the coproduct property. Its composite with the inclusion agrees with the identity on every summand and hence is the identity. Thus the union is surjective on points. Each point therefore lies in one summand image, giving the desired index and preimage.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosedEmbedding_coprod_inl_base: The left inclusion is an open embedding on points and hence an embedding. Its image is closed by the complement argument, so it is a closed embedding.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosedEmbedding_coprod_inr_base: The right inclusion is an embedding on points because it is an open immersion. Its closed image makes it a closed embedding.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosedEmbedding_sigmaι_base: The summand inclusion is an embedding on points because it is an open immersion. The assumed closedness of its range makes it a closed embedding.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosedImmersion_sigmaι: The summand inclusion is already an open immersion and therefore an embedding with the requisite map on sheaves. Its image is also closed by the summand complement argument, so it is a closed immersion.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosed_range_coprod_inl: The complement of the left range is the right range. The right inclusion is an open immersion, so this complement is open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosed_range_coprod_inr: The right range is the complement of the left range, which is open. Thus the right range is closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosed_range_sigmaι: A point outside the chosen summand lies in some other summand, since the summand images cover the coproduct. That other image is open and disjoint from the chosen summand. Thus every point of the complement has an open neighborhood in the complement, so the chosen image is closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isOpen_range_coprod_inl: The left inclusion is an open immersion, and the image of an open immersion is open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.quasiCompact_sigmaι: The summand inclusion is a closed embedding on points. The inverse image of a quasi-compact open is homeomorphic to its intersection with the closed range, which is a closed subset of that quasi-compact open. It is therefore quasi-compact.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.range_coprod_inr_eq_compl: The two summands of the coproduct have disjoint images whose union is the whole scheme. The right image is therefore the complement of the left image.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.range_sigmaι_subset_iUnion: The range of the open inclusion is the union of the summand images. A point from the chosen summand lies in this union by taking its given index.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.sigmaι_base_ne: Equality of images in the coproduct implies equality of the corresponding points of the disjoint union. Taking their first coordinates would identify the two summand indices, contrary to the hypothesis.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.surjective_base_of_comp_eq_id: For any point of the target of the second map, apply the first map to obtain a preimage. Evaluating the composite identity at the point shows that the second map sends this preimage back to it.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.appLE_congr_hom: After identifying the morphisms, the opens and the inclusion condition are the same. Their induced restricted maps on sections therefore agree.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.comap_map_of_isClosedImmersion: The general image and pullback inequality gives one containment. The factorization through the original closed subscheme for a closed immersion gives the reverse containment, proving equality.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.finite_range_connectedComponent: Every point belongs to an irreducible component, which is connected and therefore contained in the point's connected component. For each irreducible component, take the union of the connected components of its points. This equals the connected component of any one of its points. Every connected component is obtained this way from one of finitely many irreducible components.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isAffineHom_pullback_fst: The first projection in the pullback square is a base change of the affine map. Affineness is stable under base change.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isAffineHom_pullback_fst_specMap_of_fiel: The map of spectra induced by the field homomorphism is affine. The indicated first projection is its base change, so it is affine as well.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isAffineHom_specMap: A ring homomorphism gives the corresponding map of affine spectra. Its inverse image of a basic open is the spectrum of the corresponding localization, so the morphism is affine.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isClosed_setOf_connectedComponent_subset: The set is the union of the connected components that lie within the given set. Membership in one such component is equivalent to having it as one's own component. There are finitely many components, each closed, so this union is closed.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isOpen_connectedComponent_of_noetherianS: There are finitely many irreducible components, each closed. Since an irreducible component is connected, any one meeting the given connected component lies entirely in it. Every point outside belongs to some irreducible component disjoint from it. Thus the complement is the union of the finitely many irreducible components outside it. This is closed, so the connected component is open.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.isThin_directedAffineCover_I₀: Morphisms in the index category record the order relation of the opens. Between two fixed opens they are proofs of the same inclusion, so any two such morphisms coincide.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.le_comap_map_of_isClosedImmersion: The image ideal is the kernel of the closed-subscheme inclusion followed by the given closed immersion. This kernel identifies the closed subscheme of the image ideal with a subscheme factoring through that composite, by the universal property of the closed immersion. In the pullback defining the inverse image ideal, compose the projection to this image subscheme with that factorization. The resulting map to the original closed subscheme followed by its inclusion agrees with the pullback projection to the original ambient scheme, because both agree after composing with the given monomorphism. The kernel of the projection therefore contains the kernel of the original closed-subscheme inclusion, which is the original ideal.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.noetherianSpace_toScheme: The open subscheme has the topology induced by its inclusion into the original scheme. Subspaces of Noetherian spaces are Noetherian.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.presheaf_map_eq_of_parallel: The category of opens is a poset category, so parallel morphisms in its opposite category are equal. Applying the presheaf to this equality gives equality of the restriction maps.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.quasiCompact_of_compactSpace_of_subsingl: The inverse image of any open in a target with at most one point is empty or the whole source. The former is quasi-compact, and the latter is quasi-compact by the given hypothesis. This is the quasi-compactness condition for the morphism.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.range_comp_base: A point of the composite range is obtained by applying the second map to an image point of the first map. Conversely, a point in the second image of the first range is obtained from a point of the first source, so lies in the range of the composite.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Fo.small_directedAffineCover_I₀: The indexing type for the directed affine cover already lies in the specified universe, so it is small in that universe.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.functorialPrincipalizationCharZero: Take the principalization algorithm with radical centers. Its functoriality theorem supplies the hypotheses for passing from this algorithm to a characteristic-zero principalization rule.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.functorialPrincipalizationCharZero_of_al: Define the rule by converting the input simple normal crossing boundary to strict normal crossing data and then taking the underlying blowup sequence of the algorithm. Its final recorded ideal is unit by the algorithm's principalization property, so the sequence principalizes by the total-transform argument. The algorithm's smooth pullback and field extension properties apply to the same converted boundary data and give the required functoriality of the rule.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.functorialResolutionCharZero: Apply the characteristic-zero strong resolution theorem. Retain the length, tower, initial identification, centers, and blowup property of each resulting sequence. These are the blowup sequences required in the present formulation. The resolution and functoriality properties are exactly those supplied by strong resolution.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.hasSimpleNormalCrossingsWith_of_hasStric: For a point on the subscheme, use the chart and coordinate labels supplied by the strict normal crossing condition. Unpack the chart into its map, compatibility over the base, and étaleness. Keep its coordinate descriptions of the subscheme and boundary, which give the simple normal crossing condition.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.hasSimpleNormalCrossings_of_inStrictNorm: Retain the common smoothness condition. At each point unpack the strict normal crossing chart into the map, base compatibility, and étaleness. The same coordinate labels and boundary descriptions then give simple normal crossings.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.inStrictNormalCrossingPosition_of_hasSim: Keep the given smoothness condition. At each point the simple normal crossing data give an open chart, an étale map compatible with the structural maps, and coordinate labels for the boundary. Package the map and its two properties as an étale chart. The labels and their ideal descriptions then give strict normal crossing position.
Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/Ha.isPrincipalizingSequence_of_idealBlowupS:
At stage zero the total transform of the original ideal is the recorded ideal, and the exceptional product is unit. At a successor, pull back the preceding identity along the blowup. The marked step formula factors the pulled-back recorded ideal as the new exceptional ideal times the next recorded ideal. The recurrence for the exceptional product adds this factor to the pullback of the previous product. Induction gives the total-transform factorization at every stage. At the final stage the recorded ideal is unit, so the total transform equals the product of the exceptional ideals.

Use the given tracked ideals and boundary to supply the remaining principalization properties. The step and center conditions come from the marked data. The original scheme is Noetherian by local finite type and quasi-compactness over the field, so the boundary remains in strict normal crossing position at each stage. Convert the strict normal crossing data for the boundaries and the centers to the required simple normal crossing formulations.

Development/ResolutionOfSingularities/St.structMap_down: The structural map of a stage is its transition to stage zero followed by the initial isomorphism. The tower is a functor on the opposite ordered set, so the transition from the later stage to the earlier one followed by the transition to zero is the direct transition to zero. Postcompose this identity with the initial isomorphism.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.critLine:
A zero strictly to the right of the critical line contradicts the assumed nonvanishing at once. Suppose it lies strictly to the left. The gamma factor at s is nonzero, so the completed L-function also vanishes there. The inverse character is primitive because inversion preserves its conductor. Its functional equation now gives a zero of the completed L-function at 1 − s.

Dividing by the gamma factor transfers that zero to the ordinary L-function of the inverse character. The point 1 − s has real part greater than 1/2 and is distinct from 1, so this again contradicts the assumed nonvanishing. The remaining possibility is Re(s) = 1/2.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.gammaFactor_ne_zero: For an even character the factor is Γℝ(s), and for an odd character it is Γℝ(s + 1). Both arguments have positive real part. The real gamma factor is nonzero in that half-plane.
Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/CritLi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_every: Take the trivial character of modulus 1, whose L-function equals the zeta function. The assumed nonvanishing for all characters therefore excludes zeta zeros with real part greater than 1/2 away from 1. The reduction for zeros of the zeta function now gives the Riemann Hypothesis.

Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/RhOfRi.Formalism.VW.rh_of_right:
Let s be a nontrivial zero distinct from 1. The value of zeta at 0 also excludes s = 0. The assumed nonvanishing rules out Re(s) > 1/2. If Re(s) < 1/2, set t = 1 − s. Then Re(t) > 1/2 and t is distinct from 1, so ζ(t) is nonzero. The functional equation expresses ζ(s) as the product of ζ(t), Γ(t), cos(πt/2), and 2(2π)^(−t). The gamma and power factors are nonzero.

If the cosine vanished, t would equal 2k + 1 for an integer k, giving s = −2k. A negative k contradicts Re(s) < 1/2. The value k = 0 gives s = 0, and a positive k gives an excluded trivial zero. Thus the cosine factor is also nonzero. This contradicts ζ(s) = 0, so Re(s) = 1/2.

Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.FullTiedNoG.toFull_base: Completing the datum copies the underlying tied data from X and adds g. Its base projection is therefore the original base of X.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.FullTiedNoG.toFull_g: Completing the datum sets the G-data to g. The G-data are therefore the supplied g.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.adSet: The change of datum replaces the assigned G-data and its dimension certificate. The adjacency conditions use the original lattice and step data, the Hermitian columns, and the data at T. The change of datum copies the Hermitian columns and the data at T field by field. Consequently the upward, downward, and dilation conditions at level zero and at positive levels are identical to the six supplied conditions in h. Use those six fields for the new adjacency structure.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.full_setting_level_zero: The adjusted tied datum is built by applying the Hermitian change of datum to the original base. That change copies the level-zero field, so the completed datum has the original level-zero data.
Formalism/LocalToGlobal/GroupLattices/Ti.hermitian_setting_level_zero: The change of datum copies the tied Hermitian fields from H. In particular, its level-zero Hermitian data are those of H.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.int_mul: Choose elements of the ring of integers mapping to a and c. Their product maps to ac because the inclusion is multiplicative. Thus ac also lies in the image.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sum_top: Reindex the finite sum along the given embedding. Applying the summand to the selected coordinate of the image returns its original value, so the reindexed sum agrees term by term with the sum over the original set.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.block: Expand the sum over the eight residues. The four even residues contribute zero. The remaining terms are the powers at 8m + 1 and 8m + 7 with positive signs and at 8m + 3 and 8m + 5 with negative signs. This is the defining expression of the block.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi0: The residue 0 is even, so the character modulo 8 takes the value zero there.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi1: The residue 1 is congruent to 1 modulo 8, so the character takes the value one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi2: The residue 2 is even, so the character modulo 8 takes the value zero there.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi3: The residue 3 belongs to the pair of residues ±3 modulo 8, on which the character takes the value minus one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi4: The residue 4 is even, so the character modulo 8 takes the value zero there.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi5: The residue 5 is congruent to −3 modulo 8, so the character takes the value minus one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi6: The residue 6 is even, so the character modulo 8 takes the value zero there.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi7: The residue 7 is congruent to −1 modulo 8, so the character takes the value one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi_apply: The complex character is obtained by embedding the values of the integer character modulo 8 into the complex numbers. Evaluating this construction at x gives the formula.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.chi_cast: Reducing 8m + r modulo 8 gives the same residue as reducing r. The character therefore has the same value at both.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.tm_eval: Since r is positive, the index 8m + r is positive. Use the defining quotient for the Dirichlet series term and reduce its numerator modulo 8. Dividing by the positive base raised to s is multiplication by the same base raised to −s.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.tm_zero: The term at index zero is defined to be zero. At a positive index 8m + r, the numerator is the character value at r by periodicity. This value vanishes by hypothesis, so the term is zero in that case as well.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.corollary_final_model: Take μ = 0, the logarithmic term equal to 1, deletion parameter 1/8, both size parameters equal to 1, and height 32. Take x = 2, c = 5 and b = 1, so the height bound is an equality. Use e₀ = 1/131072, e = 2e₀, d = 1/36864 and C₁ = 3. The two square roots are 1/192 and 1/256, and their weighted contributions add to 1/32, which is the reciprocal of 2 to the power five. Set η to 5/32 + 3/192. These values satisfy the positivity and size conditions. Taking s equal to 1 plus the resulting error gives the final equality, while the preceding numerical bound gives s ≤ 32.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.corollary_model_side_condition: The square root of twice 1/131072 is 1/256. Substituting the parameters makes the error equal to (8/7)(4 log(33) + 6). Since 33 ≤ 64, log(33) ≤ 6 log(2). The bound log(2) < 7/10 follows because the first four terms of the exponential series at 7/10 already sum to more than 2. Hence one plus the error is less than 947/35, which is below 32.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.discriminant_windows_iff: Setting β and the initial scale to zero leaves every common window condition intact. For the two new upper bounds, the reciprocal of x² is nonnegative and remains nonnegative after multiplication by K ≥ 1. Thus both zero parameters meet their lower and upper bounds. Conversely, discard the bounds on these two parameters to recover the discriminant conditions.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.discriminant_windows_of: The discriminant conditions are precisely the ordinary window conditions with the bounds on β and the initial scale omitted. The other inequalities are inherited directly.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.io_discriminant_bound: Multiply the pointwise bound on the index by the nonnegative logarithm of p. The resulting term is the signature part of the weighted candidate sum scaled by amT. The indicator contribution is nonnegative, so including it can only increase the upper bound. Summing and using the assumed candidate bound yields amTR.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.joint_core: Take the larger of zero and the constant in the first-kind estimate. The window and large-x assumptions give the auxiliary inequalities, and the nonempty top set ensures that its size is at least one. At any unit, apply the basic loss estimate, then bound the omitted, first-kind and second-kind contributions by their corresponding prime estimates. Their sum is controlled by the total size bound. Separately apply the weighted candidate estimate to the index sum and use the ninth-power size bound. These give the explicit inequalities. Since twice log(4) is at most three, the first-prime constant is nonnegative, and the slope allowance is at most one, the explicit bounds imply the two simpler bounds in the same nonnegative unit.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.joint_discriminant_bound: Use the nonnegative constant furnished by the joint estimate. Set β and the initial scale to zero and transfer the discriminant conditions to the ordinary window conditions by the equivalence. All parameters occurring in the prime constraints and conclusions are preserved by this change. The simpler pair of joint bounds gives the conclusion.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.joint_discriminant_eventually: Keep the nonnegative constant from the joint discriminant bound. For the given ε, e and K, the eventual large-x estimate supplies a threshold above which its hypotheses hold. Substitute the specified value of the parameter ε, and apply the joint bound to each set of windows above the threshold.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.logdiv_nonneg: The logarithm of a natural number in the stated real convention is nonnegative, including zero at the zero input. The denominator is also nonnegative, so their quotient is nonnegative.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.out_discriminant_bound: For each served prime, every omitted top index must be marked bad, and any prime with such an omission belongs to the designated prime set. Thus for primes in that set the omission count is at most the bad count, and for other primes it is zero. Multiply by the nonnegative weights and extend the resulting sum to the full designated set. Factoring out 4am leaves the assumed weighted count, which is at most R.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.second_discriminant_bound: The second-prime estimate bounds the loss by summing 4amT log(p)/p over candidates whose indicator threshold is exceeded. Each such term is exactly the contribution from the indicator part of the weighted sum multiplied by 2amT. The remaining signature contributions are nonnegative, so the loss is bounded by 2amT times the full weighted sum. Use its bound by R.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sizeIo_core: The coefficient a/x⁹ is nonnegative and no larger than 2a/x⁹. The ninth-power estimate bounds the latter by b times the slope allowance. Multiplying by mT yields the index bound.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sizeOut_core: Write z = x to the power ε and r = 1/x. Since a = xb, the coefficient 4a times x to the power −2 + ε is 4bzr. The large-x estimate bounds 100zr by the slope allowance. Multiply by the nonnegative factor 4b/100 to get the desired bound by b times that allowance. Scaling by mT gives the claimed size estimate.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sizeSecond_core: The ninth-power bound controls the coefficient 2a/x⁹ by b times the slope allowance. Multiplication by the nonnegative mT gives the bound in the normalized size unit.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.size_core: Expand the total size into its eleven contributions. Apply the separate bounds for floors, the auxiliary-prime count, the low and high prime ranges, the order terms, the omitted terms, the band and high terms, the discriminant and the second-prime term. Adding the coefficients gives twice log(4) times the first-prime constant plus thirteen times the slope allowance, all multiplying the common unit.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.size_ninth_power_bound: Write r = 1/x. The coefficient 2a/x⁹ is 2br⁸ because a = xb. Since 0 < r ≤ 1, r⁷ ≤ 1. The large-x estimate at exponent zero bounds 100r by the slope allowance. Thus 2br⁸, which is (2b/100)r⁷ times 100r, is at most b times the allowance.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.deletion_eventual_holds: Since ε/7 > 0, eventually x to that power is at least six. Its exponential is at least one plus the power, hence at least seven. Taking the reciprocal gives an upper bound of 1/7 for the exponential decay and thus for the deletion parameter.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.ev_exp: For sufficiently large x ≥ 1, the growth of x to the power δ gives |A| ≤ κ times that power divided by two. Also log(x) grows more slowly than the same power, so B log(x) is at most the other half of κ times that power. Since A ≤ exp(|A|), the expression A times x to the power B is bounded above by exp(|A| + B log(x)). The two preceding bounds control this exponential by the one in the claim.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.round_window_eventual: The definitions simplify the window to xn times exp of x to the power ε/3. Use the bound on m to bound the desired left side by c times x to the power 1/2 + ε/2 + ε. Exponential domination makes this at most the exponential factor for all sufficiently large x. Since x ≥ 1 and n ≥ 1, multiplication by xn only increases that upper bound.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.rounding_rd_holds: Split the place sum according to whether the assigned prime belongs to the rounding set. Outside the set the differences are nonpositive. In the set they are at most one, so the total is bounded by twice the sum of the corresponding place weights. Group these weights by prime to get twice the sum of their logarithms. The primes at most X″ contribute at most twice log(4) times X″ by the Chebyshev bound. Every larger prime is among the three specified exceptions, whose doubled logarithms together are at most 6X″. Add both parts.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sigma_window_eventual: Take a common sufficiently large threshold for two applications of exponential domination. The logarithmic lower bound on T and m ≥ 1 give T ≥ exp(x to the power ε divided by two). Combining this with f ≤ x to the power e and the first domination estimate bounds the deficit by the square of x to the power −c_H divided by 2(C₁ + 1), with the full quotient squared. Thus C₁ times its square root is at most half of x to the power −c_H. The second domination estimate bounds sixteen times exp of minus x to the power ε/8 by x to the power −c_H. The assumed square-root bound and √2 ≤ 2 therefore give the same half bound for four times the square root of twice the other error. Add the half bounds.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.xe: The base 10 is positive, so taking the one-hundredth power of the four-hundredth power multiplies the exponents. Their product is 4.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.algebraMap_pow_ne_zero: An irreducible uniformizer is nonzero and so is each of its powers in the domain. The inclusion into the fraction field is injective, so the image of the power is nonzero.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.claim1: A vector in the cut lies in the scaled lattice and in V. The identity for intersecting a scaled lattice with V puts it in the scaled intersection, as required.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.claim2: A vector in the left-hand intersection is the uniformizer power times an element m of the lattice. The power is invertible over the fraction field, so if the product belongs to V, then m also belongs to V. This gives membership on the right. Conversely, scaling a lattice element of V leaves it in V and puts it in the scaled lattice.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.claimC_lattice_intersection: The cut is contained in the scaled intersection, and the scaled intersection is contained in the original intersection. The intersection identity identifies the middle lattice. Add lengths along this tower. The lower part contributes exactly the rank times τ, and the upper part is at most the sum of the truncated diagonal exponents. This gives all three assertions.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.cut_bottom_eq: The intersection lattice is finite and free. Apply the uniformizer-power quotient formula to it. The length is its rank multiplied by the exponent.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.cut_top_bound: Intersect the scaled lattice and its submodule given by meeting N with V. The resulting quotient injects into the quotient before intersecting with V, so its length is at most the original length. Identify the numerator with the scaled intersection and use the diagonal calculation for the original quotient.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.example:316: The p-adic integers form a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer p. The standard lattice has its coordinate basis and spans over the fraction field. Apply the lattice intersection bound with the full space, diagonal exponents 1 and 3, and scaling exponent 2. The resulting length inequality is the stated specialization.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.example:327: Under truncated natural subtraction, 1 − 2 is zero and 3 − 2 is one. Their sum is one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.latV_free: View the intersection as a submodule of the finite free lattice M. It is finitely generated because the discrete valuation ring is noetherian, and it is torsion-free because M is. Over a discrete valuation ring, a finite torsion-free module is free. The submodule inside M identifies with the original intersection.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.length_inf_le: The inclusion of B intersected with V into B gives a map of the corresponding quotients. If the image of a class is zero, its representative belongs to A, and it already belongs to V. Thus it belongs to the intersection in the denominator, so the map is injective. Length is monotone under injections.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.length_quot_diagSub: The basis isomorphism takes the diagonal submodule to the product of the coordinate ideals. Thus the quotient is the product of the quotients by those ideals. The uniformizer generates the maximal ideal, whose k-th power has quotient of length k. Add the lengths of these finitely many coordinate quotients.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.length_quot_pow_smul: Choose a finite basis of the free lattice. A vector is a uniformizer power times another lattice vector exactly when each of its coordinates is divisible by that power. The forward implication follows by scaling coordinates, and the reverse follows by taking the vector with the coordinate quotients. The diagonal length formula therefore adds the same exponent once for each basis element.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.length_top_part: Multiplication by the uniformizer power identifies M with its scaled lattice because the scalar acts injectively and the scaled lattice is its image. Under this identification, the intersection with N pulls back to the vectors whose i-th coordinates are divisible by the uniformizer to the truncated exponent eᵢ − τ. The diagonal quotient length formula now gives the sum of these exponents.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.length_tower: The inclusion of B into C induces an injection from B/A into C/A because a representative maps to zero exactly when it belongs to A. The natural map from C/A onto C/B is surjective and its kernel consists of classes represented by elements of B. These maps form a short exact sequence, so length is additive.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.mem_diagSub: In basis coordinates the diagonal submodule consists of vectors whose i-th coordinate belongs to the principal ideal generated by the i-th power of the uniformizer. Membership in that ideal is divisibility by that power, giving the coordinatewise condition.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.pow_dvd_shift: If a ≤ τ, the left divisibility is automatic and the truncated difference a − τ is zero, so the right divisibility is automatic too. If a > τ, factor the a-th power as the τ-th power times the power with exponent a − τ. Cancel the common nonzero τ-th power.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.pow_smul_eq_zero: View the scalar as a nonzero element of the fraction field. It acts invertibly on the vector space, so a vector annihilated by this scalar must be zero.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.smul_latV_le: Every vector in the scaled intersection is the uniformizer power times a vector of the intersection. The intersection is a submodule, so it contains all such scalar multiples.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.span_eq_map_diagSub: Each scaled basis vector has divisible coordinates because all but one are zero and the remaining coordinate is its prescribed power. Hence their span lies in the image of the diagonal submodule. Conversely, a vector in that diagonal submodule has each coordinate equal to the prescribed power times a coefficient. Its basis expansion expresses its image as a linear combination of the scaled basis vectors.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.stdLat_span: The standard lattice contains the two coordinate basis vectors. Their span over the p-adic field is the entire coordinate space, so the field span of the lattice is the whole space.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.first_family_transfer_holds: The finite-coordinate form uses the trace and the square trace of the weighted matrix sum. Relabeling preserves both. The matrix-to-linear-map transfer identifies them with the two operator traces, so the trace-ratio inequalities agree.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.flat_lattice_theorem_holds: Extract the individual geometric and numerical assumptions from the grouped hypotheses. Together with the given frame estimates and their parameter bounds they are exactly the hypotheses of the flat lattice theorem. Applying it gives the slope inequality.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.frame_kernel_to_lin_sub_id: The frame kernel is c times the adjoint composed with the original map. In coordinates, composition gives matrix multiplication, the adjoint gives the conjugate transpose, and the identity map gives the identity matrix. The representation preserves scalar multiplication and subtraction, giving the formula.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hilbert_schmidt_transfer_holds: Express the linear kernel minus the identity as the map of the scalar-weighted Gram matrix minus the identity. Its squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm equals the corresponding matrix norm. For a nonnegative weight the scalar-weighted Gram matrix is exactly the diagonal kernel.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hs_norm_sq_to_euclidean_lin: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the linear map is the real part of the trace of its adjoint composed with itself. The coordinate matrix of that composite is the conjugate transpose of A times A. Its real trace is the sum of the squared moduli of the entries of A.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hs_sq_reindex: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm sums the squared moduli over row and column indices. Changing both indices by their bijections permutes the terms of this double sum, leaving it unchanged.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.input_size_transfer_holds: The two input-size formulations differ only by relabeling the row and column coordinates. The off-diagonal kernel norms and the diagonal deviation norms agree by the transfer identities. The remaining dimensions and numerical bounds are the same, so each set of conditions implies the other.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.joint_a_ramified_holds: The ramification estimate supplies two slope bounds under exactly these assumptions. Its first bound is the one required here.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.kernel_matrix_reindex: Relabel the column coordinates of each matrix by its chosen finite-coordinate bijection. In the weighted product of the first conjugate transpose and the second matrix, the common ambient relabeling cancels by a change of summation index. The two remaining relabelings act on the row and column indices of the kernel.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.matrix_trace_reindex: When rows and columns are relabeled by the same bijection, the diagonal entries are permuted by that bijection. Their sum is unchanged.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.quadratic_matrix_fin_reindex: Expand both weighted matrix sums and compare each term. In a matrix times its conjugate transpose, the common relabeling of its column coordinates cancels in the sum over those coordinates. Only the ambient relabeling remains on the product, and it commutes with the weighted sum.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.quadratic_transfer_holds: Represent the frame operator by its weighted matrix sum. Its square is then represented by the square of that sum. Tracing the operator and its square gives the corresponding two matrix traces.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.ramification_condition_holds: Apply the linear compression estimate to obtain the trace-ratio bound with parameter 5 times the scale plus 3 times the square root of the deficit, and the deviation bound with parameter twice the initial error. The supplied matrix product identifies these compressed matrices with the given family. The parameters are nonnegative and the deviation bound is at most one quarter. Apply the two flat lattice inequalities to the same geometric and numerical data to obtain both conclusions.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.ramification_linear_case_holds: Transfer the finite-size and isometry assumptions to matrices on numbered coordinates. Apply the matrix bounds for the compressed trace square and the diagonal deviation. Use the compression identity to identify their family and transfer both conclusions back to the linear maps. The square-root bound and ramification-scale bound imply that twice the initial error is at most one quarter. Finally, the original total rank is positive by the dimension lower bound, and the retained-rank estimate preserves positivity because the fractional loss is below one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.ramification_transfer_holds: Under finite-coordinate relabeling, the shared middle coordinates in the compression product are merely permuted, so the product transfers directly. The compression map is an isometry exactly when its Gram matrix is the identity. That Gram matrix is carried to the same simultaneous relabeling of rows and columns, which preserves the identity and can be reversed by the inverse bijection.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.second_family_transfer_holds: The total rank is unchanged by the finite-coordinate bijections. For each nonnegative weight the squared deviation is unchanged under reindexing, and the norm transfer identifies that same deviation with the linear-map norm. Substituting these equalities in the summed bound gives the equivalence.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sharp_flat_lattice_theorem_holds: Extract the individual geometric and numerical assumptions from the grouped hypotheses and keep the given frame bounds. Apply the sharp lattice theorem with these data to obtain the slope inequality with the stated deletion and error terms.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.slope_le_max_slope: The lattice is nonzero because it spans a vector space with positive basis cardinality. Together with finite generation and the invertible metric data, it gives a realized lattice to which the maximal-slope characterization applies. That characterization bounds the slope of the lattice itself by its maximal slope.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.to_euclidean_lin_adjoint_eq: In the standard orthonormal coordinate bases, the adjoint has the conjugate transpose matrix. Translating that matrix back to a Euclidean map gives the stated adjoint.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.to_euclidean_lin_mul: In the standard Euclidean coordinate bases, the matrix of a composite is the product of the two matrices, in the same order as their action. Thus the maps represented by both sides agree.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.to_euclidean_lin_one: The identity matrix sends each coordinate basis vector to itself, so its corresponding Euclidean linear map is the identity.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.to_euclidean_lin_trace: Use the standard orthonormal coordinate basis for the map represented by A. The trace is the sum of its diagonal coefficients in that basis, which is the matrix trace of A.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.transfer_conclusion_holds: Expand the error function and its logarithmic term. Reassociate multiplication by four with the factor u. The resulting error expression is the one in the desired conclusion, so the inequalities agree.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.transfer_fin_index_holds: The kernel and Gram-deviation reindexing identities preserve the corresponding squared norms. The ambient reindexing identity preserves the trace of the quadratic matrix and the trace of its square because it preserves matrix multiplication. Finally, the labels change only by bijections, so the total rank is unchanged.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_frame_operator_to_lin: Each weighted summand of the frame operator is the map composed with its adjoint, multiplied by its weight. The corresponding matrix is the weighted product of the matrix and its conjugate transpose. Add these identities over the family using linearity of the matrix-to-map correspondence.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_gram_eq_smul: The diagonal kernel uses the weight's square root twice. Their product is the weight itself because it is nonnegative. Factor this scalar out of the Gram matrix.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_gram_sub_one_reindex: Apply the kernel reindexing identity with both arguments equal. The identity matrix is unchanged by simultaneous reindexing of rows and columns. Subtract it to obtain the reindexed deviation.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.word_count_bound_holds: Sum the common lower bound on each coordinate dimension over the words. The result is the word count times that lower bound and is at most the total rank. The word-count hypothesis bounds the count below by C₀Γ² divided by the scale. Multiplying by the nonnegative dimension lower bound cancels C₀ and Γ², leaving the dimension parameter divided by the scale. This gives the required lower bound on the total rank.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.Ga_bound5: Use the lower bound on the mean slope to isolate the gain in the assumed slope inequality. The divisor identity replaces the combined divisor and count terms by the main term and the fixed errors. For the logarithmic error, use the upper bounds on the shifted spread and height in the logarithmic estimate. Bound the other error by replacing η, the squared-error parameter and the height by their upper bounds, using monotonicity of the square root and nonnegativity. Both errors are nonnegative, so the reciprocal deletion factor can be increased to the one using the upper bound on deletion. Adding the resulting terms gives the gain estimate.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.Vvar_bound5: Bound the exponent at the second index from above and at the first index from below. Their common center cancels, leaving twice the exponent error. The height comparison bounds the remaining difference by the weighted count difference plus the height error. Factor the total place weight out of that count difference and apply its uniform bound. The three error contributions form the variation budget.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.each_unit_bound_statement: Apply the gain estimate at the unit. The loss hypothesis bounds its index term and the excess of its requested amount over the gain. The averaged local loss is at most the uniform loss expression by the bound just proved. Since its coefficient in the logarithmic error is nonnegative, the same replacement is valid there. Combining the terms gives the pointwise result with the stated error.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.exponent_ge_lower: The absolute deviation estimate bounds the exponent minus its center below by the negative of the allowed error. Add back the center and factor out m.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.exponent_le_upper: The absolute deviation estimate bounds the exponent minus its center by the allowed error. Add back the center and factor out m.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.key_identity5: Substitute the definition of the count lower bound into the divisor expression. Its terms involving m times the logarithmic congruence parameter cancel the added term. The existing divisor identity identifies the remaining uncorrected expression with the main term. What remains is the count correction multiplied by the total place weight.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.losses_of_losses5: The two pointwise losses are each bounded by the same constant. Monotonicity of the uniform mean bounds their means by the mean of that constant, which equals the constant.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.s_lower5: At each index take the lower bound on its quotient mean slope and the lower comparison with the reference lattice slope. Use the divisor bound to control the difference between the weighted logarithmic term and its global divisor contribution, and use the count lower bound multiplied by the nonnegative total place weight. The exponent upper bound enters with a minus sign. Combining these estimates gives the same index-independent lower bound after subtracting the local loss. Taking the mean with the positive degree weights gives the stated inequality.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.u_function_le_mean: Fix an index for the maximal shifted slope and compare it with the shifted mean slope at an arbitrary second index. Use the quotient upper bound at the first index and the quotient lower bound at the second. The common gain and positive correction cancel in the difference. The reference slope bounds and the variation estimate bound what remains by the common budget plus the second index's loss. Average over the second index with the positive weights, then maximize over the first. Subtracting the shifted mean gives the result.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.uniform_bound_statement: The pointwise loss assumptions give the two aggregate loss bounds by monotonicity of the uniform mean. The weighted mean result then applies with these aggregate bounds and the remaining hypotheses.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_mean_bound_statement: Insert the bound on the average local loss into the gain estimate before averaging over units. Its index contribution has a nonnegative coefficient equal to the local loss coefficient times one plus the logarithmic multiplier. Apply linearity and monotonicity of the uniform mean to the gain bounds. Add the mean of the excess over gain to recover the mean requested amount. The two aggregate loss hypotheses bound this excess mean and the mean index, yielding the stated uniform error.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_mean_lower_bound_le: The only word-dependent term in the local loss is a nonnegative coefficient times the logarithm of its count. Use the count upper bound at each word and add the remaining fixed terms. Taking the positive weighted mean preserves this common upper bound.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.exists_unif: The prime ideal defining a finite place is nonzero and proper. The strict descent of powers of such an ideal in the ring of integers gives an element in its first power outside its second power. The first power is the ideal itself.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.cj_apply: The conjugated matrix is obtained by applying complex conjugation to each entry. Its entry at row i and column j is therefore the conjugate of the corresponding original entry.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.cj_cj: At each entry, conjugating twice returns the original complex number. Equality of all entries gives the matrix identity.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.cj_sub: Complex conjugation preserves subtraction. Apply that identity to each entry of the difference to obtain the matrix equality.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hOf_mul: Both odd factors and their product are coprime to the modulus. The unit represented by the product is the product of the units represented by the factors, as seen on their underlying residues. Passing to the quotient preserves products, which are written as sums in the additive group.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hOf_of_coprime: Under the coprimality hypothesis, the construction takes the residue of m as a unit and sends it to its quotient class, written in additive notation.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hOf_one: The residue of 1 gives the identity unit. Its quotient class is the multiplicative identity, hence zero in the additive notation.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.laV_mul: In the trivial case the function is constantly one. Otherwise use multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol in its numerator. Embedding the symbol values into the complex numbers preserves the multiplication.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.laV_one: For the trivial parameter the function is constantly one. In the other case its value at 1 is the Jacobi symbol with numerator 1, which equals one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.node_sizes_explicit: The explicit parameter bounds furnish the window-size conditions with thin width b′ divided by x times the group order, with both factors in the denominator. Apply the node-size estimate to these conditions and the assumed local windows.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.node_sizes_of_windows: A thick node has positive weight because its lower bound is b > 0. Any other permitted node either is among the listed top places, where its lower bound is bₜ plus the nonnegative offset and bₜ ≥ b′ > 0, or has lower bound w″ > 0. The thick upper bound is already b + η + 1. At a non-thick top place, the upper bound is at most b′ + κb′ + b′/x + η ≤ 2b′. At any other non-thick place, the upper bound is w″ + η ≤ b′/x + η ≤ b′, which also gives the required bound.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.odd_iff_cop: The exponent e + 2 is positive, so coprimality with 2 to that power is equivalent to coprimality with 2. A natural number is coprime to 2 exactly when it is odd.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.omV_mul: When the character is trivial on the quotient factor, the function is constantly one. Otherwise an even factor causes both the product value and the corresponding factor value to vanish. When both factors are odd, the quotient class of their product is the sum of the classes, and evaluation by the additive character turns that sum into multiplication.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.omV_one: When the character is trivial on the quotient factor, the value is one by definition. Otherwise the input 1 is odd, and its quotient class is zero. The additive character takes zero to one.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.sg_ne: Project the proposed equality to the second coordinate of the first factor. It would identify zero with one in the two-element group, which is impossible.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.window_sizes_explicit: The ratio b′/x is positive and at most b′/3. Either that ratio or its floor is nonnegative and bounded above by the ratio. The group has at least one element, so dividing the ratio by the group order gives a positive thin width no larger than b′/x. The three contributions to the remaining constraint are bounded by b′/4, b′/3 and b′/4. Their sum is at most b′.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.b_power_grouped_holds: The grouped power-window statement packages all the individual hypotheses in one conjunction. Unpack the conjunction to use the statement with separate hypotheses. In the other direction, combine the separate hypotheses into the conjunction and apply the grouped statement.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.b_ramified_grouped_holds: The grouped ramified hypotheses are the conjunction of the separate ramified hypotheses. To apply the ungrouped result, extract each conjunct and supply it as the corresponding hypothesis. To apply the grouped result, assemble the separate hypotheses into the conjunction. Both statements give the same conclusion.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.c_grouped_form_holds: With the lattice and slope data fixed, the grouped form collects the same conditions as the separate-hypothesis form. Each implication follows by either taking the components of the conjunction or combining the separate assumptions into it.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.d_grouped_form_holds: The grouped local-lattice and slope conditions contain exactly the hypotheses in the separate form. Decompose the conjunction to obtain the separate hypotheses in one direction, and combine them to obtain the grouped hypothesis in the other.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.distinct_lines_gram_hs_le_one: Every Gram entry is zero or one, so the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm counts parameter pairs whose points coincide. Distinct lines meet in at most one point, and the parametrizations are injective. There is at most one such pair.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.distinct_lines_meet_at_most_once: Distinct vertical lines have different fixed first coordinates and cannot meet. For a vertical line and a nonvertical line, the fixed first coordinate determines the horizontal parameter, and the other coordinate then determines the vertical parameter. For two nonvertical lines, any intersection has a common first coordinate. If their slopes agree, their intercepts differ and they cannot meet. Otherwise subtract the two intersection equations to get the product of the nonzero slope difference and the parameter difference equal to zero. The parameter difference must vanish in the field.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.flatness_iff_holds: The flat statement presents the geometric and numerical hypotheses individually. Form the geometric and numerical conjunctions from the corresponding parts of the flat list to use the grouped theorem. Conversely, read off the individual assumptions from those two conjunctions and restore them to the flat list. The remaining conditions are supplied directly in both directions.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.hs_sq_one: The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm sums the squared moduli of all entries. Only the diagonal entries contribute, each with value one. Their number is the cardinality of the index set.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.inclusion_matrix_isometry: Each column is a different coordinate vector of the enlarged space. Their inner products are one for equal columns and zero otherwise, so their Gram matrix is the identity.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_map_ne_zero: Apply the line map to the coordinate basis vector at parameter zero. The coefficient of the image at the point with that parameter is one, so this image is nonzero and the map cannot vanish.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_matrix_gram: Each column is the coordinate vector at its corresponding point. The Gram entry is the inner product of two coordinate vectors, which is one when the points coincide and zero otherwise.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_matrix_gram_self: For two columns of one line, their points coincide exactly when their parameters coincide. The Gram formula therefore gives ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_model_input_sizes: All weights are one and each line has p coordinates. The off-diagonal bound permits squared norm p² divided by p², which is one, and the distinct-line estimate gives it. The diagonal Gram matrices are identities, so their deviations vanish. The ambient point set has p² elements and the added coordinate set is empty, giving the required dimension.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_point_injective: For a nonvertical line the first coordinate is the parameter. For a vertical line the second coordinate is the parameter. Thus equal points on the same line always have equal parameters.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.line_rank_sum_eq: There are p + 1 direction choices, including the vertical direction, and p intercepts for each. Each line has coordinate space of dimension p. Summing the ranks over all lines gives p²(p + 1).
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.local_length_self_eq_zero: The quotient of the lattice by its own restriction to itself is the zero module. Localizing preserves the zero module, whose module length is zero.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.power_hyp_to_ramified: Use x raised to −c for the ramification scale. It is positive because x is positive. Since it is the reciprocal of x to the power c, dividing by it amounts to multiplying by x to the power c. These substitutions transform the two scale inequalities into the required ramified inequalities. The other conditions are carried over directly.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.projective_lines_all_cases: Take the shifts, mean and spread from the power-window construction. Choose the height to be one plus the absolute difference between the mean and the ambient minimal slope, and choose the upper spread equal to the spread itself. These choices satisfy the construction's hypotheses. The small height is the large height divided by p + 1, so it is strictly smaller. Each line map is nonzero by the coordinate-vector argument.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.projective_lines_geometry: All metric and change-of-basis matrices are identities, so their determinants are units. The standard lattices are finitely generated and span their vector spaces, and the total line rank is positive. Each coordinate generator on a line maps to the coordinate generator at its plane point, so the maps preserve the lattices. The height function is the map height itself. With zero deletion and no added coordinates, the dimension inequality holds with equality. Finally, the incidence entries are zero or one and are fixed by every embedding, so the matrix identity follows entry by entry.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.projective_lines_model: Apply the construction at the prime p = 19. The ambient dimension p² becomes 361 and the scale p + 1 becomes 20. The same witnesses have the required strict height bound and nonzero maps.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.projective_lines_model₂: Work at p = 19 and let k be the logarithm of the number of lines. Let t be the absolute gap between the chosen mean and the ambient minimal slope. Choose the large height t + 1 + 20k and the small height equal to one-twentieth of it, so the latter dominates k. Take the unit size parameters equal to one, take the parameter a equal to twenty times the small height, and take the loss equal to the nonnegative spread. The resulting spread bound is at least the spread. Apply the power-window construction, then convert it to the ramified form with reciprocal scale 1/20. The chosen parameters satisfy the remaining equalities and inequalities.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.projective_lines_power_hypothesis: Use the map heights for the shifts and take s to be the rank-weighted mean of the shifted lattice means. The total rank is positive, so this normalizes the weighted sum correctly. Take u as the sum of the absolute differences between each shifted maximal slope and s. It is nonnegative and bounds every individual difference. The assumptions on the height and U supply the other numerical bounds. The geometric and Gram estimates furnish the matrix conditions. With x = p + 1 and exponent one, the reciprocal scale is at most 1/20 since p ≥ 19, the total rank is p²x, and the choice of small height equal to the large height divided by x saturates the height bound. The zero error parameters satisfy the remaining bounds.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.standard_lattice_fg: The standard lattice is the integral span of the coordinate basis. The coordinate index set is finite, so that basis is a finite generating set for the lattice.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.standard_lattice_ne_bot: Choose a coordinate index using nonemptiness. Its basis vector is nonzero and lies in the standard lattice. The lattice therefore contains an element other than zero.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.standard_lattice_span_eq_top: Each coordinate basis vector belongs to the integral lattice. Their span over the number field is the entire vector space. The field-linear span of the larger set of lattice points is therefore the entire space as well.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.landau_zero_free_half_plane: Apply the zeta Landau theorem in its case below the line of real part one. The assumed eventual bound gives its growth hypothesis with constant one, and the real-part condition places the given point in the resulting zero-free region.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.riemann_hypothesis_of_power_bound: It suffices to establish nonvanishing on the open half-plane to the right of one half. Apply the epsilon form of the zeta Landau theorem at one half. For any positive requested exponent allowance, choose the smaller of half the available parameter range and the allowance divided by one plus the absolute value of the growth coefficient. This choice is positive, lies below the available range, and makes the extra growth exponent at most the requested allowance. The assumed power bound therefore gives the required eventual estimate, after increasing the starting point to at least one so that increasing the exponent increases the power. The Landau theorem gives nonvanishing, and the zero-free half-plane criterion gives the Riemann hypothesis.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.example: Use two indices, with weights 1 and 2 and shifts 1 and 0, respectively. Set both maximal slopes and the old mean slope to zero, and set the new mean slope to −1. Set the common gain and all drops to zero and the remaining loss to one. The two slope inequalities then hold as equalities. Both bounds for the old slopes can be set to zero, and the shift oscillation is exactly one. The shifts differ at the two indices.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_mean_claimU: The equality for the mean slopes implies the lower inequality required by the preceding bound. The two versions have the same upper inequality for the maximal slopes and the same positivity hypotheses, so that bound applies.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.weighted_mean_lemma_ge: The pointwise lower bound on the new mean slopes gives, after subtracting the shifts and taking the positive weighted mean, a lower bound by the old shifted mean plus the common gain minus the weighted mean of the combined losses. For the maximum slopes, each new shifted value is at most the corresponding old shifted value plus the common gain because the drop is nonnegative. Taking maxima gives the same upper bound with the old maximum. Subtract the lower bound on the mean from the upper bound on the maximum. The common gain cancels, leaving the old spread plus the weighted mean of the combined losses.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.wmean_add': Distribute the weight across each addition in the numerator and split the finite sum. Dividing both terms by the same total weight gives the sum of their means.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.wmean_const': Factor the common value out of the numerator. The remaining factor is the sum of the weights, which is positive and cancels the denominator.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.wmean_mono': Multiplying the pointwise inequality by each positive weight preserves it, and summing gives the numerator inequality. The sum of the weights is positive because the index set is nonempty. Divide by this sum.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.wmean_sub: Distribute the weight across each difference and split the numerator as a difference of finite weighted sums. Division by the common total weight gives the difference of the two means.

Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.claimHigh_valid: The modified local gain is bounded above by the original local gain at each place. Subtract the same threshold and sum with the nonnegative place weights to compare the two weighted excesses. Use the assumed upper bounds on the new and intermediate maximal slopes, then substitute the signed decomposition of the original excess.
Formalism/SizeWindowBrackets/ChainSlopeW.deficit_bounds: Since T > 2, the base 1 − 1/(T − 1) lies strictly between zero and one.
