Split the integral and take out the constant coefficients. The weighted sum has the corrected logarithmic-derivative Mellin formula, and integrating the power gives the reciprocal of the complex variable minus the power exponent. Combining the two terms gives the stated transform.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaLandau.le.riemannZetaOne_ne_zero_of_integrable_mel:
On the half-plane above the chosen exponent, the Mellin transform is analytic by differentiation under the integral. Subtract the elementary power contribution and multiply by the variable, the variable minus one, and regularized zeta. This gives an analytic function on that half-plane. In the smaller half-plane to the right of one, the Mellin formula identifies it with the signed entire numerator used in the continuation. The identity theorem gives this equality throughout the larger half-plane.

Use the sign squared equal to one to rearrange the identity as a differential equation. The derivative of regularized zeta equals regularized zeta times an analytic function on the half-plane. Regularized zeta is entire and has value one at one, so the logarithmic-derivative nonvanishing criterion rules out any zero there.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaLandau.le.rint_HZ: After distributing the Mellin weight, the integrand is the sum of a constant multiple of the corrected weighted sum times that weight and a constant multiple of the power term times the weight. The first is integrable for the real exponent above one. The second is integrable because the real exponent is also above the power exponent. Their sum is integrable.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaLandau.le.zetaLandau: Choose a constant at least as large as the constant in the eventual one-sided bound and the absolute bound on the initial finite interval. Since the exponent is positive, the power of an argument at least one is at least one. Thus subtracting the given signed corrected sum from this power term gives a nonnegative function on the whole integration interval. Its sign coefficient squares to one. The Landau integrability theorem and the differential-equation criterion give nonvanishing of regularized zeta above the chosen exponent. Away from one this implies nonvanishing of ordinary zeta by the regularization identity. At one use the stated zeta nonvanishing on the line of real part one.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaLandau.le.zetaLandauEps: Choose a positive allowance no larger than half either gap, the gap from the given exponent to the point's real part and the gap to one. The shifted exponent is still below both. The given eventual bound at that shifted exponent now meets the one-sided zeta Landau theorem, which gives nonvanishing at the point.

Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.F_differentiableAt: Each summand is holomorphic and the local domination estimate gives a summable majorant throughout an open ball about the point. The series converges uniformly there by the Weierstrass test, so its sum is holomorphic on the ball and differentiable at its center.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.F_eq: For real part greater than one, the series of terms with coefficient 1 − s converges to (1 − s)ζ(s). The sum of the other two powers over the first N indices telescopes to 1 minus (N + 1) raised to 1 − s. The omitted power tends to zero because its exponent has negative real part. Adding the two series gives the identity.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.e_bound: Put x = n + 1, a = 1 − s and L = log((x + 1)/x). Factor x to the power a out of the remainder. The factor in brackets is the negative of the exponential remainder exp(aL) − 1 − aL, plus a times 1/x − L. The logarithm bounds put L between 1/(x + 1) and 1/x, so 0 ≤ 1/x − L ≤ 1/x². Also |aL| ≤ 1 by the hypothesis, so the norm of the exponential remainder is at most |aL|². The bracket is therefore bounded in norm by (|a|² + |a|)/x². The modulus of x to the power a is x to the real part of a, giving the stated estimate.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.e_crude: Apply the triangle inequality to the three defining terms and replace the moduli of the complex powers by real powers at the real parts of their exponents. Because the bases are at least one and the real part of s is positive, the first power is at most one and the other two powers are at most their bases. Adding those three bounds gives the result.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.e_differentiable: Both bases n + 1 and n + 2 are positive. Their powers are exponentials of affine functions of s with constant logarithms of the bases. The three terms are entire, so their sum is differentiable everywhere.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.e_dom: Set δ to half the real part of the center and R to one plus the distance from the center to 1. On the ball of radius min(δ, 1), the real part of w exceeds δ and |1 − w| ≤ R. For n + 1 ≥ R use the sharp remainder bound and dominate it by (R² + R) times the power of n + 1 with exponent −1 − δ. This sequence is summable. For the finitely many indices with n + 1 < R, add the crude bound with R in place of |1 − w|. The combined sequence is summable and works uniformly on the ball.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.e_ofReal: All bases are positive, so real powers agree under the real-to-complex embedding with complex powers at the same real exponents. The embedding also preserves each addition and multiplication in the remainder formula.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.er_le: By concavity, the increase of x raised to 1 − σ over the unit interval is at least its derivative at the right endpoint n + 2. Subtract this lower bound from the derivative at n + 1 to obtain the stated upper bound for the remainder.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.er_nonneg: The function x raised to 1 − σ is concave for positive x when 0 < σ < 1. Its increase from n + 1 to n + 2 is at most its derivative at n + 1 times the unit interval length. Subtracting that increase from the derivative at n + 1 gives the remainder, which is therefore nonnegative.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.norm_cpow_nat: The base n + k is positive, so its complex logarithm is the real logarithm. The modulus of its exponential with exponent w is the exponential of the real part of w log(n + k), which is the stated real power.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.riemannZetaOne_eq_one_sub_of_re_pos: The regularized zeta function and one minus the remainder series are holomorphic on the open right half-plane. On the subregion with real part above one, both equal (s − 1)ζ(s) by the Dirichlet series calculation and the definition of regularization. They therefore agree on a neighborhood of 2. The right half-plane is convex and connected, so the identity theorem extends the equality to the entire domain.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.summable_e: Apply the local domination estimate at the center of its positive-radius ball. The norms of the terms are bounded by a summable sequence, so the series converges absolutely.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.tsum_er_le: Sum the upper bounds for the first N nonnegative remainders. The differences of successive negative powers telescope to (1 − σ) times one minus the power of N + 1 with exponent −σ, which is at most 1 − σ. Thus the nonnegative partial sums are bounded and their limit satisfies the same inequality.
Formalism/ZetaNonvanishing/ZetaRealNonva.zetaRealNonvanish: At 0 < σ < 1, the remainder series equals its real counterpart and has sum at most 1 − σ. Thus one minus that sum is at least σ and is positive. This is the value of the regularized zeta function. Dividing by the nonzero factor σ − 1 shows that ζ(σ) cannot vanish.

Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re: Fix a character and a zero in the open critical strip. The critical-strip conclusion of the combined nonvanishing theorem applies to all characters and forces real part 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive: Apply the critical-line theorem for primitive characters to the given zero in the open critical strip. It gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Main.lean.LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re: Fix a Dirichlet character and a point strictly to the right of the critical line. The assumption on the character or the point excludes the exceptional pair of the principal character and s = 1, so the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem applies.
Main.lean.riemannHypothesis: Apply the reduction from right half-plane nonvanishing for Dirichlet L-functions to the Riemann Hypothesis. The nonvanishing theorem for every character supplies its hypothesis.
Main.lean.riemannZeta_eq_zero_re: Let s be a zero of the zeta function distinct from 1 and from the negative even integers. The Riemann Hypothesis established above applies to precisely these zeros and gives real part 1/2.

Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.allChi: Apply the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem for every Dirichlet character to the given character and point.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.claimAll: Start with right half-plane nonvanishing for every character. The Dirichlet critical-strip reduction and the zeta-zero reduction give the other two conclusions from this same input. Combine the three claims.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.critAll: Fix a primitive character χ and a zero s with 0 < Re(s) < 1. Apply the primitive-character critical-line criterion with the right half-plane nonvanishing theorem. The criterion gives Re(s) = 1/2.
Supplements/Kernels/MainTheorems.lean.rhOfAll: The reduction to the Riemann Hypothesis requires right half-plane nonvanishing for all characters. Apply it using the preceding nonvanishing theorem.
